**Surah 38 (Sad)**
*It has eighty-eight verses and is Meccan.*

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾ ﴿Yet those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ ﴿How many generations before them have We destroyed, and they cried out when there was no longer any escape.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾ ﴿Yet those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ ﴿How many generations before them have We destroyed, and they cried out when there was no longer any escape.﴾ On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The full discussion of such opening letters is mentioned at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, but it is fine to repeat some of the views.

The first view: It is a key to the names of God Most High, whose first letters are *sad*, as in our saying *Sadiq al-wa'd* (True to His promise), *Sani' al-masnu'at* (Maker of created things), and *Samad* (Eternal, Self-Sufficient).

The second view: Its meaning is "Muhammad spoke the truth in everything he reported from God" (ﷺ).

The third view: Its meaning is "the disbelievers turned away from accepting this religion," as God Most High said: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of God﴾ [al-Nisa' 167].

The fourth view: Its meaning is that the Qur'an is composed of these letters, and you are capable of them but are not capable of producing something to rival the Qur'an. This shows that the Qur'an is inimitable.

The fifth view: The word *sad* is read with a *kasra* on the *dal*, from *al-musadda*, which means opposition. From it comes *al-sada*, which is the echo that answers your voice in empty places free of solid bodies. Its meaning is: "Oppose the Qur'an through your action, so act on its commands and refrain from its prohibitions."

The sixth view: It is the name of the surah, and the implied sense is "This is *Sad*." If it is said that there are two problems here:

One: His saying ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ is an oath, but where is the thing sworn to?

Two: The word *bal* ("rather" / "yet") requires the lifting of a ruling that was established before it, and establishing a ruling after it contradicts the earlier ruling. So where is this meaning here?

The answer to the first problem has several aspects:

The first: The meaning of *sad* may be "Muhammad spoke the truth" (ﷺ). Then *sad* is the thing sworn to, and His saying ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ is the oath.

The second: The thing sworn to may be omitted, and the implied sense is "The surah of ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ is indeed an inimitable speech," because we have shown that His saying ﴿Sad﴾ is an alert to the challenge.

The third: *Sad* may be the name of the surah, and the implied sense is "This is *Sad*. By the Qur'an, full of reminder." Since it is well known that Muhammad (peace be upon him) claims in this surah that it is a miracle, His saying "This is *Sad*" functions in the same way

[Page 153]

as His saying "This is the miraculous surah." A parallel is the saying "This is Hatim, by God," meaning "This is the one famous for generosity."

The answer to the second problem: The ruling mentioned before the word *bal* is either what the commentator mentioned, that Muhammad was truthful in conveying the message, or that the Qur'an or this surah is a miracle. The ruling mentioned after the word *bal* here is the dispute and opposition regarding its being so. Thus the aim is achieved. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** Al-Hasan read *sadi* with a *kasra* on the *dal* because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *sadan* with a *fatha* on the *sad* and *nun*, with the omission of the oath particle and the direct attachment of its verb, like the people's saying *Allahi la-af'alanna* ("By God, I will certainly do it"). Most readers use the *jazm* (sukun) because nouns without governing particles are pronounced in pause form at their ends.

**The third issue:** In His saying ﴿*dhi al-dhikr*﴾ ("full of reminder") there are two meanings:

The first: It means "possessor of honor." God Most High said: ﴿And it is indeed a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44], and He said: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya' 10]. Its metaphorical usage comes from the people's saying "So-and-so has a *dhikr* among people," just as they say "he has *sit*" (a reputation).

The second: It means "possessor of the two explanations," that is, in it are the stories of the earlier and later peoples, and in it is the explanation of the fundamental and derivative sciences. Its metaphorical usage comes from His saying: ﴿We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar 40].

**The fourth issue:** The Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds the created nature of the Qur'an) said: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, and *dhikr* is created. The proof of the first premise is His saying Most High: ﴿And it is indeed a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44]; ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya' 50]; ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad 1]; ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ [Ya-Sin 69]. The proof of the second premise is His saying: ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord﴾ [al-Anbiya' 2], and His saying ﴿No new reminder comes to them from the Most Gracious﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 5].

The answer: We turn your evidence toward the letters and sounds, which are created.

As for His saying ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾, what is meant are the disbelievers among the leaders of Quraysh, among whom consensus on envy and arrogance that prevents submission to the truth is conceivable. Here *'izza* ("arrogance") means self-exaltation, and it refers to the inner states that a person holds about himself which prevent him from following others. This is according to God Most High's saying: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride in sin seizes him﴾ [al-Baqarah 206]. *Shiqaq* ("opposition") is the display of contrariness either on the basis of equality with the opponent or on the basis of claiming superiority over him. It is derived from *shiqq* ("side"), as if he rises above being bound to submit to him, and places himself on one side and his opponent on another. So he wants to remain on his own side and not have his opponent's ruling applied to him. Similar to it is *mu'adah* ("hostility"), where one party is on one bank and the other on the other bank, the *'udwa* being the side of a valley. Likewise *muhadda* ("defiance") means that one is on a limit different from the other's limit. It is said that so-and-so "deviated from so-and-so," and "so-and-so kept away from so-and-so," meaning he came to be on an edge and on a side other than his. And God knows best.

Then, when He described them with arrogance and opposition, He warned them, saying: ﴿How many generations before them have We destroyed﴾. The meaning is that when the punishment descended upon them in this world, they called out, but it does not mention with what they called out. There are several views:

The first, which is the most apparent, is that they called out seeking help, because the cry of one upon whom punishment descends is nothing but a plea for help.

The second: They called out with faith and repentance at the moment of witnessing the punishment.

The third: They called out, that is, they raised their voices. It is said "So-and-so is louder in voice than so-and-so," meaning he raises his voice more. Then He said: ﴿But there was no longer any escape﴾, meaning that this was not the time of fleeing from punishment. This is like His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said, "We believe"﴾ [Ghafir 84], and He said: ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out﴾ [al-Mu'minun 64]. *Ju'ar* is raising the voice in humble supplication and seeking help. It is also like His saying: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before﴾ [Yunus 91], and His saying: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir 85].

Several discussions remain here:

**The first discussion:** On the precise analysis of the word ﴿*wa-la-ta*﴾ ("but there was no"). Al-Khalil and Sibawayh claimed that *la-ta* is *la* (no), which is similar to *laysa* (is not), with a feminine *ta* added to it, just as it was added to *rubba* and *thamma* for emphasis. Because of this addition, it acquired new rulings. Among them: it only occurs before time expressions; and only one of its two components may appear, either the subject or the predicate, while both appearing together is impossible. Al-Akhfash said: it is *la* of generic negation with the *ta* added to it, and it is restricted to negating time expressions. ﴿*hina manas*﴾ ("a time of escape") is in the accusative governed by it, as if you said: "There is no time of escape for them," and it can be in the nominative by the inchoative, meaning "and there is no time of escape belonging to them."

**The second discussion:** Most readers pause on the *ta* in ﴿*wa-la-ta*﴾, but al-Kisa'i pauses on it with a *ha*, as one does with feminine nouns. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: As for the view of Abu 'Ubayda that the *ta* is attached to *hin* ("time"), there is no basis for it. His argument that the *ta* is joined to *hin* in the Mushaf of 'Uthman is weak, because many things in the Mushaf are outside the rules of orthography.

**The third discussion:** *Manas* means escape and rescue. It is said *nasahu yanusuhu* when one helps him, and *istanasa* means he sought escape. And God knows best.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: As for the view of Abu 'Ubayda that the *ta* is attached to *hin* ("time"), there is no basis for it. The first: they said, "Muhammad is equal to us in outward form, inward character, lineage, appearance and figure. How is it conceivable that he alone among us should be singled out for this lofty station and exalted rank?"

A man came to them calling them to monotheism, to the glorification of the angels, to desire for the Hereafter and aversion from this world. Moreover, this man is one of their own kin, and they know that he was far from lying and accusation. All of this necessitates acknowledging the truth of his message. Then He said: "And they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them." Its meaning is that Muhammad was of their clan and tribe, and was equal to them in worldly means. So they disdained to submit to his authority and to comply with his obligations, and they wondered that he alone among them should be singled out for the message of God and be distinguished from them by this noble attribute. In sum, the cause of this wonder was nothing but envy.

Then the Exalted said: "And the disbelievers say, 'This is a sorcerer, a great liar.'" He did not say "and they said" but rather "and the disbelievers said," to express wonder and to indicate that this statement can only issue from complete disbelief. For the sorcerer is one who prevents obedience to God and calls to obedience to Satan, whereas he, in your view, is the reverse of that. The liar is one who reports about a thing other than as it is, whereas he reports the existence of the eternal, wise, knowing Creator, and the resurrection and gathering, and all other matters whose soundness is established by rational proofs. How then could he be a liar? Then He related all that they relied upon to establish his being a liar, and these are three things:

One: what relates to divinity (al-ilahiyyat).

Second: what relates to prophethood (al-nubuwwat).

Third: what relates to the return (al-ma'ad).

As for the doubt relating to divinity, it is their saying: "Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing." It is narrated that when 'Umar embraced Islam, the Muslims rejoiced greatly, and this grieved the Quraysh. Twenty-five of their chiefs gathered and went to Abu Talib and said: "You are our shaykh and our elder, and you know what these fools have done"—meaning the Muslims—"so we have come to you that you may judge between us and your nephew." Abu Talib summoned the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "O son of my brother, these are your people; they ask you a request, so do not incline entirely away from your people." He ﷺ said: "What do they ask of me?" They said: "Leave us and leave the mention of our gods, and we will leave you and your God." He ﷺ said: "Tell me, if I give you what you ask, will you give me one word by which you will rule the Arabs and the non-Arabs will submit to you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Say: There is no god but God." Then they stood up and said: "Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing," meaning, extremely wondrous.

I say: the source of the wonder is of two aspects:

The first: these people were not men of reflection and inference; rather their imaginations followed what is sensed. When they found in the observable world that a single agent's power and knowledge is not sufficient to preserve this great creation, they analogized the unseen to the seen and said: there must be in preserving this vast world many gods, each one of whom undertakes the preservation of a different kind.

The second aspect: their forefathers, by their multitude and the strength of their minds, were unanimous in polytheism, so they said, with extreme wonder, that it is astonishing that those peoples, despite their multitude and the strength of their minds, were ignorant and in error, while this single man should be right and truthful. And I say, by my life, if we were to grant the application of the judgment of the observable to the unseen without proof or argument, the first doubt would be necessary. And since we agree on its corruption, we know with certainty that applying the judgment of the observable to the unseen is corrupt. When this principle is void, the foundation of the speech of the anthropomorphists (al-mushabbiha) regarding the essence is void, and the speech of the anthropomorphists regarding the acts is void. As for the anthropomorphists regarding the essence, they say: since everything existent in the observable must be a body and occupy a place, it must be so in the unseen. As for the anthropomorphists regarding the acts, they are the Mu'tazilites who say: such-and-such an act is ugly from us, therefore it must be ugly from God. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that if the speech of these anthropomorphists regarding the essence and the acts is sound, it necessarily follows that the doubt of these polytheists is certainly sound. And since we agree on its corruption, we know that the foundation of the corporealists (al-mujassima) and the speech of the Mu'tazilites is false and corrupt.

As for the second doubt, by my life, if imitation (al-taqlid) were true, this doubt would be necessary; and since it is corrupt, we know that imitation is false.

Twenty-five of their chiefs gathered and went to Abu Talib and said: "You are our shaykh and our elder, and you know what these fools have done"—meaning the Muslims—"so we have come to you that you may judge between us and your nephew." Abu Talib summoned the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "O son of my brother, these are your people; they ask you a request, so do not incline entirely away from your people." He ﷺ said: "What do they ask of me?" They said: "Leave us and leave the mention of our gods, and we will leave you and your God." He ﷺ said: "Tell me, if I give you what you ask, will you give me one word by which you will rule the Arabs and the non-Arabs will submit to you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Say: There is no god but God." Then they stood up and said: "Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing," meaning, extremely wondrous.

I say: the source of the wonder is of two aspects:

The first: these people were not men of reflection and inference; rather their imaginations followed what is sensed. When they found in the observable world that a single agent's power and knowledge is not sufficient to preserve this great creation, they analogized the unseen to the seen and said: there must be in preserving this vast world many gods, each one of whom undertakes the preservation of a different kind.

The second aspect: their forefathers, by their multitude and the strength of their minds, were unanimous in polytheism, so they said, with extreme wonder, that it is astonishing that those peoples, despite their multitude and the strength of their minds, were ignorant and in error, while this single man should be right and truthful. And I say, by my life, if we were to grant the application of the judgment of the observable to the unseen without proof or argument, the first doubt would be necessary. And since we agree on its corruption, we know with certainty that applying the judgment of the observable to the unseen is corrupt. When this principle is void, the foundation of the speech of the anthropomorphists (al-mushabbiha) regarding the essence is void, and the speech of the anthropomorphists regarding the acts is void. As for the anthropomorphists regarding the essence, they say: since everything existent in the observable must be a body and occupy a place, it must be so in the unseen. As for the anthropomorphists regarding the acts, they are the Mu'tazilites who say: such-and-such an act is ugly from us, therefore it must be ugly from God. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that if the speech of these anthropomorphists regarding the essence and the acts is sound, it necessarily follows that the doubt of these polytheists is certainly sound. And since we agree on its corruption, we know that the foundation of the corporealists (al-mujassima) and the speech of the Mu'tazilites is false and corrupt.

As for the second doubt, by my life, if imitation (al-taqlid) were true, this doubt would be necessary; and since it is corrupt, we know that imitation is false.

Remaining here are some discussions:

First discussion: "'Ujab" means "'ajib" (wondrous), but it is more intensive than "'ajib," like their saying "tawil" and "tuwal," "'arid" and "'urad," "kabir" and "kubar." It may be doubled for intensity, as in His saying: "And they schemed a great scheme (makran kubbaran)" (Nuh: 22).

Second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "'Ujab" has been read with light and with heavy pronunciation, and he said: the heavy form is more intensive than the light, as in His saying: "makran kubbaran."

Then the Exalted said: "And the chiefs went forth, [saying], 'Walk on, and be steadfast for your gods.'" We have mentioned that "al-mala'" refers to the people who, when present in an assembly, the hearts and eyes are filled with awe of them and their greatness. His words "from among them" mean from Quraysh. They departed from the assembly of Abu Talib after the Messenger of God ﷺ had silenced them with a ready reply, saying to one another: "Walk on, and be steadfast for your gods." Concerning this there are discussions:

First discussion: the well-known reading is "an-imshu" (that walk on). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "imshu" with "an" omitted. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "an" here means "ay" (that is), because those departing from the assembly of speech must speak and discuss what took place in the previous assembly; so their departing was implicitly containing the meaning of saying. And from Ibn 'Abbas: "And the chiefs went forth among them, walking."

Second discussion: the meaning of "an-imshu" is that some of them said to others: walk on and be steadfast; there is no stratagem for you to repel the affair of Muhammad. "Indeed, this is a thing that is intended." Regarding this there are three aspects:

One: the rise of the religion of Muhammad ﷺ has no apparent cause that establishes that its increasing manifestation is due to nothing but God willing it, and what God wills to exist, there is none to repel it.

Second: the matter is like one of the calamities of time, and there is no escape for us from it.

Third: your religion is a thing that is sought, that is, desired to be taken from you. Al-Qaffal said: this is a phrase used for threat and intimidation, and its meaning seems to be that Muhammad's purpose in this speech is not the establishment of religion, but rather his aim is to seize power over us, so that he may rule over our wealth and children as he wishes.

* * *

Then He said: "We have not heard of this in the latter religion." The latter religion is the religion of the Christians, so they said: this monotheism which Muhammad ﷺ brought, we have not heard of it in the religion of the Christians. Or the intended meaning of "the latter religion" is the religion of Quraysh which they inherited from their fathers. Then they said: "This is nothing but fabrication," that is, invention and lying. The essence of the speech from this aspect is that they said: we have not heard from our forefathers the saying of monotheism, so it must be false. And if the saying of imitation were true, the speech of these polytheists would be true; and since it is false, we know that the saying of imitation is false.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 8–10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ ﴿Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Almighty, the Bestower?﴾ ﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them ascend by the means.﴾ ﴿A host of the factions there, routed.﴾

Know that this is the third doubt of those disbelievers, and it is the doubt concerning prophethood. It is their saying that Muhammad, since he was equal to others in essence, attributes, outward form and inward character, how is it conceivable that he should be singled out for this lofty rank and noble station? This is what is meant by their saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾, for it is a question in the manner of denial. God Exalted related of the people of Salih that they said the like of this saying, so they said:

صفحة ١٥٧
﴿Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us? Rather, he is a liar, an insolent one.﴾ [al-Qamar: 25]. God Exalted also related of the people of Muhammad ﷺ that they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. The complete statement in establishing this doubt is: they said, prophethood is the most exalted of ranks, so it must not be attained except by the most noble of people, and Muhammad is not the most noble of people, therefore prophethood must not be attained by him. The first two premises are true, but the third is false. The reason this error gained currency among them is that they supposed nobility is attained only through wealth and helpers, and that is false. For the levels of happiness are three: the highest are the psychic (nafsaniyya), the middle are the bodily (badaniyya), and the lowest are the external (kharijiyya), namely wealth and standing. Thus the people reversed the matter, and they supposed the lowest of the ranks to be the most noble. So when they found wealth and standing greater with others, they supposed that others were nobler than him, and then this corrupt syllogism took hold in their minds.

Then God Exalted answered this doubt in several ways:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ In this there are two aspects:

One of them: His saying ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾, that is, about the proofs which, if they reflected upon them, this doubt would be removed from them. This is because all the doubts they have raised are weak words, whereas the proofs that indicate by themselves the soundness of his prophethood are decisive proofs. Had they contemplated the speech with due contemplation, they would have come to know the weakness of the doubts with which they clung to deny prophethood, and they would have recognized the soundness of the proofs indicating the soundness of his prophethood. Since they did not know this, it was because they abandoned reflection and inference. As for His saying ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, its place in this discourse is that He, exalted is He, says: these people only abandoned reflection and inference because I have not made them taste My punishment; had they tasted it, nothing would have proceeded from them except turning toward performing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden.

The second: that what is meant by His saying ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾ is that the Prophet ﷺ used to warn them of the punishment of God should they persist in disbelief; then they persisted in disbelief, and the punishment did not descend upon them, and that became a cause of their doubt regarding his truthfulness, and they said: ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. So He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾, its meaning being what we have mentioned, and His saying ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ means that this doubt arose only because of the non-descent of the punishment.

The second of the aspects which God Exalted mentioned in answering that doubt is His saying: ﴿Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Almighty, the Bestower?﴾ The explanation of this answer is that the station of prophethood is a great station and a lofty rank, and the one able to bestow it must be Almighty, i.e., of complete power, and Bestower, i.e., of great generosity; and that is God, glorified and exalted. Since He, exalted is He, is of complete power and complete generosity, His being the bestower of this blessing does not depend upon whether the one from whom it is bestowed is rich or poor, nor does that differ because His enemies love Him or hate Him.

The third aspect in the answer to this doubt is His saying: ﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them ascend by the means.﴾ Know that the meaning of this statement must be different from the meaning of His saying ﴿Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord﴾. The difference is that the treasuries of God, exalted is He, are not finite, as He said: ﴿And there is nothing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾ [al-Hijr: 21], and among those treasuries are these heavens and earth. So when He mentioned the treasuries first in their generality, He followed it with the mention of ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, meaning that these things are one kind of the treasuries of God. So if you are incapable of this category, then being incapable of all the treasuries of God is more fitting. This is what I was able to mention regarding the difference between the two statements.

As for His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾, the meaning is that if they claim that they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth, then at this point it is said to them: ascend by the means and climb the ladders by which one reaches the Throne, so that they may ascend upon it, manage the affairs of the world and the dominion of God, and send down revelation upon whomever they choose. Know that the philosophers of Islam have used His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾ as evidence that the celestial bodies and the powers and properties God placed in them are causes for the events of the lower world, because God, exalted is He, named the celestial things "means" (asbab), and that indicates what we have said. And God knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A host of the factions there, routed﴾, in it there are two sections of discussion:

One of them: concerning the explanation of these words.

The second: concerning how it is connected to what precedes it.

As for the first section: His saying ﴿jund﴾ (host) is the subject, and ﴿ma﴾ is for indefiniteness, like His saying "I came for a certain matter (li-amrin ma)" and "I have some food (ta'amun ma)". ﴿Min al-ahzab﴾ (of the factions) is an attribute of ﴿jund﴾, and ﴿mahzum﴾ (routed) is the predicate of the subject. As for His saying ﴿hunalika﴾ (there), it is permissible that it be an attribute of ﴿jund﴾, meaning a host established there, and it is permissible that it be connected to ﴿mahzum﴾, meaning that the host of the factions is routed there, that is, in that place where they used to utter these words that impugn the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

As for the second section: when He, exalted is He, said that if they possess the heavens and the earth, let them ascend by the means, He mentioned after it that they are a host of factions, weak, so how could they be possessors of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Qatada said: "there" refers to the Day of Badr. God informed them in Mecca that the host of the polytheists would be routed, and its fulfilment came on the Day of Badr. It was also said: the Day of the Trench. But the more correct view in my opinion is to take it as referring to the Day of the Conquest of Mecca, because the meaning is that they are a host who will be routed in the place where they uttered these words, and that place is Mecca; so it must be that they will be routed in Mecca, and that is none other than the Day of the Conquest. And God knows best.

* * *

The meaning is that the condition of those factions, despite their complete strength, ended in destruction and perdition, so how much more the condition of these weak and wretched ones.

The first: that it means a punishment that will seize them and come upon them suddenly in one stroke, as one says "time has cried out against them" when they are destroyed. The poet said:

*"Time cried out against the family of Barmak with a cry, and they fell on their chins from its severity."*

The second opinion: this blast is the first blast of the trumpet, as He said in Surah Ya Sin: ﴿They wait for nothing but a single blast that will seize them while they are disputing﴾ [Ya Sin 36:49]. The meaning is that although they have not tasted My punishment in this world, it is prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection. So it is as though that punishment has already come upon them. He made them waiting for it, in the sense of its nearness to them, like the man who awaits a thing: he keeps his gaze fixed upon it, hoping every moment for its arrival. Then He, glorified is He, described this blast, saying: ﴿with no respite from it.﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *fuwaq* with a *damma* on the *fa'*, while the rest read it with a *fatha*. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', Abu ʿUbaydah, and al-Akhfash said: they are two dialects, from *fawaq* of the she-camel, which is the interval between the two milkings of the she-camel. Its root is return, as one says "he recovered (afaqa) from his illness," meaning he returned to health. And God knows best.
