So the time between the two milkings, during which the milk returns to the udder, is called *fawaq* with a *fatha* and with a *damma*, as in your saying *qasas al-sha'r* and *qusas-uhu* (the cutting of the hair).

Al-Wahidi said: *al-fuwaq* and *al-fawaq* are both nouns derived from *al-ifaqah* (recovery), and *al-ifaqah* means return and calm, like the recovery of the sick person. However, *fawaq* with a *fatha* may be used in the place of the verbal noun, while *fuwaq* with a *damma* is the name of that time in which the milk returns to the udder.

Al-Wahidi narrated in *al-Basit* from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said concerning this verse: "Israfil will be commanded, and he will blow the blast of terror." He said: "He will prolong it and extend it." And this is the one of which He says: ﴿with no respite from it.﴾ Then al-Wahidi said: This may bear two meanings:

One of them: there will be no calm in it.

The second: there will be no return from it. The meaning is that the blast will not subside and will not return to calm. It is said of everyone who remains in one state that he does not recover from it and does not regain his senses.

And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 11–15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and ʿAd, and Pharaoh, the lord of the stakes, denied,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket. Those were the factions.﴾ ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My punishment was justified.﴾ ﴿These [people] wait for nothing but a single blast, with no respite from it.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned, in answer to the doubt of the people, that they were only slow and lax in reflection and inference because the punishment had not descended upon them, He explained in this verse that the peoples of all the other prophets were likewise, and then the punishment descended upon them at last. The purpose of this is to frighten those disbelievers who used to deny the Messenger regarding his report of the descent of punishment upon them. So God mentioned six categories of them:

The first is the people of Noah, peace be upon him. When they denied Noah, God destroyed them by drowning and the flood.

The second is the people of Hud. When they denied him, God destroyed them by the wind.

The third is Pharaoh. When he denied Moses, God destroyed him along with his people by drowning.

The fourth is Thamud, the people of Salih. When they denied him, they were destroyed by the Blast (al-Sayhah).

The fifth is the people of Lot. They denied him, and they were destroyed by being swallowed up (al-Khasf).

The sixth is the companions of the Thicket, who were the people of Shuʿayb. They denied him, and they were destroyed by the punishment of the Day of the Canopy. They said: God described Pharaoh as "lord of the stakes" for several reasons.

The first: the original meaning of this word is the stability of a tent fixed by its stakes, and then it was borrowed to express the establishment of power and sovereignty. The poet said:

*"They lived in it in the most pleasant comfort, in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firm."*

The judge (al-Qadi) said: Taking the phrase in this sense is preferable, because he is described as one who denied the messengers, so what he is described by should be a magnification of the matter of his kingdom, so that the warning, with the destruction that came upon him from God, Exalted is He, despite the strength of his affair, would be more eloquent.

The second: he used to set up wooden posts in the air, and he would stretch the limbs of the one being tortured, his hands and feet, to those four pieces of wood, and he would drive a stake into each of these limbs, leaving him suspended in the air until he died.

The third: he would stretch the one being tortured between four stakes in the ground and send scorpions and snakes upon him.

The fourth: Qatadah said: they were stakes, ropes, and playthings with which they amused themselves in his presence.

The fifth: his soldiers were numerous, they had abundant equipment and great provisions, and they used many stakes for their tents, so he became known by them.

The sixth: "lord of the stakes" means lord of the armies and the great multitudes. The armies were called stakes because they uphold his command and strengthen his kingdom, just as a stake strengthens a building.

As for *al-Ayka*, it is the dense, thickly intertwined thicket.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those were the factions.﴾ Regarding this there are several opinions:

The first: those whom we have mentioned from the nations are those who formed factions against their prophets, so We destroyed them. Likewise We shall do to your people. This is because He, exalted is He, made clear by His saying: ﴿A host of the factions, routed, is there﴾ that the people of Muhammad (ﷺ) are a host of the factions, that is, of the same kind as the earlier factions. So when He mentioned that He dealt with the earlier factions by destruction, this was a severe warning to the people of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second: the meaning of His saying ﴿Those were the factions﴾ is an intensification to describe them as strong and numerous, as one says "So-and-so is the man." The meaning is that the condition of those factions, despite their complete strength, ended in destruction and perdition, so how much more the condition of these weak and wretched ones.

Know that if these peoples believe these reports, it is a warning; and if they do not believe them, it is also a warning, because the traces of these events remain, and it gives strong conjecture, so they take heed. And because it is repeated in a manner that also necessitates caution. Then He said: ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My punishment was justified.﴾ That is, all these groups, when they denied their prophets concerning both encouragement and warning, the punishment indeed descended upon them, even though that was after a time. Its purpose is to restrain the listeners. Then God explained that although the destruction of these deniers is delayed, it is as though it has already befallen them, so He said: ﴿These [people] wait for nothing but a single blast, with no respite from it.﴾ Regarding the interpretation of this blast there are two opinions:

The first: that it means a punishment that will seize them and come upon them suddenly in one stroke, as one says "time has cried out against them" when they are destroyed. The poet said:

*"Time cried out against the family of Barmak with a cry, and they fell on their chins from its severity."*

It is likely that the origin of this is a raid, when it overtakes a people and the cry falls upon them. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ [Yunus 10:102], and so on.

The second opinion: this blast is the first blast of the trumpet, as He said in Surah Ya Sin: ﴿They wait for nothing but a single blast that will seize them while they are disputing﴾ [Ya Sin 36:49]. The meaning is that although they have not tasted My punishment in this world, it is prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection. So it is as though that punishment has already come upon them. He made them waiting for it, in the sense of its nearness to them, like the man who awaits a thing: he keeps his gaze fixed upon it, hoping every moment for its arrival. Then He, glorified is He, described this blast, saying: ﴿with no respite from it.﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *fuwaq* with a *damma* on the *fa'*, while the rest read it with a *fatha*. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', Abu ʿUbaydah, and al-Akhfash said: they are two dialects, from *fawaq* of the she-camel, which is the interval between the two milkings of the she-camel. Its root is return, as one says "he recovered (afaqa) from his illness," meaning he returned to health. So the time between the two milkings, during which the milk returns to the udder, is called *fawaq* with a *fatha* and with a *damma*, as in your saying *qasas al-sha'r* and *qusas-uhu* (the cutting of the hair).

Al-Wahidi said: *al-fuwaq* and *al-fawaq* are both nouns derived from *al-ifaqah* (recovery), and *al-ifaqah* means return and calm, like the recovery of the sick person. However, *fawaq* with a *fatha* may be used in the place of the verbal noun, while *fuwaq* with a *damma* is the name of that time in which the milk returns to the udder.

Al-Wahidi narrated in *al-Basit* from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said concerning this verse: "Israfil will be commanded, and he will blow the blast of terror." He said: "He will prolong it and extend it." And this is the one of which He says: ﴿with no respite from it.﴾ Then al-Wahidi said: This may bear two meanings:

One of them: there will be no calm in it.

The second: there will be no return from it. The meaning is that the blast will not subside and will not return to calm. It is said of everyone who remains in one state that he does not recover from it and does not regain his senses.

And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 16–20 (part 1 of 2):

[Qur'an] ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength (dha al-ayd). Indeed, he was constantly turning back (to Allah).﴾

Know that we mentioned in the tafsir of His words, ﴿And they wondered that a warner from among them had come to them, and the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾, that the people were only astonished because of three doubts:

The first concerns divinity, and it is His words, ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾

The second concerns prophethood, and it is His words, ﴿Has the Reminder been revealed to him from among us?﴾

The third concerns the return (al-ma'ad), and it is the words of the Exalted, ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ This is because the people were at the extreme of denial regarding the teaching of resurrection and gathering (al-hashr wa al-nashr). They would argue that the corruption of the doctrine of resurrection proves the corruption of his prophethood. The qitt is a piece of something, because it has been cut off from it, from "qattahu" (he cut it), and the written document of a reward is called qitt. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the promise of Paradise to the believers, they said, mockingly, "Hasten to us our portion of Paradise," or, "Hasten to us the record of our deeds so that we may look into it."

Know that when the disbelievers exceeded all bounds in foolishness against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, "This is a sorcerer, a liar," and said to him by way of mockery, "Hasten to us our qitt," Allah commanded him to be patient with their foolishness, saying, ﴿Be patient over what they say.﴾ If it is asked: what connection is there between His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, and His words, ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾? We say: the explanation of this connection is in several aspects:

The first: it is as if it were said, "If you have witnessed from these ignorant people their audacity against Allah and their denial of gathering and resurrection, then remember the story of Dawud, so that you may know the intensity of his fear of Allah the Exalted and of the Day of Gathering. For as one of two opposites increases in nobility, the other opposite decreases in worth."

The second: it is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Do not let your chest be constrained by their denial of your words and your religion, for if they oppose you, the great prophets have agreed with you."

The third: people hold two views about the story of Dawud. Some say it indicates his sin, and others say it does not indicate it. (As for the one who holds the first view), the aspect of relevance is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Your grief is nothing compared to his, because the disbelievers deny you, whereas Dawud's grief was due to his falling into that sin. There is no doubt that his grief was greater. So reflect on the story of Dawud and the great grief he had, so that what you are suffering of grief may become lighter for you." (As for the one who holds the second view), he said: the two adversaries who entered upon Dawud were humans, and they entered upon him only with the intent to kill him, so Dawud feared them. Yet he did not harm them, nor did he invoke evil upon them, but rather he asked forgiveness for them, as the explanation of this method will come later. Therefore, Allah the Exalted commanded Muhammad (peace be upon him) to follow him in good character.

The fifth: the Quraysh only denied Muhammad (peace be upon him) and treated him lightly because, for the most part, they said that he was an orphan and poor. Then the Exalted related to Muhammad the perfection of the kingdom of Dawud, then He explained that, despite that, he was not spared from sorrows and griefs, so that it would be known that there is no way to be free of grief in this world.

The sixth: His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud﴾, are not restricted to Dawud alone. Rather, after the story of Dawud, He mentioned the stories of the rest of the prophets. It is as if He said, "Be patient over what they say, and take a lesson from the condition of the rest of the prophets," so that He would teach him that each of them was occupied with a particular concern and a particular grief. Then he would know that the world does not cease from worries and sorrows, and that attaining high ranks with Allah is achieved only by bearing hardships and toils in this world. These are aspects that we have mentioned in this context. Here there is another aspect, stronger and better than all that preceded it, which will be mentioned, Allah willing, when we reach the tafsir of His words, ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses﴾ [Sad: 29]. Know that after that, He mentioned the condition of nine prophets: He mentioned the condition of three of them in detail and the condition of six others in summary.

So the first story is the story of Dawud. Know that the essential contents of what Allah the Exalted mentioned in this story are three kinds of speech.

The first: the detailing of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud, which bring about happiness in the Hereafter and in this world.

The second: the explanation of that event which befell him concerning the matter of the two adversaries.

The third: Allah the Exalted's appointing him as successor (istikhlaf) after the occurrence of that event.

As for the first kind, namely the explanation of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud that bring about complete happiness, they are ten.

The first: His words to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud.﴾ So He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), despite his high station, to follow Dawud in patience in obeying Allah. This is a great honor and a noble tribute to Dawud, in that Allah commanded the best of creation, Muhammad (ﷺ), to follow him in noble morals.

The second: that He said concerning him, ﴿Our servant Dawud﴾. He described him as His servant and spoke of Himself in the plural form, which indicates the utmost glorification. This is the highest honor. Do you not see that when the Glorified and Exalted One wished to honor Muhammad (peace be upon him) on the night of the Ascension, He said, ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Here, then, this indicates that same honor for Dawud, and that was a sign of the elevation of his rank also. For the Exalted's describing the prophets by their servitude indicates that they had realized the meaning of servitude through striving in obedience.

The third: His words, ﴿dha al-ayd﴾, meaning possessing strength to perform obedience and to guard against disobedience. This is because when the Exalted praised him with strength, that strength must necessarily be something that merits praise, and the strength which merits great praise is nothing but strength to do what is commanded and to abstain from what is forbidden. The word ﴿al-ayd﴾ mentioned here is like the strength mentioned in His words, ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12], and His words, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailing of everything, so take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], meaning: with diligence in performing the trust and firmness in carrying out the call, and not displaying weakness or frailty. "Al-ayd" and "al-quwwa" (strength) are the same. From it is His words, ﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and His words, ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqara: 87], and He said, ﴿And the heaven We built with ayd﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47]. From Qatada: he was given strength in worship and understanding of the religion, and he used to stand in prayer at night and fast every other day.

The fourth: His words, ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back﴾, meaning that Dawud used to return in all his affairs to My obedience. "Awwab" is an intensive form (fa''al) from "aba," meaning to return, as the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 25]. And the form fa''al is the pattern of intensification, as one says qattal and darrab, for it is more emphatic than qatil and darib.

The fifth: His words, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾. A similar verse is His words, ﴿O mountains, repeat the praise with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. Concerning this there are several discussions.

The first discussion: in it there are several views.

The first: Allah the Glorified created in the body of the mountain life, intellect, power, and speech, and then the mountain became one that glorifies Allah the Exalted. A parallel is His words, ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], for its meaning is that He the Exalted created in the mountain intellect and understanding, then He created in it the vision of Allah the Exalted. So it is likewise here.

The second: regarding interpretation, what al-Qaffal narrated in his tafsir: it is permissible to say that Dawud (peace be upon him) was given such intensity and beauty of voice that the mountains would echo with a beautiful resonance, and the birds would listen to it because of its beauty. So the echo of the mountains and the chirping of the birds with him, and their listening to him, would be glorification. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also mentioned that Allah the Exalted did not give any of His creatures a voice like the voice of Dawud, to the extent that when he recited the Psalms (al-Zabur), the wild animals would approach him until he could take them by their necks.

The third: Allah the Glorified subjected the mountains so that they would move wherever Dawud wished, and that movement was made into glorification, because it indicated the perfection of the power and wisdom of Allah the Exalted.

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said, "﴿yusabbihna﴾ is in the sense of musabbihat (glorifying)." If they say, "Is there any difference between yusabbihna and musabbihat?" We say: yes. The verbal form indicates occurrence and renewal, while the nominal form indicates permanence, as explained by Abd al-Qahir al-Nahwi (the grammarian) in the book Dala'il al-I'jaz. If this is established, we say: His words, ﴿yusabbihna﴾, indicate that the glorification by the mountains occurs gradually, one thing after another and state after state, and the hearer who was present at those mountains would hear them glorifying.

The third discussion: al-Zajjaj said: it is said "sharaqat al-shams" when the sun rises, and "ashraqat" when it shines; and it was said the two have the same meaning, though the first is more common. The Arabs say, "sharaqat al-shams wa al-ma'u yushriq" (the sun rose and the water shines).

The fourth discussion: they have argued for the legality of the Duha prayer (salat al-duha) from this verse. From Umm Hani, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon us, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the Duha prayer, and said, 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq (shining).'" And from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Do you find mention of the Duha prayer in the Qur'an?" They said, "No." So he recited, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾, and said, "Dawud used to pray it." And he said, "There was always something in my mind about the Duha prayer until I found it in His words, ﴿glorify at evening and at sunrise﴾."

* * *

The sixth quality of Dawud (peace be upon him) is the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the birds gathered, each one returning to him.﴾ Concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: His words, ﴿and the birds﴾, are conjoined to the mountains, and the implied meaning is "And We subjected the birds, gathered." Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: when Dawud glorified, the mountains responded to him, and the birds gathered to him and glorified with him. Their gathering to him is their "hashr" (gathering), so according to this interpretation, the one who gathers them is Allah. (If it is asked): how can the glorification of Allah come from the birds, given that they have no intellect? We say: it is not far-fetched to say that Allah the Exalted would create intellect for them so that they would know Allah and then glorify Him. All of that was a miracle for Dawud (peace be upon him).

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: His words, ﴿mahshura (gathered)﴾, correspond to ﴿yusabbihna﴾, except that gathering does not carry the same implication as glorifying, namely indicating occurrence one thing after another. Therefore it was brought as a noun, not a verb. For He said: if it had been said, "And We subjected the birds gathered, glorifying," on the supposition that the gathering was accomplished by the One who gathers them all at once, that indicates the stated measure. And Allah knows best.

The third discussion: it has been read as "wa al-tayru mahshurah" with the nominative case (raf').

The seventh quality of Dawud (peace be upon him): His words, ﴿Each one returning to him.﴾ Its meaning: each of the mountains and the birds is "awwab," that is, returning, meaning whenever Dawud returned to glorification, they responded to him. So these things also used to return to their glorifications. The difference between this quality and the one before it is that in what preceded, we learned that the mountains and the birds glorified along with Dawud's glorification, and by this wording we understood the continuation of that agreement. It has also been said that the pronoun in His words, ﴿Each one returning to him﴾, refers to Allah the Exalted, meaning: each of Dawud, the mountains, and the birds is returning to Allah, that is, glorifying Him and returning to glorification.

[Page 161, 162, 163 markers as in source]

Ninth attribute... Let me translate carefully.

The eighth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾, that is, We made it strong. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. It was also said that "shaddadna" is for intensification. As for the causes that bring about this strengthening, they are many, and they are either worldly causes or religious causes. As for the first, they mention two aspects regarding it:

The first: al-Wahidi narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that every night there would guard him thirty-six thousand men, and when he woke in the morning it was said: "Return, for the Prophet of Allah is pleased with you." Others added and mentioned forty thousand. They said: He was the mightiest of the kings of the earth in authority.

And from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that a man brought a claim before Dawud against another man, saying that he had taken a cow from him. The accused denied it. Dawud said to the claimant: "Bring the evidence," but he did not bring it. Then Dawud saw in his dream that Allah was commanding him to kill the accused. Dawud held firm and said: "It is merely a dream." Then after that the revelation came to him that he must kill him. So he summoned him and informed him that Allah had commanded him to kill him. The accused said: "Allah has spoken the truth. Indeed, I had killed this man's father by treachery." So Dawud killed him. This incident strengthened his kingdom.

As for the religious causes that bring about this strengthening, they are patience, complete reflection, and perfect caution.

The ninth attribute: His saying: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾. Know that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. Know that virtues are of three kinds: soul-related (nafsaniyyah), bodily (badaniyyah), and external (kharijiyyah). Soul-related virtues are confined to two types: knowledge ('ilm) and action ('amal). As for knowledge, it is that the soul becomes, through true conceptions and soul-related assents, in accordance with human capacity. As for action, it is that a person performs the action that is most suitable and most correct for the interests of this world and the Hereafter. This is what wisdom (hikmah) is. It was named "wisdom" because the derivation of sound wisdom does not accept abrogation (naskh) or annulment (naqd), so it is at the utmost level of firmness (ihkam). As for the actions that conform to the interests of this world and the Hereafter, they are binding to observe and do not accept annulment or abrogation. For this reason we named those cognitions and these actions "wisdom."

The tenth attribute: His saying: ﴿And decisive speech (fasl al-khitab)﴾. Know that the bodies of this world are of three kinds:

The first: those that are devoid of perception and awareness, namely inanimate objects (jamadat) and plants (nabatat).

The second: those that have perception and awareness but are not able to make others know the states they have come to know, for the most part. This kind is the entirety of animals other than man.

The third: that which has perception and awareness and has the ability to make others know the states known to it, and that is man. His ability to make others know the states known to him is by speech and address. Then people differ in degrees of ability to express what is in the heart. Among them is one for whom it is difficult to produce ordered, coherent speech, but rather his speech is jumbled and disordered. Among them is one for whom ordering is difficult in some respects. Among them is one who is able to master meaning and express it to the utmost degree. Whoever has this ability in its most complete form, the effects emanating from the rational soul (al-nafs al-nutqiyyah) in him are most complete, and whoever has that ability to a lesser degree, those effects are weaker. When Allah, exalted is He, described the perfection of the essence of the rational soul that belonged to Dawud by His saying: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾, He followed it with an explanation of the perfection of his state in speech, utterance and expression, saying: ﴿and decisive speech﴾. This ordering is of the utmost grandeur. Among the exegetes is one who explained it as meaning that Dawud was the first to say in his speech "Amma ba'd." I say: Truly, those who follow such phrases have been deprived of grasping the meanings of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, with a great deprivation. And Allah knows best. The view of one who said the intended meaning is knowledge of the matters by which disputants are separated, namely requiring evidence and oath, is also far-fetched, because decisive speech is an expression of being able to articulate everything that comes to mind and appears in the imagination, such that nothing becomes confused with anything, and each situation is distinct from another. This is a general meaning that encompasses all the categories. And Allah knows best.

Here ends the discussion of the ten attributes which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in praise of Dawud, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 16–20 (part 1 of 2):

[Qur'an] ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength (dha al-ayd). Indeed, he was constantly turning back (to Allah).﴾

Know that we mentioned in the tafsir of His words, ﴿And they wondered that a warner from among them had come to them, and the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾, that the people were only astonished because of three doubts:

The first concerns divinity, and it is His words, ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾

The second concerns prophethood, and it is His words, ﴿Has the Reminder been revealed to him from among us?﴾

The third concerns the return (al-ma'ad), and it is the words of the Exalted, ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ This is because the people were at the extreme of denial regarding the teaching of resurrection and gathering (al-hashr wa al-nashr). They would argue that the corruption of the doctrine of resurrection proves the corruption of his prophethood. The qitt is a piece of something, because it has been cut off from it, from "qattahu" (he cut it), and the written document of a reward is called qitt. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the promise of Paradise to the believers, they said, mockingly, "Hasten to us our portion of Paradise," or, "Hasten to us the record of our deeds so that we may look into it."

Know that when the disbelievers exceeded all bounds in foolishness against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, "This is a sorcerer, a liar," and said to him by way of mockery, "Hasten to us our qitt," Allah commanded him to be patient with their foolishness, saying, ﴿Be patient over what they say.﴾ If it is asked: what connection is there between His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, and His words, ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾? We say: the explanation of this connection is in several aspects:

The first: it is as if it were said, "If you have witnessed from these ignorant people their audacity against Allah and their denial of gathering and resurrection, then remember the story of Dawud, so that you may know the intensity of his fear of Allah the Exalted and of the Day of Gathering. For as one of two opposites increases in nobility, the other opposite decreases in worth."

The second: it is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Do not let your chest be constrained by their denial of your words and your religion, for if they oppose you, the great prophets have agreed with you."

The third: people hold two views about the story of Dawud. Some say it indicates his sin, and others say it does not indicate it. (As for the one who holds the first view), the aspect of relevance is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Your grief is nothing compared to his, because the disbelievers deny you, whereas Dawud's grief was due to his falling into that sin. There is no doubt that his grief was greater. So reflect on the story of Dawud and the great grief he had, so that what you are suffering of grief may become lighter for you." (As for the one who holds the second view), he said: the two adversaries who entered upon Dawud were humans, and they entered upon him only with the intent to kill him, so Dawud feared them. Yet he did not harm them, nor did he invoke evil upon them, but rather he asked forgiveness for them, as the explanation of this method will come later. Therefore, Allah the Exalted commanded Muhammad (peace be upon him) to follow him in good character.

The fifth: the Quraysh only denied Muhammad (peace be upon him) and treated him lightly because, for the most part, they said that he was an orphan and poor. Then the Exalted related to Muhammad the perfection of the kingdom of Dawud, then He explained that, despite that, he was not spared from sorrows and griefs, so that it would be known that there is no way to be free of grief in this world.

The sixth: His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud﴾, are not restricted to Dawud alone. Rather, after the story of Dawud, He mentioned the stories of the rest of the prophets. It is as if He said, "Be patient over what they say, and take a lesson from the condition of the rest of the prophets," so that He would teach him that each of them was occupied with a particular concern and a particular grief. Then he would know that the world does not cease from worries and sorrows, and that attaining high ranks with Allah is achieved only by bearing hardships and toils in this world. These are aspects that we have mentioned in this context. Here there is another aspect, stronger and better than all that preceded it, which will be mentioned, Allah willing, when we reach the tafsir of His words, ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses﴾ [Sad: 29]. Know that after that, He mentioned the condition of nine prophets: He mentioned the condition of three of them in detail and the condition of six others in summary.

So the first story is the story of Dawud. Know that the essential contents of what Allah the Exalted mentioned in this story are three kinds of speech.

The first: the detailing of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud, which bring about happiness in the Hereafter and in this world.

The second: the explanation of that event which befell him concerning the matter of the two adversaries.

The third: Allah the Exalted's appointing him as successor (istikhlaf) after the occurrence of that event.

As for the first kind, namely the explanation of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud that bring about complete happiness, they are ten.

The first: His words to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud.﴾ So He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), despite his high station, to follow Dawud in patience in obeying Allah. This is a great honor and a noble tribute to Dawud, in that Allah commanded the best of creation, Muhammad (ﷺ), to follow him in noble morals.

The second: that He said concerning him, ﴿Our servant Dawud﴾. He described him as His servant and spoke of Himself in the plural form, which indicates the utmost glorification. This is the highest honor. Do you not see that when the Glorified and Exalted One wished to honor Muhammad (peace be upon him) on the night of the Ascension, He said, ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Here, then, this indicates that same honor for Dawud, and that was a sign of the elevation of his rank also. For the Exalted's describing the prophets by their servitude indicates that they had realized the meaning of servitude through striving in obedience.

The third: His words, ﴿dha al-ayd﴾, meaning possessing strength to perform obedience and to guard against disobedience. This is because when the Exalted praised him with strength, that strength must necessarily be something that merits praise, and the strength which merits great praise is nothing but strength to do what is commanded and to abstain from what is forbidden. The word ﴿al-ayd﴾ mentioned here is like the strength mentioned in His words, ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12], and His words, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailing of everything, so take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], meaning: with diligence in performing the trust and firmness in carrying out the call, and not displaying weakness or frailty. "Al-ayd" and "al-quwwa" (strength) are the same. From it is His words, ﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and His words, ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqara: 87], and He said, ﴿And the heaven We built with ayd﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47]. From Qatada: he was given strength in worship and understanding of the religion, and he used to stand in prayer at night and fast every other day.

The fourth: His words, ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back﴾, meaning that Dawud used to return in all his affairs to My obedience. "Awwab" is an intensive form (fa''al) from "aba," meaning to return, as the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 25]. And the form fa''al is the pattern of intensification, as one says qattal and darrab, for it is more emphatic than qatil and darib.

The fifth: His words, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾. A similar verse is His words, ﴿O mountains, repeat the praise with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. Concerning this there are several discussions.

The first discussion: in it there are several views.

The first: Allah the Glorified created in the body of the mountain life, intellect, power, and speech, and then the mountain became one that glorifies Allah the Exalted. A parallel is His words, ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], for its meaning is that He the Exalted created in the mountain intellect and understanding, then He created in it the vision of Allah the Exalted. So it is likewise here.

The second: regarding interpretation, what al-Qaffal narrated in his tafsir: it is permissible to say that Dawud (peace be upon him) was given such intensity and beauty of voice that the mountains would echo with a beautiful resonance, and the birds would listen to it because of its beauty. So the echo of the mountains and the chirping of the birds with him, and their listening to him, would be glorification. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also mentioned that Allah the Exalted did not give any of His creatures a voice like the voice of Dawud, to the extent that when he recited the Psalms (al-Zabur), the wild animals would approach him until he could take them by their necks.

The third: Allah the Glorified subjected the mountains so that they would move wherever Dawud wished, and that movement was made into glorification, because it indicated the perfection of the power and wisdom of Allah the Exalted.

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said, "﴿yusabbihna﴾ is in the sense of musabbihat (glorifying)." If they say, "Is there any difference between yusabbihna and musabbihat?" We say: yes. The verbal form indicates occurrence and renewal, while the nominal form indicates permanence, as explained by Abd al-Qahir al-Nahwi (the grammarian) in the book Dala'il al-I'jaz. If this is established, we say: His words, ﴿yusabbihna﴾, indicate that the glorification by the mountains occurs gradually, one thing after another and state after state, and the hearer who was present at those mountains would hear them glorifying.

The third discussion: al-Zajjaj said: it is said "sharaqat al-shams" when the sun rises, and "ashraqat" when it shines; and it was said the two have the same meaning, though the first is more common. The Arabs say, "sharaqat al-shams wa al-ma'u yushriq" (the sun rose and the water shines).

The fourth discussion: they have argued for the legality of the Duha prayer (salat al-duha) from this verse. From Umm Hani, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon us, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the Duha prayer, and said, 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq (shining).'" And from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Do you find mention of the Duha prayer in the Qur'an?" They said, "No." So he recited, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾, and said, "Dawud used to pray it." And he said, "There was always something in my mind about the Duha prayer until I found it in His words, ﴿glorify at evening and at sunrise﴾."

* * *

The sixth quality of Dawud (peace be upon him) is the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the birds gathered, each one returning to him.﴾ Concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: His words, ﴿and the birds﴾, are conjoined to the mountains, and the implied meaning is "And We subjected the birds, gathered." Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: when Dawud glorified, the mountains responded to him, and the birds gathered to him and glorified with him. Their gathering to him is their "hashr" (gathering), so according to this interpretation, the one who gathers them is Allah. (If it is asked): how can the glorification of Allah come from the birds, given that they have no intellect? We say: it is not far-fetched to say that Allah the Exalted would create intellect for them so that they would know Allah and then glorify Him. All of that was a miracle for Dawud (peace be upon him).

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: His words, ﴿mahshura (gathered)﴾, correspond to ﴿yusabbihna﴾, except that gathering does not carry the same implication as glorifying, namely indicating occurrence one thing after another. Therefore it was brought as a noun, not a verb. For He said: if it had been said, "And We subjected the birds gathered, glorifying," on the supposition that the gathering was accomplished by the One who gathers them all at once, that indicates the stated measure. And Allah knows best.

The third discussion: it has been read as "wa al-tayru mahshurah" with the nominative case (raf').

The seventh quality of Dawud (peace be upon him): His words, ﴿Each one returning to him.﴾ Its meaning: each of the mountains and the birds is "awwab," that is, returning, meaning whenever Dawud returned to glorification, they responded to him. So these things also used to return to their glorifications. The difference between this quality and the one before it is that in what preceded, we learned that the mountains and the birds glorified along with Dawud's glorification, and by this wording we understood the continuation of that agreement. It has also been said that the pronoun in His words, ﴿Each one returning to him﴾, refers to Allah the Exalted, meaning: each of Dawud, the mountains, and the birds is returning to Allah, that is, glorifying Him and returning to glorification.

[Page 161, 162, 163 markers as in source]

Ninth attribute... Let me translate carefully.

The eighth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾, that is, We made it strong. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. It was also said that "shaddadna" is for intensification. As for the causes that bring about this strengthening, they are many, and they are either worldly causes or religious causes. As for the first, they mention two aspects regarding it:

The first: al-Wahidi narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that every night there would guard him thirty-six thousand men, and when he woke in the morning it was said: "Return, for the Prophet of Allah is pleased with you." Others added and mentioned forty thousand. They said: He was the mightiest of the kings of the earth in authority.

And from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that a man brought a claim before Dawud against another man, saying that he had taken a cow from him. The accused denied it. Dawud said to the claimant: "Bring the evidence," but he did not bring it. Then Dawud saw in his dream that Allah was commanding him to kill the accused. Dawud held firm and said: "It is merely a dream." Then after that the revelation came to him that he must kill him. So he summoned him and informed him that Allah had commanded him to kill him. The accused said: "Allah has spoken the truth. Indeed, I had killed this man's father by treachery." So Dawud killed him. This incident strengthened his kingdom.

As for the religious causes that bring about this strengthening, they are patience, complete reflection, and perfect caution.

The ninth attribute: His saying: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾. Know that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. Know that virtues are of three kinds: soul-related (nafsaniyyah), bodily (badaniyyah), and external (kharijiyyah). Soul-related virtues are confined to two types: knowledge ('ilm) and action ('amal). As for knowledge, it is that the soul becomes, through true conceptions and soul-related assents, in accordance with human capacity. As for action, it is that a person performs the action that is most suitable and most correct for the interests of this world and the Hereafter. This is what wisdom (hikmah) is. It was named "wisdom" because the derivation of sound wisdom does not accept abrogation (naskh) or annulment (naqd), so it is at the utmost level of firmness (ihkam). As for the actions that conform to the interests of this world and the Hereafter, they are binding to observe and do not accept annulment or abrogation. For this reason we named those cognitions and these actions "wisdom."

The tenth attribute: His saying: ﴿And decisive speech (fasl al-khitab)﴾. Know that the bodies of this world are of three kinds:

The first: those that are devoid of perception and awareness, namely inanimate objects (jamadat) and plants (nabatat).

The second: those that have perception and awareness but are not able to make others know the states they have come to know, for the most part. This kind is the entirety of animals other than man.

The third: that which has perception and awareness and has the ability to make others know the states known to it, and that is man. His ability to make others know the states known to him is by speech and address. Then people differ in degrees of ability to express what is in the heart. Among them is one for whom it is difficult to produce ordered, coherent speech, but rather his speech is jumbled and disordered. Among them is one for whom ordering is difficult in some respects. Among them is one who is able to master meaning and express it to the utmost degree. Whoever has this ability in its most complete form, the effects emanating from the rational soul (al-nafs al-nutqiyyah) in him are most complete, and whoever has that ability to a lesser degree, those effects are weaker. When Allah, exalted is He, described the perfection of the essence of the rational soul that belonged to Dawud by His saying: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾, He followed it with an explanation of the perfection of his state in speech, utterance and expression, saying: ﴿and decisive speech﴾. This ordering is of the utmost grandeur. Among the exegetes is one who explained it as meaning that Dawud was the first to say in his speech "Amma ba'd." I say: Truly, those who follow such phrases have been deprived of grasping the meanings of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, with a great deprivation. And Allah knows best. The view of one who said the intended meaning is knowledge of the matters by which disputants are separated, namely requiring evidence and oath, is also far-fetched, because decisive speech is an expression of being able to articulate everything that comes to mind and appears in the imagination, such that nothing becomes confused with anything, and each situation is distinct from another. This is a general meaning that encompasses all the categories. And Allah knows best.

Here ends the discussion of the ten attributes which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in praise of Dawud, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 16–20 (part 1 of 2):

[Qur'an] ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength (dha al-ayd). Indeed, he was constantly turning back (to Allah).﴾

Know that we mentioned in the tafsir of His words, ﴿And they wondered that a warner from among them had come to them, and the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾, that the people were only astonished because of three doubts:

The first concerns divinity, and it is His words, ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾

The second concerns prophethood, and it is His words, ﴿Has the Reminder been revealed to him from among us?﴾

The third concerns the return (al-ma'ad), and it is the words of the Exalted, ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ This is because the people were at the extreme of denial regarding the teaching of resurrection and gathering (al-hashr wa al-nashr). They would argue that the corruption of the doctrine of resurrection proves the corruption of his prophethood. The qitt is a piece of something, because it has been cut off from it, from "qattahu" (he cut it), and the written document of a reward is called qitt. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the promise of Paradise to the believers, they said, mockingly, "Hasten to us our portion of Paradise," or, "Hasten to us the record of our deeds so that we may look into it."

Know that when the disbelievers exceeded all bounds in foolishness against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, "This is a sorcerer, a liar," and said to him by way of mockery, "Hasten to us our qitt," Allah commanded him to be patient with their foolishness, saying, ﴿Be patient over what they say.﴾ If it is asked: what connection is there between His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, and His words, ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾? We say: the explanation of this connection is in several aspects:

The first: it is as if it were said, "If you have witnessed from these ignorant people their audacity against Allah and their denial of gathering and resurrection, then remember the story of Dawud, so that you may know the intensity of his fear of Allah the Exalted and of the Day of Gathering. For as one of two opposites increases in nobility, the other opposite decreases in worth."

The second: it is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Do not let your chest be constrained by their denial of your words and your religion, for if they oppose you, the great prophets have agreed with you."

The third: people hold two views about the story of Dawud. Some say it indicates his sin, and others say it does not indicate it. (As for the one who holds the first view), the aspect of relevance is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Your grief is nothing compared to his, because the disbelievers deny you, whereas Dawud's grief was due to his falling into that sin. There is no doubt that his grief was greater. So reflect on the story of Dawud and the great grief he had, so that what you are suffering of grief may become lighter for you." (As for the one who holds the second view), he said: the two adversaries who entered upon Dawud were humans, and they entered upon him only with the intent to kill him, so Dawud feared them. Yet he did not harm them, nor did he invoke evil upon them, but rather he asked forgiveness for them, as the explanation of this method will come later. Therefore, Allah the Exalted commanded Muhammad (peace be upon him) to follow him in good character.

The fifth: the Quraysh only denied Muhammad (peace be upon him) and treated him lightly because, for the most part, they said that he was an orphan and poor. Then the Exalted related to Muhammad the perfection of the kingdom of Dawud, then He explained that, despite that, he was not spared from sorrows and griefs, so that it would be known that there is no way to be free of grief in this world.

The sixth: His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud﴾, are not restricted to Dawud alone. Rather, after the story of Dawud, He mentioned the stories of the rest of the prophets. It is as if He said, "Be patient over what they say, and take a lesson from the condition of the rest of the prophets," so that He would teach him that each of them was occupied with a particular concern and a particular grief. Then he would know that the world does not cease from worries and sorrows, and that attaining high ranks with Allah is achieved only by bearing hardships and toils in this world. These are aspects that we have mentioned in this context. Here there is another aspect, stronger and better than all that preceded it, which will be mentioned, Allah willing, when we reach the tafsir of His words, ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses﴾ [Sad: 29]. Know that after that, He mentioned the condition of nine prophets: He mentioned the condition of three of them in detail and the condition of six others in summary.

So the first story is the story of Dawud. Know that the essential contents of what Allah the Exalted mentioned in this story are three kinds of speech.

The first: the detailing of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud, which bring about happiness in the Hereafter and in this world.

The second: the explanation of that event which befell him concerning the matter of the two adversaries.

The third: Allah the Exalted's appointing him as successor (istikhlaf) after the occurrence of that event.

As for the first kind, namely the explanation of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud that bring about complete happiness, they are ten.

The first: His words to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud.﴾ So He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), despite his high station, to follow Dawud in patience in obeying Allah. This is a great honor and a noble tribute to Dawud, in that Allah commanded the best of creation, Muhammad (ﷺ), to follow him in noble morals.

The second: that He said concerning him, ﴿Our servant Dawud﴾. He described him as His servant and spoke of Himself in the plural form, which indicates the utmost glorification. This is the highest honor. Do you not see that when the Glorified and Exalted One wished to honor Muhammad (peace be upon him) on the night of the Ascension, He said, ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Here, then, this indicates that same honor for Dawud, and that was a sign of the elevation of his rank also. For the Exalted's describing the prophets by their servitude indicates that they had realized the meaning of servitude through striving in obedience.

The third: His words, ﴿dha al-ayd﴾, meaning possessing strength to perform obedience and to guard against disobedience. This is because when the Exalted praised him with strength, that strength must necessarily be something that merits praise, and the strength which merits great praise is nothing but strength to do what is commanded and to abstain from what is forbidden. The word ﴿al-ayd﴾ mentioned here is like the strength mentioned in His words, ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12], and His words, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailing of everything, so take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], meaning: with diligence in performing the trust and firmness in carrying out the call, and not displaying weakness or frailty. "Al-ayd" and "al-quwwa" (strength) are the same. From it is His words, ﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and His words, ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqara: 87], and He said, ﴿And the heaven We built with ayd﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47]. From Qatada: he was given strength in worship and understanding of the religion, and he used to stand in prayer at night and fast every other day.

The fourth: His words, ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back﴾, meaning that Dawud used to return in all his affairs to My obedience. "Awwab" is an intensive form (fa''al) from "aba," meaning to return, as the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 25]. And the form fa''al is the pattern of intensification, as one says qattal and darrab, for it is more emphatic than qatil and darib.

The fifth: His words, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾. A similar verse is His words, ﴿O mountains, repeat the praise with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. Concerning this there are several discussions.

The first discussion: in it there are several views.

The first: Allah the Glorified created in the body of the mountain life, intellect, power, and speech, and then the mountain became one that glorifies Allah the Exalted. A parallel is His words, ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], for its meaning is that He the Exalted created in the mountain intellect and understanding, then He created in it the vision of Allah the Exalted. So it is likewise here.

The second: regarding interpretation, what al-Qaffal narrated in his tafsir: it is permissible to say that Dawud (peace be upon him) was given such intensity and beauty of voice that the mountains would echo with a beautiful resonance, and the birds would listen to it because of its beauty. So the echo of the mountains and the chirping of the birds with him, and their listening to him, would be glorification. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also mentioned that Allah the Exalted did not give any of His creatures a voice like the voice of Dawud, to the extent that when he recited the Psalms (al-Zabur), the wild animals would approach him until he could take them by their necks.

The third: Allah the Glorified subjected the mountains so that they would move wherever Dawud wished, and that movement was made into glorification, because it indicated the perfection of the power and wisdom of Allah the Exalted.

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said, "﴿yusabbihna﴾ is in the sense of musabbihat (glorifying)." If they say, "Is there any difference between yusabbihna and musabbihat?" We say: yes. The verbal form indicates occurrence and renewal, while the nominal form indicates permanence, as explained by Abd al-Qahir al-Nahwi (the grammarian) in the book Dala'il al-I'jaz. If this is established, we say: His words, ﴿yusabbihna﴾, indicate that the glorification by the mountains occurs gradually, one thing after another and state after state, and the hearer who was present at those mountains would hear them glorifying.

The third discussion: al-Zajjaj said: it is said "sharaqat al-shams" when the sun rises, and "ashraqat" when it shines; and it was said the two have the same meaning, though the first is more common. The Arabs say, "sharaqat al-shams wa al-ma'u yushriq" (the sun rose and the water shines).

The fourth discussion: they have argued for the legality of the Duha prayer (salat al-duha) from this verse. From Umm Hani, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon us, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the Duha prayer, and said, 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq (shining).'" And from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Do you find mention of the Duha prayer in the Qur'an?" They said, "No." So he recited, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾, and said, "Dawud used to pray it." And he said, "There was always something in my mind about the Duha prayer until I found it in His words, ﴿glorify at evening and at sunrise﴾."

* * *

The sixth quality of Dawud (peace be upon him) is the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the birds gathered, each one returning to him.﴾ Concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: His words, ﴿and the birds﴾, are conjoined to the mountains, and the implied meaning is "And We subjected the birds, gathered." Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: when Dawud glorified, the mountains responded to him, and the birds gathered to him and glorified with him. Their gathering to him is their "hashr" (gathering), so according to this interpretation, the one who gathers them is Allah. (If it is asked): how can the glorification of Allah come from the birds, given that they have no intellect? We say: it is not far-fetched to say that Allah the Exalted would create intellect for them so that they would know Allah and then glorify Him. All of that was a miracle for Dawud (peace be upon him).

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: His words, ﴿mahshura (gathered)﴾, correspond to ﴿yusabbihna﴾, except that gathering does not carry the same implication as glorifying, namely indicating occurrence one thing after another. Therefore it was brought as a noun, not a verb. For He said: if it had been said, "And We subjected the birds gathered, glorifying," on the supposition that the gathering was accomplished by the One who gathers them all at once, that indicates the stated measure. And Allah knows best.

The third discussion: it has been read as "wa al-tayru mahshurah" with the nominative case (raf').

The seventh quality of Dawud (peace be upon him): His words, ﴿Each one returning to him.﴾ Its meaning: each of the mountains and the birds is "awwab," that is, returning, meaning whenever Dawud returned to glorification, they responded to him. So these things also used to return to their glorifications. The difference between this quality and the one before it is that in what preceded, we learned that the mountains and the birds glorified along with Dawud's glorification, and by this wording we understood the continuation of that agreement. Ninth attribute... Let me translate carefully.

The eighth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾, that is, We made it strong. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. It was also said that "shaddadna" is for intensification. As for the causes that bring about this strengthening, they are many, and they are either worldly causes or religious causes. As for the first, they mention two aspects regarding it:

The first: al-Wahidi narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that every night there would guard him thirty-six thousand men, and when he woke in the morning it was said: "Return, for the Prophet of Allah is pleased with you." Others added and mentioned forty thousand. They said: He was the mightiest of the kings of the earth in authority.

And from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that a man brought a claim before Dawud against another man, saying that he had taken a cow from him. The accused denied it. Dawud said to the claimant: "Bring the evidence," but he did not bring it. Then Dawud saw in his dream that Allah was commanding him to kill the accused. Dawud held firm and said: "It is merely a dream." Then after that the revelation came to him that he must kill him. So he summoned him and informed him that Allah had commanded him to kill him. The accused said: "Allah has spoken the truth. Indeed, I had killed this man's father by treachery." So Dawud killed him. This incident strengthened his kingdom.

As for the religious causes that bring about this strengthening, they are patience, complete reflection, and perfect caution.

As for knowledge, it is that the soul becomes, through true conceptions and soul-related assents, in accordance with human capacity. As for action, it is that a person performs the action that is most suitable and most correct for the interests of this world and the Hereafter. This is what wisdom (hikmah) is. It was named "wisdom" because the derivation of sound wisdom does not accept abrogation (naskh) or annulment (naqd), so it is at the utmost level of firmness (ihkam). As for the actions that conform to the interests of this world and the Hereafter, they are binding to observe and do not accept annulment or abrogation. For this reason we named those cognitions and these actions "wisdom."

The second: those that have perception and awareness but are not able to make others know the states they have come to know, for the most part. This kind is the entirety of animals other than man.

The third: that which has perception and awareness and has the ability to make others know the states known to it, and that is man. His ability to make others know the states known to him is by speech and address. Then people differ in degrees of ability to express what is in the heart. Among them is one for whom it is difficult to produce ordered, coherent speech, but rather his speech is jumbled and disordered. Among them is one for whom ordering is difficult in some respects. Among them is one who is able to master meaning and express it to the utmost degree. Whoever has this ability in its most complete form, the effects emanating from the rational soul (al-nafs al-nutqiyyah) in him are most complete, and whoever has that ability to a lesser degree, those effects are weaker. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 16–20 (part 1 of 2):

[Qur'an] ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength (dha al-ayd). Indeed, he was constantly turning back (to Allah).﴾

Know that we mentioned in the tafsir of His words, ﴿And they wondered that a warner from among them had come to them, and the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾, that the people were only astonished because of three doubts:

The first concerns divinity, and it is His words, ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾

The second concerns prophethood, and it is His words, ﴿Has the Reminder been revealed to him from among us?﴾

The third concerns the return (al-ma'ad), and it is the words of the Exalted, ﴿They say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ This is because the people were at the extreme of denial regarding the teaching of resurrection and gathering (al-hashr wa al-nashr). They would argue that the corruption of the doctrine of resurrection proves the corruption of his prophethood. The qitt is a piece of something, because it has been cut off from it, from "qattahu" (he cut it), and the written document of a reward is called qitt. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the promise of Paradise to the believers, they said, mockingly, "Hasten to us our portion of Paradise," or, "Hasten to us the record of our deeds so that we may look into it."

Know that when the disbelievers exceeded all bounds in foolishness against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, "This is a sorcerer, a liar," and said to him by way of mockery, "Hasten to us our qitt," Allah commanded him to be patient with their foolishness, saying, ﴿Be patient over what they say.﴾ If it is asked: what connection is there between His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, and His words, ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾? We say: the explanation of this connection is in several aspects:

The first: it is as if it were said, "If you have witnessed from these ignorant people their audacity against Allah and their denial of gathering and resurrection, then remember the story of Dawud, so that you may know the intensity of his fear of Allah the Exalted and of the Day of Gathering. For as one of two opposites increases in nobility, the other opposite decreases in worth."

The second: it is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Do not let your chest be constrained by their denial of your words and your religion, for if they oppose you, the great prophets have agreed with you."

The third: people hold two views about the story of Dawud. Some say it indicates his sin, and others say it does not indicate it. (As for the one who holds the first view), the aspect of relevance is as if it were said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "Your grief is nothing compared to his, because the disbelievers deny you, whereas Dawud's grief was due to his falling into that sin. There is no doubt that his grief was greater. So reflect on the story of Dawud and the great grief he had, so that what you are suffering of grief may become lighter for you." (As for the one who holds the second view), he said: the two adversaries who entered upon Dawud were humans, and they entered upon him only with the intent to kill him, so Dawud feared them. Yet he did not harm them, nor did he invoke evil upon them, but rather he asked forgiveness for them, as the explanation of this method will come later. Therefore, Allah the Exalted commanded Muhammad (peace be upon him) to follow him in good character.

The fifth: the Quraysh only denied Muhammad (peace be upon him) and treated him lightly because, for the most part, they said that he was an orphan and poor. Then the Exalted related to Muhammad the perfection of the kingdom of Dawud, then He explained that, despite that, he was not spared from sorrows and griefs, so that it would be known that there is no way to be free of grief in this world.

The sixth: His words, ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud﴾, are not restricted to Dawud alone. Rather, after the story of Dawud, He mentioned the stories of the rest of the prophets. It is as if He said, "Be patient over what they say, and take a lesson from the condition of the rest of the prophets," so that He would teach him that each of them was occupied with a particular concern and a particular grief. Then he would know that the world does not cease from worries and sorrows, and that attaining high ranks with Allah is achieved only by bearing hardships and toils in this world. These are aspects that we have mentioned in this context. Here there is another aspect, stronger and better than all that preceded it, which will be mentioned, Allah willing, when we reach the tafsir of His words, ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses﴾ [Sad: 29]. Know that after that, He mentioned the condition of nine prophets: He mentioned the condition of three of them in detail and the condition of six others in summary.

So the first story is the story of Dawud. Know that the essential contents of what Allah the Exalted mentioned in this story are three kinds of speech.

The first: the detailing of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud, which bring about happiness in the Hereafter and in this world.

The second: the explanation of that event which befell him concerning the matter of the two adversaries.

The third: Allah the Exalted's appointing him as successor (istikhlaf) after the occurrence of that event.

As for the first kind, namely the explanation of the qualities which Allah gave Dawud that bring about complete happiness, they are ten.

The first: His words to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud.﴾ So He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), despite his high station, to follow Dawud in patience in obeying Allah. This is a great honor and a noble tribute to Dawud, in that Allah commanded the best of creation, Muhammad (ﷺ), to follow him in noble morals.

The second: that He said concerning him, ﴿Our servant Dawud﴾. He described him as His servant and spoke of Himself in the plural form, which indicates the utmost glorification. This is the highest honor. Do you not see that when the Glorified and Exalted One wished to honor Muhammad (peace be upon him) on the night of the Ascension, He said, ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Here, then, this indicates that same honor for Dawud, and that was a sign of the elevation of his rank also. For the Exalted's describing the prophets by their servitude indicates that they had realized the meaning of servitude through striving in obedience.

The third: His words, ﴿dha al-ayd﴾, meaning possessing strength to perform obedience and to guard against disobedience. This is because when the Exalted praised him with strength, that strength must necessarily be something that merits praise, and the strength which merits great praise is nothing but strength to do what is commanded and to abstain from what is forbidden. The word ﴿al-ayd﴾ mentioned here is like the strength mentioned in His words, ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12], and His words, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailing of everything, so take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], meaning: with diligence in performing the trust and firmness in carrying out the call, and not displaying weakness or frailty. "Al-ayd" and "al-quwwa" (strength) are the same. From it is His words, ﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and His words, ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqara: 87], and He said, ﴿And the heaven We built with ayd﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47]. From Qatada: he was given strength in worship and understanding of the religion, and he used to stand in prayer at night and fast every other day.

The fourth: His words, ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back﴾, meaning that Dawud used to return in all his affairs to My obedience. "Awwab" is an intensive form (fa''al) from "aba," meaning to return, as the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 25]. And the form fa''al is the pattern of intensification, as one says qattal and darrab, for it is more emphatic than qatil and darib.

The fifth: His words, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾. A similar verse is His words, ﴿O mountains, repeat the praise with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. Concerning this there are several discussions.

The first discussion: in it there are several views.

The first: Allah the Glorified created in the body of the mountain life, intellect, power, and speech, and then the mountain became one that glorifies Allah the Exalted. A parallel is His words, ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], for its meaning is that He the Exalted created in the mountain intellect and understanding, then He created in it the vision of Allah the Exalted. So it is likewise here.

The second: regarding interpretation, what al-Qaffal narrated in his tafsir: it is permissible to say that Dawud (peace be upon him) was given such intensity and beauty of voice that the mountains would echo with a beautiful resonance, and the birds would listen to it because of its beauty. So the echo of the mountains and the chirping of the birds with him, and their listening to him, would be glorification. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also mentioned that Allah the Exalted did not give any of His creatures a voice like the voice of Dawud, to the extent that when he recited the Psalms (al-Zabur), the wild animals would approach him until he could take them by their necks.

The third: Allah the Glorified subjected the mountains so that they would move wherever Dawud wished, and that movement was made into glorification, because it indicated the perfection of the power and wisdom of Allah the Exalted.

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said, "﴿yusabbihna﴾ is in the sense of musabbihat (glorifying)." If they say, "Is there any difference between yusabbihna and musabbihat?" We say: yes. The verbal form indicates occurrence and renewal, while the nominal form indicates permanence, as explained by Abd al-Qahir al-Nahwi (the grammarian) in the book Dala'il al-I'jaz. If this is established, we say: His words, ﴿yusabbihna﴾, indicate that the glorification by the mountains occurs gradually, one thing after another and state after state, and the hearer who was present at those mountains would hear them glorifying.

The third discussion: al-Zajjaj said: it is said "sharaqat al-shams" when the sun rises, and "ashraqat" when it shines; and it was said the two have the same meaning, though the first is more common. The Arabs say, "sharaqat al-shams wa al-ma'u yushriq" (the sun rose and the water shines).

The fourth discussion: they have argued for the legality of the Duha prayer (salat al-duha) from this verse. From Umm Hani, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon us, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the Duha prayer, and said, 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq (shining).'" And from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Do you find mention of the Duha prayer in the Qur'an?" They said, "No." So he recited, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾, and said, "Dawud used to pray it." And he said, "There was always something in my mind about the Duha prayer until I found it in His words, ﴿glorify at evening and at sunrise﴾."

* * *

The sixth quality of Dawud (peace be upon him) is the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the birds gathered, each one returning to him.﴾ Concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: His words, ﴿and the birds﴾, are conjoined to the mountains, and the implied meaning is "And We subjected the birds, gathered." Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: when Dawud glorified, the mountains responded to him, and the birds gathered to him and glorified with him. Their gathering to him is their "hashr" (gathering), so according to this interpretation, the one who gathers them is Allah. (If it is asked): how can the glorification of Allah come from the birds, given that they have no intellect? We say: it is not far-fetched to say that Allah the Exalted would create intellect for them so that they would know Allah and then glorify Him. All of that was a miracle for Dawud (peace be upon him).

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: His words, ﴿mahshura (gathered)﴾, correspond to ﴿yusabbihna﴾, except that gathering does not carry the same implication as glorifying, namely indicating occurrence one thing after another. Therefore it was brought as a noun, not a verb. For He said: if it had been said, "And We subjected the birds gathered, glorifying," on the supposition that the gathering was accomplished by the One who gathers them all at once, that indicates the stated measure. And Allah knows best.

The third discussion: it has been read as "wa al-tayru mahshurah" with the nominative case (raf').

The seventh quality of Dawud (peace be upon him): His words, ﴿Each one returning to him.﴾ Its meaning: each of the mountains and the birds is "awwab," that is, returning, meaning whenever Dawud returned to glorification, they responded to him. So these things also used to return to their glorifications. The difference between this quality and the one before it is that in what preceded, we learned that the mountains and the birds glorified along with Dawud's glorification, and by this wording we understood the continuation of that agreement. It has also been said that the pronoun in His words, ﴿Each one returning to him﴾, refers to Allah the Exalted, meaning: each of Dawud, the mountains, and the birds is returning to Allah, that is, glorifying Him and returning to glorification.
