Do you not see that when the Glorified and Exalted One wished to honor Muhammad (peace be upon him) on the night of the Ascension, He said, ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Here, then, this indicates that same honor for Dawud, and that was a sign of the elevation of his rank also. For the Exalted's describing the prophets by their servitude indicates that they had realized the meaning of servitude through striving in obedience.

The third: His words, ﴿dha al-ayd﴾, meaning possessing strength to perform obedience and to guard against disobedience. This is because when the Exalted praised him with strength, that strength must necessarily be something that merits praise, and the strength which merits great praise is nothing but strength to do what is commanded and to abstain from what is forbidden. The word ﴿al-ayd﴾ mentioned here is like the strength mentioned in His words, ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12], and His words, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailing of everything, so take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], meaning: with diligence in performing the trust and firmness in carrying out the call, and not displaying weakness or frailty. "Al-ayd" and "al-quwwa" (strength) are the same. From it is His words, ﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and His words, ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqara: 87], and He said, ﴿And the heaven We built with ayd﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47]. From Qatada: he was given strength in worship and understanding of the religion, and he used to stand in prayer at night and fast every other day.

The fourth: His words, ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back﴾, meaning that Dawud used to return in all his affairs to My obedience. "Awwab" is an intensive form (fa''al) from "aba," meaning to return, as the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 25]. And the form fa''al is the pattern of intensification, as one says qattal and darrab, for it is more emphatic than qatil and darib.

The fifth: His words, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾. A similar verse is His words, ﴿O mountains, repeat the praise with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. Concerning this there are several discussions.

The first discussion: in it there are several views.

The first: Allah the Glorified created in the body of the mountain life, intellect, power, and speech, and then the mountain became one that glorifies Allah the Exalted. A parallel is His words, ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], for its meaning is that He the Exalted created in the mountain intellect and understanding, then He created in it the vision of Allah the Exalted. So it is likewise here.

The second: regarding interpretation, what al-Qaffal narrated in his tafsir: it is permissible to say that Dawud (peace be upon him) was given such intensity and beauty of voice that the mountains would echo with a beautiful resonance, and the birds would listen to it because of its beauty. So the echo of the mountains and the chirping of the birds with him, and their listening to him, would be glorification. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also mentioned that Allah the Exalted did not give any of His creatures a voice like the voice of Dawud, to the extent that when he recited the Psalms (al-Zabur), the wild animals would approach him until he could take them by their necks.

The third: Allah the Glorified subjected the mountains so that they would move wherever Dawud wished, and that movement was made into glorification, because it indicated the perfection of the power and wisdom of Allah the Exalted.

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said, "﴿yusabbihna﴾ is in the sense of musabbihat (glorifying)." If they say, "Is there any difference between yusabbihna and musabbihat?" We say: yes. The verbal form indicates occurrence and renewal, while the nominal form indicates permanence, as explained by Abd al-Qahir al-Nahwi (the grammarian) in the book Dala'il al-I'jaz. If this is established, we say: His words, ﴿yusabbihna﴾, indicate that the glorification by the mountains occurs gradually, one thing after another and state after state, and the hearer who was present at those mountains would hear them glorifying.

The third discussion: al-Zajjaj said: it is said "sharaqat al-shams" when the sun rises, and "ashraqat" when it shines; and it was said the two have the same meaning, though the first is more common. The Arabs say, "sharaqat al-shams wa al-ma'u yushriq" (the sun rose and the water shines).

The fourth discussion: they have argued for the legality of the Duha prayer (salat al-duha) from this verse. From Umm Hani, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon us, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the Duha prayer, and said, 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq (shining).'" And from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Do you find mention of the Duha prayer in the Qur'an?" They said, "No." So he recited, ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾, and said, "Dawud used to pray it." And he said, "There was always something in my mind about the Duha prayer until I found it in His words, ﴿glorify at evening and at sunrise﴾."

* * *

The sixth quality of Dawud (peace be upon him) is the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the birds gathered, each one returning to him.﴾ Concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: His words, ﴿and the birds﴾, are conjoined to the mountains, and the implied meaning is "And We subjected the birds, gathered." Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: when Dawud glorified, the mountains responded to him, and the birds gathered to him and glorified with him. Their gathering to him is their "hashr" (gathering), so according to this interpretation, the one who gathers them is Allah. (If it is asked): how can the glorification of Allah come from the birds, given that they have no intellect? We say: it is not far-fetched to say that Allah the Exalted would create intellect for them so that they would know Allah and then glorify Him. All of that was a miracle for Dawud (peace be upon him).

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: His words, ﴿mahshura (gathered)﴾, correspond to ﴿yusabbihna﴾, except that gathering does not carry the same implication as glorifying, namely indicating occurrence one thing after another. Therefore it was brought as a noun, not a verb. For He said: if it had been said, "And We subjected the birds gathered, glorifying," on the supposition that the gathering was accomplished by the One who gathers them all at once, that indicates the stated measure. And Allah knows best.

The third discussion: it has been read as "wa al-tayru mahshurah" with the nominative case (raf').

The seventh quality of Dawud (peace be upon him): His words, ﴿Each one returning to him.﴾ Its meaning: each of the mountains and the birds is "awwab," that is, returning, meaning whenever Dawud returned to glorification, they responded to him. So these things also used to return to their glorifications. The difference between this quality and the one before it is that in what preceded, we learned that the mountains and the birds glorified along with Dawud's glorification, and by this wording we understood the continuation of that agreement. It has also been said that the pronoun in His words, ﴿Each one returning to him﴾, refers to Allah the Exalted, meaning: each of Dawud, the mountains, and the birds is returning to Allah, that is, glorifying Him and returning to glorification.

[Page 161, 162, 163 markers as in source]

Ninth attribute... Let me translate carefully.

The eighth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾, that is, We made it strong. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. It was also said that "shaddadna" is for intensification. As for the causes that bring about this strengthening, they are many, and they are either worldly causes or religious causes. As for the first, they mention two aspects regarding it:

The first: al-Wahidi narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that every night there would guard him thirty-six thousand men, and when he woke in the morning it was said: "Return, for the Prophet of Allah is pleased with you." Others added and mentioned forty thousand. They said: He was the mightiest of the kings of the earth in authority.

And from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that a man brought a claim before Dawud against another man, saying that he had taken a cow from him. The accused denied it. Dawud said to the claimant: "Bring the evidence," but he did not bring it. Then Dawud saw in his dream that Allah was commanding him to kill the accused. Dawud held firm and said: "It is merely a dream." Then after that the revelation came to him that he must kill him. So he summoned him and informed him that Allah had commanded him to kill him. The accused said: "Allah has spoken the truth. Indeed, I had killed this man's father by treachery." So Dawud killed him. This incident strengthened his kingdom.

As for the religious causes that bring about this strengthening, they are patience, complete reflection, and perfect caution.

The ninth attribute: His saying: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾. Know that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. Know that virtues are of three kinds: soul-related (nafsaniyyah), bodily (badaniyyah), and external (kharijiyyah). Soul-related virtues are confined to two types: knowledge ('ilm) and action ('amal). As for knowledge, it is that the soul becomes, through true conceptions and soul-related assents, in accordance with human capacity. As for action, it is that a person performs the action that is most suitable and most correct for the interests of this world and the Hereafter. This is what wisdom (hikmah) is. It was named "wisdom" because the derivation of sound wisdom does not accept abrogation (naskh) or annulment (naqd), so it is at the utmost level of firmness (ihkam). As for the actions that conform to the interests of this world and the Hereafter, they are binding to observe and do not accept annulment or abrogation. For this reason we named those cognitions and these actions "wisdom."

The tenth attribute: His saying: ﴿And decisive speech (fasl al-khitab)﴾. Know that the bodies of this world are of three kinds:

The first: those that are devoid of perception and awareness, namely inanimate objects (jamadat) and plants (nabatat).

The second: those that have perception and awareness but are not able to make others know the states they have come to know, for the most part. This kind is the entirety of animals other than man.

The third: that which has perception and awareness and has the ability to make others know the states known to it, and that is man. His ability to make others know the states known to him is by speech and address. Then people differ in degrees of ability to express what is in the heart. Among them is one for whom it is difficult to produce ordered, coherent speech, but rather his speech is jumbled and disordered. Among them is one for whom ordering is difficult in some respects. Among them is one who is able to master meaning and express it to the utmost degree. Whoever has this ability in its most complete form, the effects emanating from the rational soul (al-nafs al-nutqiyyah) in him are most complete, and whoever has that ability to a lesser degree, those effects are weaker. When Allah, exalted is He, described the perfection of the essence of the rational soul that belonged to Dawud by His saying: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾, He followed it with an explanation of the perfection of his state in speech, utterance and expression, saying: ﴿and decisive speech﴾. This ordering is of the utmost grandeur. Among the exegetes is one who explained it as meaning that Dawud was the first to say in his speech "Amma ba'd." I say: Truly, those who follow such phrases have been deprived of grasping the meanings of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, with a great deprivation. And Allah knows best. The view of one who said the intended meaning is knowledge of the matters by which disputants are separated, namely requiring evidence and oath, is also far-fetched, because decisive speech is an expression of being able to articulate everything that comes to mind and appears in the imagination, such that nothing becomes confused with anything, and each situation is distinct from another. This is a general meaning that encompasses all the categories. And Allah knows best.

Here ends the discussion of the ten attributes which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in praise of Dawud, peace be upon him.

[Page 165]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you, when they climbed over the wall into the prayer niche?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud and he was alarmed by them, they said, "Do not fear. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth, do not be unjust, and guide us to the right path." ﴾ ﴿"Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said, 'Entrust it to me,' and he overcame me in speech."﴾ ﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes. Indeed, many associates oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And Dawud thought that We had only tested him, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance.﴾ ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has nearness to Us and a good final return.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, praised him and commended him in ten respects, He followed this with the mention of a story, to show by it that the circumstances occurring in this story do not indicate anything that would make him (peace be upon him) deserving of such great praise and commendation.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you?﴾, it is similar to His saying, ﴿Has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9]. The purpose of this interrogative is to draw attention to the greatness of the story being asked about, so that it serves as a call to listen to it and to take a lesson from it. I will state three views on this story:

The first: it is mentioned in a manner that indicates that he committed a major sin.

The second: it indicates a minor sin.

The third: it does not indicate either a major or a minor sin.

As for the first view, the essence of what they say about it is that Dawud fell in love with the wife of Uriya, so he devised many schemes until he killed her husband and then married her. God then sent two angels to him in the form of litigants in a case similar to his own, and they presented that case to him. Dawud gave a judgment which necessarily implied his admission that he was guilty, and then he became aware of this and occupied himself with repentance.

What I hold and adopt is that this is false, and the following points indicate this.

The first: if this account were attributed to the most immoral and most debauched of people, he would be ashamed of it. And the vile, wicked man who narrates this story, if he were attributed with such an action, would strongly deny it and perhaps curse the one who attributes it to him. If this is so, how is it fitting for a sensible person to attribute such a thing to one who is protected from sin?

The second: the essence of the story reduces to two matters: striving to kill a Muslim man without right, and desiring his wife. As for the first, it is a reprehensible matter. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever participates in the shedding of a Muslim's blood, even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: 'Despairing of the mercy of God.'"

As for the second, it is a grave wrong. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe." Uriya was not safe from Dawud, neither in his life nor in his wife.

The third: God, exalted is He, described Dawud (peace be upon him) before the mention of this story with the ten attributes mentioned, and He also described him with many attributes after the mention of this story. All of these attributes are incompatible with his being described with this reprehensible act and this ugly deed. There is no harm in repeating these attributes for the sake of emphasis in clarification.

So we say: as for the first attributes, they are that God, exalted is He, commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to take Dawud as a model in patient endurance with hardship. If we say that Dawud did not endure restraining the self, but rather strove to shed the blood of a Muslim man for the sake of his desire, how would it be fitting for the Most Wise of the wise to command Muhammad, the best of the messengers, to take Dawud as a model in patience in obedience to God?

As for the second attribute: He described him as His servant, and we have explained that the purpose of this description is to show that the one so described is perfect in the station of servitude, complete in performing acts of obedience and in abstaining from what is forbidden. If we say that Dawud (peace be upon him) occupied himself with those false actions, then Dawud would not have been perfect in his servitude to God, exalted is He, but rather perfect in obeying his desire and lust.

The third attribute: He said ﴿the one with strength﴾, that is, the one with power. There is no doubt that what is meant by this is strength in religion, because strength in other than religion was present in the kings of the disbelievers, and there is no meaning to strength in religion except complete ability to perform obligations

صفحة ١٦٦
and to avoid what is forbidden. And what strength is there for one who does not master himself against killing and against desire for the wife of a Muslim?

The fourth attribute: that he was one who turns back frequently to God, exalted is He. How is this fitting for one whose heart is enamoured with killing and debauchery?

The fifth attribute: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him﴾. Do you think the mountains were subjected to him so that he might make them a means to killing and debauchery?

The sixth attribute: His saying, ﴿and the birds gathered﴾. It has been said that it was forbidden for him to hunt any kind of bird. How is it conceivable that the birds are safe from him, yet a Muslim man is not safe from him regarding his life and his wife?

The seventh attribute: His saying, ﴿and We strengthened his kingdom﴾. It is impossible that what is meant is that God strengthened his kingdom through worldly means. Rather, what is meant is that God strengthened his kingdom by means that strengthen religion and the causes of happiness in the Hereafter, and what is meant is the strengthening of his kingdom in religion and in the world. And one who does not master himself against killing and debauchery, how is such a thing fitting for him?

The eighth attribute: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾. Wisdom is a comprehensive term for everything that ought to be known and done. How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to say, "We gave him wisdom and decisive speech," while he persists in what the vile Satan would shrink from, namely competing with his most sincere companion over his life and his wife? Therefore, these attributes mentioned before the explanation of that story indicate the innocence of his reputation from those falsehoods.

* * *

As for the attributes mentioned after the mention of the story, they are ten:

The first: His saying, ﴿And indeed he has nearness to Us and a good final return﴾. The mention of this statement is only appropriate if the preceding story indicates his obedience to God. But if the preceding story indicated his striving in killing and debauchery, His saying ﴿indeed he has nearness to Us﴾ would not be fitting for him.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿O Dawud, We have made you a successor on the earth﴾ [Sad: 26]. This indicates the falsity of that story in several respects:

One of them: when a great king relates about one of his servants that he targeted the lives, wealth, and wives of people, and after finishing the explanation of the story before a gathering of people, it would be shameful for him to say afterward, "O servant, I have entrusted to you my caliphate and my representation." This is because the mention of such vices and reprehensible acts calls for censure and restraint, whereas appointing him as a deputy and successor for himself is absolutely not fitting.

The second: it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that mentioning a ruling immediately after a description indicates that the ruling is caused by that description. So when God related about him that disgraceful incident, and then said after it, ﴿We have made you a successor on the earth﴾, this indicates that the cause for entrusting this succession was his committing those reprehensible acts. And it is known that this is false. But if the story were mentioned in a way that indicates his innocence from sins and transgressions, and the intensity of his perseverance in obedience to God, then it would be appropriate to mention after it, ﴿We have made you a successor on the earth﴾ [Sad: 26]. Thus it is established that what we choose is more correct.

The third: since the introduction of the verse indicates the praise and magnification of Dawud (peace be upon him), and its conclusion also indicates that, then if the intermediate part indicated vices and faults, it would be like saying: "So-and-so is of great rank, high in standing in obedience to God, who kills, commits adultery, and steals, and God has made him a successor on His earth and the arbiter of His judgments." Just as this statement is not fitting for a sensible person, so too here. And it is known that the mention of passion and the striving in killing is among the greatest sources of faults.

The fourth: that the proponents of this view mention in this narration that Dawud (peace be upon him) wished to obtain in religion the high ranks that the earlier prophets had attained, such as what the Friend (Abraham) attained through being cast into the fire, what the one who was sacrificed attained through the sacrifice, and what Ya'qub attained through hardships that bring abundant reward. So God revealed to him that they only attained those ranks because when they were tested, they endured patiently. Thereupon Dawud (peace be upon him) asked for a trial, and God revealed to him that he would be tested on such-and-such a day. He took great precautions, but then the event occurred. So we say: the beginning of their account indicates that God tests him with a trial that increases his merit and perfects the degrees of his sincerity. So striving to kill a soul without right and excessive passion, how is that fitting in this state? And it is established that the story they mention contradicts its beginning with its end.

The third: since the introduction of the verse indicates the praise and magnification of Dawud (peace be upon him), and its conclusion also indicates that, then if the intermediate part indicated vices and faults, it would be like saying: "So-and-so is of great rank, high in standing in obedience to God, who kills, commits adultery, and steals, and God has made him a successor on His earth and the arbiter of His judgments." Just as this statement is not fitting for a sensible person, so too here. And it is known that the mention of passion and the striving in killing is among the greatest sources of faults.

The fourth: that the proponents of this view mention in this narration that Dawud (peace be upon him) wished to obtain in religion the high ranks that the earlier prophets had attained, such as what the Friend (Abraham) attained through being cast into the fire, what the one who was sacrificed attained through the sacrifice, and what Ya'qub attained through hardships that bring abundant reward. So God revealed to him that they only attained those ranks because when they were tested, they endured patiently. Thereupon Dawud (peace be upon him) asked for a trial, and God revealed to him that he would be tested on such-and-such a day. He took great precautions, but then the event occurred. So we say: the beginning of their account indicates that God tests him with a trial that increases his merit and perfects the degrees of his sincerity. So striving to kill a soul without right and excessive passion, how is that fitting in this state? And it is established that the story they mention contradicts its beginning with its end.

[Page 165]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you, when they climbed over the wall into the prayer niche?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud and he was alarmed by them, they said, "Do not fear. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth, do not be unjust, and guide us to the right path." ﴾ ﴿"Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said, 'Entrust it to me,' and he overcame me in speech."﴾ ﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes. Indeed, many associates oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And Dawud thought that We had only tested him, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance.﴾ ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has nearness to Us and a good final return.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, praised him and commended him in ten respects, He followed this with the mention of a story, to show by it that the circumstances occurring in this story do not indicate anything that would make him (peace be upon him) deserving of such great praise and commendation.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you?﴾, it is similar to His saying, ﴿Has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9]. The purpose of this interrogative is to draw attention to the greatness of the story being asked about, so that it serves as a call to listen to it and to take a lesson from it. I will state three views on this story:

The first: it is mentioned in a manner that indicates that he committed a major sin.

The second: it indicates a minor sin.

The third: it does not indicate either a major or a minor sin.

As for the first view, the essence of what they say about it is that Dawud fell in love with the wife of Uriya, so he devised many schemes until he killed her husband and then married her. God then sent two angels to him in the form of litigants in a case similar to his own, and they presented that case to him. Dawud gave a judgment which necessarily implied his admission that he was guilty, and then he became aware of this and occupied himself with repentance.

What I hold and adopt is that this is false, and the following points indicate this.

The first: if this account were attributed to the most immoral and most debauched of people, he would be ashamed of it. And the vile, wicked man who narrates this story, if he were attributed with such an action, would strongly deny it and perhaps curse the one who attributes it to him. If this is so, how is it fitting for a sensible person to attribute such a thing to one who is protected from sin?

The second: the essence of the story reduces to two matters: striving to kill a Muslim man without right, and desiring his wife. As for the first, it is a reprehensible matter. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever participates in the shedding of a Muslim's blood, even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: 'Despairing of the mercy of God.'"

As for the second, it is a grave wrong. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe." Uriya was not safe from Dawud, neither in his life nor in his wife.

The third: God, exalted is He, described Dawud (peace be upon him) before the mention of this story with the ten attributes mentioned, and He also described him with many attributes after the mention of this story. All of these attributes are incompatible with his being described with this reprehensible act and this ugly deed. There is no harm in repeating these attributes for the sake of emphasis in clarification.

So we say: as for the first attributes, they are that God, exalted is He, commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to take Dawud as a model in patient endurance with hardship. If we say that Dawud did not endure restraining the self, but rather strove to shed the blood of a Muslim man for the sake of his desire, how would it be fitting for the Most Wise of the wise to command Muhammad, the best of the messengers, to take Dawud as a model in patience in obedience to God?

As for the second attribute: He described him as His servant, and we have explained that the purpose of this description is to show that the one so described is perfect in the station of servitude, complete in performing acts of obedience and in abstaining from what is forbidden. If we say that Dawud (peace be upon him) occupied himself with those false actions, then Dawud would not have been perfect in his servitude to God, exalted is He, but rather perfect in obeying his desire and lust.

The third attribute: He said ﴿the one with strength﴾, that is, the one with power. There is no doubt that what is meant by this is strength in religion, because strength in other than religion was present in the kings of the disbelievers, and there is no meaning to strength in religion except complete ability to perform obligations

صفحة ١٦٦
and to avoid what is forbidden. And what strength is there for one who does not master himself against killing and against desire for the wife of a Muslim?

The fourth attribute: that he was one who turns back frequently to God, exalted is He. How is this fitting for one whose heart is enamoured with killing and debauchery?

The fifth attribute: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him﴾. Do you think the mountains were subjected to him so that he might make them a means to killing and debauchery?

The sixth attribute: His saying, ﴿and the birds gathered﴾. It has been said that it was forbidden for him to hunt any kind of bird. How is it conceivable that the birds are safe from him, yet a Muslim man is not safe from him regarding his life and his wife?

The seventh attribute: His saying, ﴿and We strengthened his kingdom﴾. It is impossible that what is meant is that God strengthened his kingdom through worldly means. Rather, what is meant is that God strengthened his kingdom by means that strengthen religion and the causes of happiness in the Hereafter, and what is meant is the strengthening of his kingdom in religion and in the world. And one who does not master himself against killing and debauchery, how is such a thing fitting for him?

The eighth attribute: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾. Wisdom is a comprehensive term for everything that ought to be known and done. How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to say, "We gave him wisdom and decisive speech," while he persists in what the vile Satan would shrink from, namely competing with his most sincere companion over his life and his wife? Therefore, these attributes mentioned before the explanation of that story indicate the innocence of his reputation from those falsehoods.

* * *

As for the attributes mentioned after the mention of the story, they are ten:

The first: His saying, ﴿And indeed he has nearness to Us and a good final return﴾. The mention of this statement is only appropriate if the preceding story indicates his obedience to God. But if the preceding story indicated his striving in killing and debauchery, His saying ﴿indeed he has nearness to Us﴾ would not be fitting for him.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿O Dawud, We have made you a successor on the earth﴾ [Sad: 26]. This indicates the falsity of that story in several respects:

One of them: when a great king relates about one of his servants that he targeted the lives, wealth, and wives of people, and after finishing the explanation of the story before a gathering of people, it would be shameful for him to say afterward, "O servant, I have entrusted to you my caliphate and my representation." This is because the mention of such vices and reprehensible acts calls for censure and restraint, whereas appointing him as a deputy and successor for himself is absolutely not fitting.

The second: it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that mentioning a ruling immediately after a description indicates that the ruling is caused by that description. So when God related about him that disgraceful incident, and then said after it, ﴿We have made you a successor on the earth﴾, this indicates that the cause for entrusting this succession was his committing those reprehensible acts. And it is known that this is false. But if the story were mentioned in a way that indicates his innocence from sins and transgressions, and the intensity of his perseverance in obedience to God, then it would be appropriate to mention after it, ﴿We have made you a successor on the earth﴾ [Sad: 26]. Thus it is established that what we choose is more correct.

The third: since the introduction of the verse indicates the praise and magnification of Dawud (peace be upon him), and its conclusion also indicates that, then if the intermediate part indicated vices and faults, it would be like saying: "So-and-so is of great rank, high in standing in obedience to God, who kills, commits adultery, and steals, and God has made him a successor on His earth and the arbiter of His judgments." Just as this statement is not fitting for a sensible person, so too here. And it is known that the mention of passion and the striving in killing is among the greatest sources of faults.

The fourth: that the proponents of this view mention in this narration that Dawud (peace be upon him) wished to obtain in religion the high ranks that the earlier prophets had attained, such as what the Friend (Abraham) attained through being cast into the fire, what the one who was sacrificed attained through the sacrifice, and what Ya'qub attained through hardships that bring abundant reward. So God revealed to him that they only attained those ranks because when they were tested, they endured patiently. Thereupon Dawud (peace be upon him) asked for a trial, and God revealed to him that he would be tested on such-and-such a day. He took great precautions, but then the event occurred. So we say: the beginning of their account indicates that God tests him with a trial that increases his merit and perfects the degrees of his sincerity. So striving to kill a soul without right and excessive passion, how is that fitting in this state? And it is established that the story they mention contradicts its beginning with its end.

The fifth: Dawud, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And indeed many of the partners wrong one another, except those who believe﴾. He excepted those who believe from wronging. So if we said that he was described with wronging, it would follow that he had passed judgment against himself regarding lack of faith, and that is false.

The sixth: I attended some gatherings in which one of the great kings was present, and he wished to be zealous in establishing that corrupt saying and that wicked story for a reason that required it. So I said to him: There is no doubt that Dawud, peace be upon him, was among the greatest of the prophets and messengers, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Whoever Allah the Exalted has praised with such great praise, it is not permissible for us to exaggerate in criticizing him. Furthermore, even if he was not a prophet, there is no doubt that he was a Muslim, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not mention your dead except with good." Then, even if we pay no attention to any of these proofs, we say that it is known by necessity that, supposing the story you have mentioned were true and correct, its narration and mention would bring no reward whatsoever, for if spreading indecency does not necessitate punishment, then at least it does not necessitate reward. As for supposing this story is false and corrupt, then the one who mentions it deserves the greatest punishment, and an event of this nature and description, sound reason requires silence about it. Thus it is established that the truth is what we have adopted, and that explaining that story is forbidden and prohibited. When that king heard this speech, he fell silent and mentioned nothing.

The seventh: The mention of this story and the mention of the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, entail the spreading of indecency, so it must be forbidden, because of His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 19].

The eighth: If Dawud had striven to kill that man, he would have fallen under his saying: "Whoever strives toward the blood of a Muslim, even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: despairing of the mercy of Allah." Moreover, if he had done that, he would have been a wrongdoer, and so he would have fallen under His saying: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18].

The ninth: From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever narrates to you the story of Dawud as the storytellers relate it, I will flog him a hundred and sixty times," and that is the punishment for slander against the prophets. Something that strengthens this is that when they claimed that al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba had committed adultery, and three of the upright Companions testified to that, while the fourth did not say, "I saw that act." Meaning: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab denied those three and flogged each one of them eighty lashes because they had slandered. If this is the situation with one of the ordinary Companions, then how much more so with Dawud, peace be upon him, although he is among the greatest of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The tenth: It is related that some people mentioned this story as it is in the Book of Allah the Exalted, and said: it is not proper to add to it, even if the event was as it has been described. Then He the Exalted did not mention it except to conceal that event concerning Dawud, peace be upon him, so it is not permissible for a sensible person to strive to tear that veil after a thousand years or less or more. Then 'Umar said: "My hearing this statement is dearer to me than what the sun has risen upon."

Thus it is established, by these aspects we have mentioned, that the story they related is corrupt and false. If someone says: Many of the great narrators and exegetes have mentioned this story, so what is the situation regarding it? The true answer is that when there is a conflict between decisive proofs and a single report from the solitary reports, returning to the decisive proofs is more appropriate. Also, the original state is the absence of liability. Also, when the evidence of prohibition and permission conflicts, the side of prohibition is preferable. Also, the way of caution requires preferring our view. Also, we know by necessity that, supposing this event occurred, Allah will not say to us on the Day of Resurrection: why did you not strive to publicize this event? As for supposing it is false, then in mentioning it we would bear the greatest punishment. Also, he, peace be upon him, said: "When you know something like the sun, then testify." Here, neither knowledge nor probable opinion has arisen concerning the soundness of this account, rather the overpowering proofs we have mentioned stand, so it is necessary that testimony by it not be permitted. Also, all the exegetes have not agreed upon this view; rather the majority of the discerning and the verifying among them reject it and judge it to be lying and corrupt. Also, if the statements of the exegetes and the narrators conflict regarding it, they cancel each other out, and what remains is returning to the proofs we have mentioned. This is the complete discussion concerning this story.

As for the second possibility: that this story be understood in a way that entails a minor sin but does not entail a major sin, we say that regarding how this story is to be understood on this supposition there are several aspects:

The first: that this woman was proposed to by Uriya, and they accepted him, then Dawud proposed to her and her family preferred him. So his fault was that he proposed upon the proposal of his believing brother, despite the multitude of his wives.

The second: they said that his gaze fell upon her and his heart inclined toward her, and there is absolutely no sin for him in this. As for his gaze falling upon her without intention, that is not a sin, and as for the inclination arising after the glance, that too is not a sin, because this inclination is not within his capacity, so he is not held accountable for it. Rather, when it happened that her husband was killed, he was not greatly distressed by his killing, because he hoped to marry that woman; so the slip occurred due to this matter, namely that the killing of that man did not trouble him.

The third: that the people of Dawud's time used to ask one another to divorce their wives so that they could marry them, and their custom in this matter was familiar and well known; or that the Ansar used to equal the Muhajirun in this matter. It happened that Dawud's eye fell upon that woman and he loved her, so he asked him to relinquish her, and he was ashamed to refuse him, so he did it, and she was the mother of Sulayman. It was said to him: this, although it is permissible in the outward Shari'a, does not befit you, for the good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near. These are three aspects; if we understood this story according to any one of them, nothing would be attributed to Dawud, peace be upon him, except leaving what is better and more fitting.

* * *

As for the third possibility: that this story is in a way that does not necessitate attributing a major or minor sin to Dawud, peace be upon him, but rather entails attributing to him the greatest kind of praise and commendation. It is that we say: it is related that a group of enemies coveted killing the Prophet of Allah Dawud, peace be upon him, and he had a day in which he was alone with himself and occupied with obedience to his Lord. They seized the opportunity on that day and scaled the mihrab. When they entered upon him, they found with him people who prevented them from him, so they feared, and they fabricated a lie, saying: "Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other," up to the end of the story. There is nothing in the wording of the Qur'an that could be used as an argument to attribute sin to Dawud except four words:

One of them: His saying: ﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tried him﴾.

The second: His saying the Exalted: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾.

The third: His saying: ﴿and turned in repentance﴾.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾. Then we say: none of these words indicates what they have claimed, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: When they entered upon him to seek his killing by this means, and Dawud, peace be upon him, knew that, anger urged him to occupy himself with taking revenge upon them. However, he inclined toward pardon and overlooking them, seeking the pleasure of Allah. He said: this incident was the trial, because it runs in the manner of a test and examination. Then he sought forgiveness from his Lord for what he had intended of retaliation against them, and repented of that concern and turned in repentance, so He forgave him that measure of concern and resolve.

The second: that although it prevailed upon his assumption that they had entered upon him to kill him, he regretted that assumption and said: since no proof or sign has established that the matter is so, how evil is what you knew of them, in that you assumed this bad assumption about them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tried him, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord and fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾, from him, so Allah forgave him that.

The third: that their entering upon him was a trial for Dawud, peace be upon him, yet he, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness for that intruder who was resolved to kill him, just as He said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad: 19]. So Dawud, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness for them and turned in repentance, meaning he returned to Allah the Exalted seeking the forgiveness of that intruder who intended to kill. His saying: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ means: We forgave him that sin for the sake of honoring Dawud and exalting him, just as some exegetes said regarding His saying the Exalted: ﴿That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin﴾ [al-Fath: 2], that its meaning is that Allah the Exalted forgives you, and for your sake, what preceded of the sin of your community.

The fourth: Suppose Dawud, peace be upon him, repented of a slip that issued from him; yet we do not grant that this slip occurred because of the woman. Why is it not permissible to say that this slip only occurred because he judged for one of the two adversaries before hearing the words of the second adversary? For when he said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes﴾, he ruled against him as a wrongdoer merely on the claim of the adversary without evidence, and that judgment was contrary to what is right. At this point he occupied himself with seeking forgiveness and repentance. However, this falls under leaving what is better and more fitting. Thus it is established by these clarifications that if we take these verses in this way, it does not necessitate attributing any sin to Dawud, peace be upon him, but rather it entails attributing to him the greatest acts of obedience. Then we say: taking the verse this way is more appropriate for several reasons.

The first: that the original state of a Muslim is distance from prohibited things, especially since he is a man among the greatest of the prophets and messengers.

The second: that it is more cautious.

The third: that He the Exalted said at the beginning of the verse to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud﴾. When the people of Muhammad, peace be upon him, displayed foolishness by saying: ﴿This is a lying sorcerer﴾, and mocked him by saying: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning﴾, He the Exalted said at the beginning of the verse: O Muhammad, be patient over their foolishness, endure, show forbearance, do not display anger, and remember Our servant Dawud. This remembrance is only fitting if Dawud, peace be upon him, had been patient in the face of their harm, had endured their foolishness, had shown forbearance, and had not displayed haste and anger. This meaning is only attained if we take the verse as we have explained, whereas if we take it as they say, the speech becomes contradictory and corrupt.

The fourth: that this narration only holds if we say the two adversaries were two angels; and since they were of the angels, and there was no litigation between them and neither wronged the other, their saying "two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other" would be a lie. This narration cannot be sustained except by two things:

One of them: attributing a lie to the angels.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 24–25 (part 2 of 3):

The second possibility is to seek a way out by attributing the lie to the angels, or attributing the most shameful of vices to a great man among the prophets. But if we take the verse in the sense we have mentioned, we are spared both attributing a lie to the angels and attributing an ugly act to the prophets. So our view is the better one. This is what we have on this subject, and God knows best the secrets of His speech. Now we return to the explanation of the verses.

As for His saying, ﴿And has the news of the litigants reached you?﴾ al-Wahidi said: "Khasm" is a verbal noun from "khasamtuhu, akhsimuhu, khaṣman." It is then used for two persons and for a group, and it is not made dual or plural. One says, "They two are a khasm," and "they (plural) are a khasm," just as one says, "they two are ʿadl" and "they are ʿadl." The meaning is "possessors of a dispute" (dhawā khaṣm) and "possessors of disputes" (dhawū khaṣm). By "al-khasm" here is meant the two persons who entered upon David, peace be upon him.

His saying, ﴿when they climbed over the wall into the prayer chamber﴾: one says, "tasawwartu al-sūr tasawwuran" when one climbs over the wall. The meaning of ﴿they climbed over the wall into the prayer chamber﴾ is that they came to it over its wall, which is its upper part. One says, "tasawwara fulān al-dār" when he comes to the house through its wall. As for al-miḥrāb, it means the room in which David would enter and occupy himself with obedience to his Lord. That room was called al-miḥrāb because it contained a miḥrāb, just as a thing is named after its most noble part.

Here there is a question from the science of legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh): some people hold that the minimum of the plural is two. Those who hold this have relied on this verse, because God has used the plural form in these verses in four places:

The first is His saying, ﴿when they climbed over the wall into the prayer chamber﴾.
The second is His saying, ﴿when they entered upon﴾.
The third is His saying, ﴿from them﴾.
The fourth is His saying, ﴿They said, "Fear not"﴾.

All these four words are plural forms, while they were two, as shown by their saying, "two litigants (khaṣmān)." They said: this verse indicates that the minimum of the plural is two.

The answer: there is nothing to prevent each of the two litigants from being a plural, a group of many persons, because we have shown that when khasm is used as a noun it is neither made dual nor plural. Then He said, ﴿when they entered upon David﴾. The benefit of this is that they might have climbed over the wall without entering upon him. So when He said, ﴿when they entered upon﴾, it shows that after climbing over they entered upon him. Al-Farra' said: "idh" may be used twice, and its two occurrences are taken as one, as when you say, "I struck you when you entered upon me when you dared," even though the time of entering and the time of daring are one.

Then He said, ﴿he was frightened of them﴾. The reason is that when David saw them entering upon him not by the usual way, he knew that they had entered upon him for evil, so he was indeed frightened of them.

Then He said, ﴿They said, "Fear not. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other."﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: "khaṣmān" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "we are two litigants."

The second issue: here there are two opinions.

The first: they were two angels who descended from heaven, and they intended to alert David, peace be upon him, to the ugliness of the act he had undertaken.

The second: they were two humans who entered upon him for evil and killing. They thought they would find him alone, but when they saw a group of servants with him, they fabricated that falsehood to ward off the evil.

As for those who deny that they were two angels, they argued against this view that if they were two angels, they would be lying in their saying "two litigants," since there is no litigation among angels; and they would be lying in their saying, "one of whom has wronged the other"; and they would be lying in their saying, ﴿This is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes﴾. Thus it is established that if they were two angels they would be liars, and lying about an angel is not permissible, because of His saying, ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiya᾽: 27], and His saying, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. Those who hold the first view answered this argument by saying: the two angels mentioned this statement by way of illustration, not as an actual assertion, so no lying was involved. This answer is refuted: what you have mentioned requires departing from the apparent meaning of the wording, and it is well known that this goes against the principle.

As for taking the speech to mean that the two litigants were two men who entered upon him for the purpose of evil and then fabricated this false story, then it follows that the lie is attributed to two wicked persons, and this is better than the first view. God knows best.

As for those who hold that they were two angels, they argued with several points:

The first: the agreement of most of the exegetes upon it.

The second: he is too exalted in rank for ordinary subjects to climb over the wall upon him while he was in worship, so it must have been angels who did so.

The third: His saying, ﴿They said, "Fear not"﴾ is like an indication that they were two angels, because one of his subjects would hardly say such a thing to him given his high rank.

The fourth: their saying, ﴿and do not deviate﴾ is like an indication that they were two angels, because none of his subjects would dare to say to him, "Do not wrong, and do not go beyond the truth." You should know that the weakness of these proofs is evident, and there is no need to answer them. God knows best.

* * *

The third issue: ﴿one of whom has wronged the other﴾ means: transgressed and went beyond the limit. One says, "baghā al-jurḥ" when the pain of the wound intensifies and reaches its extreme. And one says, "baghat al-mar'ah" when a woman commits adultery, because fornication is a grave and abominable sin. He said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. Then He said, ﴿So judge between us with truth﴾. The meaning of judgment (ḥukm) is establishing the matter by carrying out God's obligation upon the two of them in this incident. From this comes "ḥikmah" for a beast, because it is restrained from bolting; and from it comes "a firm building (bināʾ muḥkam)" when it is strong. His saying, ﴿with truth﴾ means with the true judgment, which is the one God has decreed. ﴿And do not deviate﴾: one says, "shaṭṭa al-rajul" when he went far away, and from it comes the saying, "shaṭṭat al-dār" when the house became distant. He said: ﴿We would have uttered an outrageous lie﴾ [al-Kahf: 14], meaning a statement far from the truth. So His saying, ﴿and do not deviate﴾ means: do not go far from the truth in this judgment. Then He said, ﴿And guide us to the even path﴾, and "sawāʾ al-ṣirāṭ" is its middle. He said: ﴿So he looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55]. The middle of a thing is its best and most just part. He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

I say: they expressed a single intended meaning in three expressions:

The first is their saying, "judge with truth."
The second is their saying, "and do not deviate," which is a prohibition against falsehood.
The third is their saying, "and guide us to the even path," meaning: your effort must be directed toward establishing this truth, and in avoiding this falsehood, to turn us from the false path to the true path. This is a complete emphasis in establishing what is sought.

You should know that when they had informed him of the occurrence of the dispute in a general way, they followed it with an explanation of the cause of that dispute in detail, and they said: ﴿This is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "akhī" is either an appositive to "hādhā" or a predicate of "inna." The intended meaning is brotherhood of religion, or brotherhood of friendship and affection, or brotherhood of partnership and association, because of His saying, ﴿And indeed many partners wrong one another﴾ [Sad: 24]. Each of these kinds of brotherhood requires abstaining from injustice and transgression.

The second issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said that it was read "tis'un wa-tis'ūna" with a fatḥah on the tā᾽, and "niʿjatan" with a kasrah on the nūn. This is among the differences of dialects, like "naṭʿ" and "niṭʿ," and "laqwah" and "liqwah," which means the female of the eagles.

The third issue: al-Layth said: "al-naʿjah" is the female of the sheep, the wild cow, and the mountain goat; its plural is "naʿajāt." The Arabs have a custom of making "al-naʿjah" and "al-ẓabyah" a metaphor for a woman.

The fourth issue: ʿAbdullah read: "tis'un wa-tis'ūna naʿjatan unthā," and this is for emphasis, like His saying, ﴿And God said, "Do not take two gods; He is only one God"﴾ [al-Nahl: 51]. Then He said: ﴿Give her to me, and he overpowered me in speech.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "akfilnīhā" literally means "make me its guardian, as I guard what is under my hand." ﴿And he overpowered me﴾ means he defeated me. One says, "ʿazzahu yaʿizzuhu," and the meaning is: he came to me with an argument I could not counter with what he had brought against me. It was also read "waʿāzanī" from al-muʿāzah, which is contention by overpowering.

You should know that those who said these two litigants were angels thought that the purpose of mentioning the ewes was an illustration, because David had under him ninety-nine wives, while Uriah had only one wife. So the angels mentioned that incident by way of symbol and illustration.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe to add to his ewes."﴾ That is, by asking to add your ewe to his ewes. It is narrated that he said to him: "If you insist on that, we will strike from you this and this," and he pointed to the nose and the forehead. Then he said: "O David, you are more deserving that we strike from you this and this, and you did such and such." Then David looked and saw no one, and he understood the situation.

If it is asked: how was it permissible for David to rule against one of the two litigants merely on the word of his opponent? We say: they mentioned several answers:

The first: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: when the first litigant finished his speech, David looked at the other litigant, who had not spoken, and said, "If he is truthful, you have certainly wronged him." The point is that this judgment was conditional upon the condition that the claimant was truthful in his claim.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: when one of the two litigants made a claim, the second acknowledged it, so David ruled against him. God did not mention that acknowledgment, because the apparent meaning of the speech indicates it, just as you say, "I commanded you to trade, so you earned," meaning you traded and so you earned. And He said: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara᾽: 63], meaning he struck it and it parted.

The third: the meaning is that the litigant whose situation is this has certainly wronged you.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And indeed many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they.﴾ Al-Layth said: "khalīl al-rajul" is his associate. al-Zajjaj said: "al-khulaṭā᾽" are the partners. If it is asked: why did David specify the partners as those who wrong one another, when non-partners also do so? The answer: there is no doubt that association causes much contention and dispute, because when two persons are closely associated, each of them comes to know the circumstances of the other. So whatever precious thing one of them owns, when the other sees it, his desire for it becomes great, and this leads to increased dispute and contention. For this reason, David, peace be upon him, specified the partners with increased transgression and aggression. Then He excepted from this ruling those who believe and do righteous deeds, because the association of these people occurs only for the sake of religion and the pursuit of true spiritual felicity, so their association does not cause contention. But those whose association is for love of worldly things, their association will inevitably become a cause of increased transgression and aggression.

You should know that this exception indicates that those who believe and do righteous deeds do not wrong one another. So if David had transgressed and overstepped against that man, then by the verdict of David it would follow that he was not among those who believe and do righteous deeds. It is well known that this is false. Thus it is established that the view of one who says that the subject of the ewe incident is the story of David is false.

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And few are they﴾. Know that the judgment that the people of good are few is frequent in the Qur'an. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13]. Dawud, peace be upon him, said in this same context: ﴿And few are they﴾. God, Exalted is He, related of Iblis that he said: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 17]. The reason for the fewness is that the impulses toward this world are numerous: they are the inner and outer senses, which are ten, along with desire and anger, and the seven natural powers. The total is nineteen, standing at the gate of Hell, which is the body, and all of them call toward creation, this world, and sensual pleasure. As for the caller to the truth and religion, it is none other than the intellect. The dominance of the sensory and natural powers over people is greater than the intellectual power in them. For this reason, fewness occurred on the side of the people of good and abundance on the side of the people of evil. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the "ma" in His saying ﴿And few are they﴾ is for vagueness (ibham), and it carries an expression of wonder at their fewness. He said: if you want to verify its benefit and its place, remove it from the line of Imru' al-Qays: "And a night, for all its shortness—see whether it ever retains any meaning at all."

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And David thought that We had tested him﴾. They said its meaning is: David knew that We had tested him, i.e., examined him. They said: the reason that required interpreting the word "thought" (zann) as "knowledge" (ʿilm) here is that when David, peace be upon him, judged between the two, one of them looked at his companion and laughed, then ascended to the sky, facing him. David knew that God had tried him with this. Thus it is established that David knew it. The interpretation of the word "thought" as "knowledge" is permissible because inferential knowledge (al-ʿilm al-istidlali) resembles thought to a great degree, and resemblance is a cause for the permissibility of metaphor (majaz). I say: this statement applies only if we say the two litigants were angels. If we do not say that, we are not obliged to interpret "thought" as "knowledge." Rather, one may say that when the supposition of being tested by God predominated over his thought, he occupied himself with seeking forgiveness and turning in repentance.

As for His saying ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾: that is, he asked his Lord for forgiveness. Here there are two views:

If we say that a lapse had proceeded from him, we interpret this seeking of forgiveness as referring to it. If we do not say so, there are several views.

The first: when the people entered upon him intending to kill him, and he was a ruler of great might and powerful strength, then, despite his great capacity for retaliation and despite the fear arising in his heart, he pardoned them and said nothing to them. It was close to the matter entering his heart with some self-admiration, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord for that state and turned in repentance to God, acknowledging that his undertaking of that good was only by God's grace. So God forgave him and overlooked it because of the occurrence of that passing thought.

The second: perhaps he intended to harm the people, then he said: no decisive proof had established that these people intended evil, so he pardoned them, then he sought forgiveness for that intention.

The third: perhaps the people repented to God and asked him to seek forgiveness from God on their behalf so that He would accept their repentance. So he sought forgiveness and humbled himself before God, and God forgave their sins because of his intercession and supplication. All these views are plausible and apparent, and the Qur'an is full of the like of these views. When the wording admits what we have mentioned, and no definitive or probable proof has established the commission of the abhorrent acts they mention, then what compels us to adopt them and to affirm them? What confirms that what we have mentioned is closer and stronger is that God concluded this story with His saying: ﴿And indeed for him with Us is nearness and a good return﴾. Such a conclusion is fitting only for one from whom much work in service and obedience has proceeded, and who has borne various kinds of hardships in compliance and submission. As for when the preceding mention is the committing of a transgression and sin, such a conclusion does not befit him. Malik ibn Dinar said: on the Day of Resurrection, a high pulpit will be brought and placed in Paradise, and it will be said: "O David, glorify Me with that beautiful, melodious voice with which you used to glorify Me in the world." And God knows best.

Several discussions remain here:

The first: it was read as "fatanahu" and "fattanahu," with the alif being a pronoun for the two angels.

The second: it is well known that the seeking of forgiveness was because of the story of the ewe and the ewes. It was also said that it was because he ruled for one of the two litigants before hearing the words of the second, and that is impermissible.

The third: His saying ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ indicates that bowing occurred. As for prostration, it is established by reports, and likewise intense weeping for a period of forty days is established by reports.

The fourth: the position of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, is that there is no prostration of recitation in this place. He said: because it is the repentance of a prophet, so it does not require a prostration of recitation.

The fifth: Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, cited this verse regarding the prostration of recitation to show that bowing takes the place of prostration.

The fifth: Dawud, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And indeed many of the partners wrong one another, except those who believe﴾. He excepted those who believe from wronging. So if we said that he was described with wronging, it would follow that he had passed judgment against himself regarding lack of faith, and that is false.

The sixth: I attended some gatherings in which one of the great kings was present, and he wished to be zealous in establishing that corrupt saying and that wicked story for a reason that required it. So I said to him: There is no doubt that Dawud, peace be upon him, was among the greatest of the prophets and messengers, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Whoever Allah the Exalted has praised with such great praise, it is not permissible for us to exaggerate in criticizing him. Furthermore, even if he was not a prophet, there is no doubt that he was a Muslim, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not mention your dead except with good." Then, even if we pay no attention to any of these proofs, we say that it is known by necessity that, supposing the story you have mentioned were true and correct, its narration and mention would bring no reward whatsoever, for if spreading indecency does not necessitate punishment, then at least it does not necessitate reward. As for supposing this story is false and corrupt, then the one who mentions it deserves the greatest punishment, and an event of this nature and description, sound reason requires silence about it. Thus it is established that the truth is what we have adopted, and that explaining that story is forbidden and prohibited. When that king heard this speech, he fell silent and mentioned nothing.

The seventh: The mention of this story and the mention of the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, entail the spreading of indecency, so it must be forbidden, because of His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 19].

The eighth: If Dawud had striven to kill that man, he would have fallen under his saying: "Whoever strives toward the blood of a Muslim, even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: despairing of the mercy of Allah." Moreover, if he had done that, he would have been a wrongdoer, and so he would have fallen under His saying: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18].

The ninth: From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever narrates to you the story of Dawud as the storytellers relate it, I will flog him a hundred and sixty times," and that is the punishment for slander against the prophets. Something that strengthens this is that when they claimed that al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba had committed adultery, and three of the upright Companions testified to that, while the fourth did not say, "I saw that act." Meaning: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab denied those three and flogged each one of them eighty lashes because they had slandered. If this is the situation with one of the ordinary Companions, then how much more so with Dawud, peace be upon him, although he is among the greatest of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The tenth: It is related that some people mentioned this story as it is in the Book of Allah the Exalted, and said: it is not proper to add to it, even if the event was as it has been described. Then He the Exalted did not mention it except to conceal that event concerning Dawud, peace be upon him, so it is not permissible for a sensible person to strive to tear that veil after a thousand years or less or more. Then 'Umar said: "My hearing this statement is dearer to me than what the sun has risen upon."

Thus it is established, by these aspects we have mentioned, that the story they related is corrupt and false. If someone says: Many of the great narrators and exegetes have mentioned this story, so what is the situation regarding it? The true answer is that when there is a conflict between decisive proofs and a single report from the solitary reports, returning to the decisive proofs is more appropriate. Also, the original state is the absence of liability. Also, when the evidence of prohibition and permission conflicts, the side of prohibition is preferable. Also, the way of caution requires preferring our view. Also, we know by necessity that, supposing this event occurred, Allah will not say to us on the Day of Resurrection: why did you not strive to publicize this event? As for supposing it is false, then in mentioning it we would bear the greatest punishment. Also, he, peace be upon him, said: "When you know something like the sun, then testify." Here, neither knowledge nor probable opinion has arisen concerning the soundness of this account, rather the overpowering proofs we have mentioned stand, so it is necessary that testimony by it not be permitted. Also, all the exegetes have not agreed upon this view; rather the majority of the discerning and the verifying among them reject it and judge it to be lying and corrupt. Also, if the statements of the exegetes and the narrators conflict regarding it, they cancel each other out, and what remains is returning to the proofs we have mentioned. This is the complete discussion concerning this story.

As for the second possibility: that this story be understood in a way that entails a minor sin but does not entail a major sin, we say that regarding how this story is to be understood on this supposition there are several aspects:

The first: that this woman was proposed to by Uriya, and they accepted him, then Dawud proposed to her and her family preferred him. So his fault was that he proposed upon the proposal of his believing brother, despite the multitude of his wives.

The second: they said that his gaze fell upon her and his heart inclined toward her, and there is absolutely no sin for him in this. As for his gaze falling upon her without intention, that is not a sin, and as for the inclination arising after the glance, that too is not a sin, because this inclination is not within his capacity, so he is not held accountable for it. Rather, when it happened that her husband was killed, he was not greatly distressed by his killing, because he hoped to marry that woman; so the slip occurred due to this matter, namely that the killing of that man did not trouble him.

The third: that the people of Dawud's time used to ask one another to divorce their wives so that they could marry them, and their custom in this matter was familiar and well known; or that the Ansar used to equal the Muhajirun in this matter. It happened that Dawud's eye fell upon that woman and he loved her, so he asked him to relinquish her, and he was ashamed to refuse him, so he did it, and she was the mother of Sulayman. It was said to him: this, although it is permissible in the outward Shari'a, does not befit you, for the good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near. These are three aspects; if we understood this story according to any one of them, nothing would be attributed to Dawud, peace be upon him, except leaving what is better and more fitting.

* * *

As for the third possibility: that this story is in a way that does not necessitate attributing a major or minor sin to Dawud, peace be upon him, but rather entails attributing to him the greatest kind of praise and commendation. It is that we say: it is related that a group of enemies coveted killing the Prophet of Allah Dawud, peace be upon him, and he had a day in which he was alone with himself and occupied with obedience to his Lord. They seized the opportunity on that day and scaled the mihrab. When they entered upon him, they found with him people who prevented them from him, so they feared, and they fabricated a lie, saying: "Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other," up to the end of the story. There is nothing in the wording of the Qur'an that could be used as an argument to attribute sin to Dawud except four words:

One of them: His saying: ﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tried him﴾.

The second: His saying the Exalted: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾.

The third: His saying: ﴿and turned in repentance﴾.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾. Then we say: none of these words indicates what they have claimed, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: When they entered upon him to seek his killing by this means, and Dawud, peace be upon him, knew that, anger urged him to occupy himself with taking revenge upon them. However, he inclined toward pardon and overlooking them, seeking the pleasure of Allah. He said: this incident was the trial, because it runs in the manner of a test and examination. Then he sought forgiveness from his Lord for what he had intended of retaliation against them, and repented of that concern and turned in repentance, so He forgave him that measure of concern and resolve.

The second: that although it prevailed upon his assumption that they had entered upon him to kill him, he regretted that assumption and said: since no proof or sign has established that the matter is so, how evil is what you knew of them, in that you assumed this bad assumption about them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tried him, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord and fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾, from him, so Allah forgave him that.

The third: that their entering upon him was a trial for Dawud, peace be upon him, yet he, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness for that intruder who was resolved to kill him, just as He said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad: 19]. So Dawud, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness for them and turned in repentance, meaning he returned to Allah the Exalted seeking the forgiveness of that intruder who intended to kill. His saying: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ means: We forgave him that sin for the sake of honoring Dawud and exalting him, just as some exegetes said regarding His saying the Exalted: ﴿That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin﴾ [al-Fath: 2], that its meaning is that Allah the Exalted forgives you, and for your sake, what preceded of the sin of your community.

The fourth: Suppose Dawud, peace be upon him, repented of a slip that issued from him; yet we do not grant that this slip occurred because of the woman. Why is it not permissible to say that this slip only occurred because he judged for one of the two adversaries before hearing the words of the second adversary? For when he said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes﴾, he ruled against him as a wrongdoer merely on the claim of the adversary without evidence, and that judgment was contrary to what is right. At this point he occupied himself with seeking forgiveness and repentance. However, this falls under leaving what is better and more fitting. Thus it is established by these clarifications that if we take these verses in this way, it does not necessitate attributing any sin to Dawud, peace be upon him, but rather it entails attributing to him the greatest acts of obedience. Then we say: taking the verse this way is more appropriate for several reasons.

The first: that the original state of a Muslim is distance from prohibited things, especially since he is a man among the greatest of the prophets and messengers.

The second: that it is more cautious.

The third: that He the Exalted said at the beginning of the verse to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud﴾. When the people of Muhammad, peace be upon him, displayed foolishness by saying: ﴿This is a lying sorcerer﴾, and mocked him by saying: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning﴾, He the Exalted said at the beginning of the verse: O Muhammad, be patient over their foolishness, endure, show forbearance, do not display anger, and remember Our servant Dawud. This remembrance is only fitting if Dawud, peace be upon him, had been patient in the face of their harm, had endured their foolishness, had shown forbearance, and had not displayed haste and anger. This meaning is only attained if we take the verse as we have explained, whereas if we take it as they say, the speech becomes contradictory and corrupt.
