The fourth: that this narration only holds if we say the two adversaries were two angels; and since they were of the angels, and there was no litigation between them and neither wronged the other, their saying "two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other" would be a lie. This narration cannot be sustained except by two things:

One of them: attributing a lie to the angels.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 24–25 (part 2 of 3):

The second possibility is to seek a way out by attributing the lie to the angels, or attributing the most shameful of vices to a great man among the prophets. But if we take the verse in the sense we have mentioned, we are spared both attributing a lie to the angels and attributing an ugly act to the prophets. So our view is the better one. This is what we have on this subject, and God knows best the secrets of His speech. Now we return to the explanation of the verses.

As for His saying, ﴿And has the news of the litigants reached you?﴾ al-Wahidi said: "Khasm" is a verbal noun from "khasamtuhu, akhsimuhu, khaṣman." It is then used for two persons and for a group, and it is not made dual or plural. One says, "They two are a khasm," and "they (plural) are a khasm," just as one says, "they two are ʿadl" and "they are ʿadl." The meaning is "possessors of a dispute" (dhawā khaṣm) and "possessors of disputes" (dhawū khaṣm). By "al-khasm" here is meant the two persons who entered upon David, peace be upon him.

His saying, ﴿when they climbed over the wall into the prayer chamber﴾: one says, "tasawwartu al-sūr tasawwuran" when one climbs over the wall. The meaning of ﴿they climbed over the wall into the prayer chamber﴾ is that they came to it over its wall, which is its upper part. One says, "tasawwara fulān al-dār" when he comes to the house through its wall. As for al-miḥrāb, it means the room in which David would enter and occupy himself with obedience to his Lord. That room was called al-miḥrāb because it contained a miḥrāb, just as a thing is named after its most noble part.

Here there is a question from the science of legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh): some people hold that the minimum of the plural is two. Those who hold this have relied on this verse, because God has used the plural form in these verses in four places:

The first is His saying, ﴿when they climbed over the wall into the prayer chamber﴾.
The second is His saying, ﴿when they entered upon﴾.
The third is His saying, ﴿from them﴾.
The fourth is His saying, ﴿They said, "Fear not"﴾.

All these four words are plural forms, while they were two, as shown by their saying, "two litigants (khaṣmān)." They said: this verse indicates that the minimum of the plural is two.

The answer: there is nothing to prevent each of the two litigants from being a plural, a group of many persons, because we have shown that when khasm is used as a noun it is neither made dual nor plural. Then He said, ﴿when they entered upon David﴾. The benefit of this is that they might have climbed over the wall without entering upon him. So when He said, ﴿when they entered upon﴾, it shows that after climbing over they entered upon him. Al-Farra' said: "idh" may be used twice, and its two occurrences are taken as one, as when you say, "I struck you when you entered upon me when you dared," even though the time of entering and the time of daring are one.

Then He said, ﴿he was frightened of them﴾. The reason is that when David saw them entering upon him not by the usual way, he knew that they had entered upon him for evil, so he was indeed frightened of them.

Then He said, ﴿They said, "Fear not. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other."﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: "khaṣmān" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "we are two litigants."

The second issue: here there are two opinions.

The first: they were two angels who descended from heaven, and they intended to alert David, peace be upon him, to the ugliness of the act he had undertaken.

The second: they were two humans who entered upon him for evil and killing. They thought they would find him alone, but when they saw a group of servants with him, they fabricated that falsehood to ward off the evil.

As for those who deny that they were two angels, they argued against this view that if they were two angels, they would be lying in their saying "two litigants," since there is no litigation among angels; and they would be lying in their saying, "one of whom has wronged the other"; and they would be lying in their saying, ﴿This is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes﴾. Thus it is established that if they were two angels they would be liars, and lying about an angel is not permissible, because of His saying, ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiya᾽: 27], and His saying, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. Those who hold the first view answered this argument by saying: the two angels mentioned this statement by way of illustration, not as an actual assertion, so no lying was involved. This answer is refuted: what you have mentioned requires departing from the apparent meaning of the wording, and it is well known that this goes against the principle.

As for taking the speech to mean that the two litigants were two men who entered upon him for the purpose of evil and then fabricated this false story, then it follows that the lie is attributed to two wicked persons, and this is better than the first view. God knows best.

As for those who hold that they were two angels, they argued with several points:

The first: the agreement of most of the exegetes upon it.

The second: he is too exalted in rank for ordinary subjects to climb over the wall upon him while he was in worship, so it must have been angels who did so.

The third: His saying, ﴿They said, "Fear not"﴾ is like an indication that they were two angels, because one of his subjects would hardly say such a thing to him given his high rank.

The fourth: their saying, ﴿and do not deviate﴾ is like an indication that they were two angels, because none of his subjects would dare to say to him, "Do not wrong, and do not go beyond the truth." You should know that the weakness of these proofs is evident, and there is no need to answer them. God knows best.

* * *

The third issue: ﴿one of whom has wronged the other﴾ means: transgressed and went beyond the limit. One says, "baghā al-jurḥ" when the pain of the wound intensifies and reaches its extreme. And one says, "baghat al-mar'ah" when a woman commits adultery, because fornication is a grave and abominable sin. He said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. Then He said, ﴿So judge between us with truth﴾. The meaning of judgment (ḥukm) is establishing the matter by carrying out God's obligation upon the two of them in this incident. From this comes "ḥikmah" for a beast, because it is restrained from bolting; and from it comes "a firm building (bināʾ muḥkam)" when it is strong. His saying, ﴿with truth﴾ means with the true judgment, which is the one God has decreed. ﴿And do not deviate﴾: one says, "shaṭṭa al-rajul" when he went far away, and from it comes the saying, "shaṭṭat al-dār" when the house became distant. He said: ﴿We would have uttered an outrageous lie﴾ [al-Kahf: 14], meaning a statement far from the truth. So His saying, ﴿and do not deviate﴾ means: do not go far from the truth in this judgment. Then He said, ﴿And guide us to the even path﴾, and "sawāʾ al-ṣirāṭ" is its middle. He said: ﴿So he looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55]. The middle of a thing is its best and most just part. He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

I say: they expressed a single intended meaning in three expressions:

The first is their saying, "judge with truth."
The second is their saying, "and do not deviate," which is a prohibition against falsehood.
The third is their saying, "and guide us to the even path," meaning: your effort must be directed toward establishing this truth, and in avoiding this falsehood, to turn us from the false path to the true path. This is a complete emphasis in establishing what is sought.

You should know that when they had informed him of the occurrence of the dispute in a general way, they followed it with an explanation of the cause of that dispute in detail, and they said: ﴿This is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "akhī" is either an appositive to "hādhā" or a predicate of "inna." The intended meaning is brotherhood of religion, or brotherhood of friendship and affection, or brotherhood of partnership and association, because of His saying, ﴿And indeed many partners wrong one another﴾ [Sad: 24]. Each of these kinds of brotherhood requires abstaining from injustice and transgression.

The second issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said that it was read "tis'un wa-tis'ūna" with a fatḥah on the tā᾽, and "niʿjatan" with a kasrah on the nūn. This is among the differences of dialects, like "naṭʿ" and "niṭʿ," and "laqwah" and "liqwah," which means the female of the eagles.

The third issue: al-Layth said: "al-naʿjah" is the female of the sheep, the wild cow, and the mountain goat; its plural is "naʿajāt." The Arabs have a custom of making "al-naʿjah" and "al-ẓabyah" a metaphor for a woman.

The fourth issue: ʿAbdullah read: "tis'un wa-tis'ūna naʿjatan unthā," and this is for emphasis, like His saying, ﴿And God said, "Do not take two gods; He is only one God"﴾ [al-Nahl: 51]. Then He said: ﴿Give her to me, and he overpowered me in speech.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "akfilnīhā" literally means "make me its guardian, as I guard what is under my hand." ﴿And he overpowered me﴾ means he defeated me. One says, "ʿazzahu yaʿizzuhu," and the meaning is: he came to me with an argument I could not counter with what he had brought against me. It was also read "waʿāzanī" from al-muʿāzah, which is contention by overpowering.

You should know that those who said these two litigants were angels thought that the purpose of mentioning the ewes was an illustration, because David had under him ninety-nine wives, while Uriah had only one wife. So the angels mentioned that incident by way of symbol and illustration.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe to add to his ewes."﴾ That is, by asking to add your ewe to his ewes. It is narrated that he said to him: "If you insist on that, we will strike from you this and this," and he pointed to the nose and the forehead. Then he said: "O David, you are more deserving that we strike from you this and this, and you did such and such." Then David looked and saw no one, and he understood the situation.

If it is asked: how was it permissible for David to rule against one of the two litigants merely on the word of his opponent? We say: they mentioned several answers:

The first: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: when the first litigant finished his speech, David looked at the other litigant, who had not spoken, and said, "If he is truthful, you have certainly wronged him." The point is that this judgment was conditional upon the condition that the claimant was truthful in his claim.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: when one of the two litigants made a claim, the second acknowledged it, so David ruled against him. God did not mention that acknowledgment, because the apparent meaning of the speech indicates it, just as you say, "I commanded you to trade, so you earned," meaning you traded and so you earned. And He said: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara᾽: 63], meaning he struck it and it parted.

The third: the meaning is that the litigant whose situation is this has certainly wronged you.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And indeed many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they.﴾ Al-Layth said: "khalīl al-rajul" is his associate. al-Zajjaj said: "al-khulaṭā᾽" are the partners. If it is asked: why did David specify the partners as those who wrong one another, when non-partners also do so? The answer: there is no doubt that association causes much contention and dispute, because when two persons are closely associated, each of them comes to know the circumstances of the other. So whatever precious thing one of them owns, when the other sees it, his desire for it becomes great, and this leads to increased dispute and contention. For this reason, David, peace be upon him, specified the partners with increased transgression and aggression. Then He excepted from this ruling those who believe and do righteous deeds, because the association of these people occurs only for the sake of religion and the pursuit of true spiritual felicity, so their association does not cause contention. But those whose association is for love of worldly things, their association will inevitably become a cause of increased transgression and aggression.

You should know that this exception indicates that those who believe and do righteous deeds do not wrong one another. So if David had transgressed and overstepped against that man, then by the verdict of David it would follow that he was not among those who believe and do righteous deeds. It is well known that this is false. Thus it is established that the view of one who says that the subject of the ewe incident is the story of David is false.

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And few are they﴾. Know that the judgment that the people of good are few is frequent in the Qur'an. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13]. Dawud, peace be upon him, said in this same context: ﴿And few are they﴾. God, Exalted is He, related of Iblis that he said: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 17]. The reason for the fewness is that the impulses toward this world are numerous: they are the inner and outer senses, which are ten, along with desire and anger, and the seven natural powers. The total is nineteen, standing at the gate of Hell, which is the body, and all of them call toward creation, this world, and sensual pleasure. As for the caller to the truth and religion, it is none other than the intellect. The dominance of the sensory and natural powers over people is greater than the intellectual power in them. For this reason, fewness occurred on the side of the people of good and abundance on the side of the people of evil. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the "ma" in His saying ﴿And few are they﴾ is for vagueness (ibham), and it carries an expression of wonder at their fewness. He said: if you want to verify its benefit and its place, remove it from the line of Imru' al-Qays: "And a night, for all its shortness—see whether it ever retains any meaning at all."

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And David thought that We had tested him﴾. They said its meaning is: David knew that We had tested him, i.e., examined him. They said: the reason that required interpreting the word "thought" (zann) as "knowledge" (ʿilm) here is that when David, peace be upon him, judged between the two, one of them looked at his companion and laughed, then ascended to the sky, facing him. David knew that God had tried him with this. Thus it is established that David knew it. The interpretation of the word "thought" as "knowledge" is permissible because inferential knowledge (al-ʿilm al-istidlali) resembles thought to a great degree, and resemblance is a cause for the permissibility of metaphor (majaz). I say: this statement applies only if we say the two litigants were angels. If we do not say that, we are not obliged to interpret "thought" as "knowledge." Rather, one may say that when the supposition of being tested by God predominated over his thought, he occupied himself with seeking forgiveness and turning in repentance.

As for His saying ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾: that is, he asked his Lord for forgiveness. Here there are two views:

If we say that a lapse had proceeded from him, we interpret this seeking of forgiveness as referring to it. If we do not say so, there are several views.

The first: when the people entered upon him intending to kill him, and he was a ruler of great might and powerful strength, then, despite his great capacity for retaliation and despite the fear arising in his heart, he pardoned them and said nothing to them. It was close to the matter entering his heart with some self-admiration, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord for that state and turned in repentance to God, acknowledging that his undertaking of that good was only by God's grace. So God forgave him and overlooked it because of the occurrence of that passing thought.

The second: perhaps he intended to harm the people, then he said: no decisive proof had established that these people intended evil, so he pardoned them, then he sought forgiveness for that intention.

The third: perhaps the people repented to God and asked him to seek forgiveness from God on their behalf so that He would accept their repentance. So he sought forgiveness and humbled himself before God, and God forgave their sins because of his intercession and supplication. All these views are plausible and apparent, and the Qur'an is full of the like of these views. When the wording admits what we have mentioned, and no definitive or probable proof has established the commission of the abhorrent acts they mention, then what compels us to adopt them and to affirm them? What confirms that what we have mentioned is closer and stronger is that God concluded this story with His saying: ﴿And indeed for him with Us is nearness and a good return﴾. Such a conclusion is fitting only for one from whom much work in service and obedience has proceeded, and who has borne various kinds of hardships in compliance and submission. As for when the preceding mention is the committing of a transgression and sin, such a conclusion does not befit him. Malik ibn Dinar said: on the Day of Resurrection, a high pulpit will be brought and placed in Paradise, and it will be said: "O David, glorify Me with that beautiful, melodious voice with which you used to glorify Me in the world." And God knows best.

Several discussions remain here:

The first: it was read as "fatanahu" and "fattanahu," with the alif being a pronoun for the two angels.

The second: it is well known that the seeking of forgiveness was because of the story of the ewe and the ewes. It was also said that it was because he ruled for one of the two litigants before hearing the words of the second, and that is impermissible.

The third: His saying ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ indicates that bowing occurred. As for prostration, it is established by reports, and likewise intense weeping for a period of forty days is established by reports.

The fourth: the position of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, is that there is no prostration of recitation in this place. He said: because it is the repentance of a prophet, so it does not require a prostration of recitation.

The fifth: Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, cited this verse regarding the prostration of recitation to show that bowing takes the place of prostration.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verses 26–29 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah (vicegerent) upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your] desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them without purpose. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ ﴿Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ ﴿[This is] a Book We have revealed to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, finished speaking about the explanation of the story, He followed it with a statement that He, exalted is He, entrusted to David the vicegerency (khilafah) over the earth. This is among the strongest proofs against the well-known view about that story, because it is extremely far-fetched to describe a man as striving to shed the blood of the Muslims and desiring to take their wives from them, and then to mention right after it that Allah, exalted is He, entrusted to him the vicegerency over the earth. Then we say, regarding the meaning of his being a khalifah, there are two views:

The first: We made you succeed those prophets who came before you in calling to Allah, exalted is He, and in governing the people, because a man's khalifah is one who succeeds him. This is only conceivable regarding one who may be absent, and that is impossible for Allah.

The second: We made you one who possesses the people and whose judgment is binding over them. By this interpretation he is called a khalifah, and from this comes the expression "the khulafa' of Allah on His earth." The sum of it is that a man's khalifah is one whose judgment is binding over his subjects, and true vicegerency is impossible with respect to Allah; so when the literal sense was impossible, the word was made to signify its necessary consequence, which is the binding execution of judgment.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So judge between the people in truth.﴾ Know that man is created civil by nature, because a single person's interests cannot be organized except in the presence of a complete city, to the extent that this one plows, that one grinds, that one bakes, that one weaves, and this one sews; in sum, each of them is occupied with an important task, and from the work of all of them the interests of all are organized. Thus it is established that man is civil by nature. When they gather in one place, disputes and quarrels arise among them, and there must be a powerful, dominating person who cuts off those disputes, and that is the sultan whose judgment is binding over all. Thus it is established that the interests of creation cannot be organized except by a dominant, governing sultan. Then, if that dominant governing sultan's judgment follows his own desire and seeks the interests of his worldly life, his harm upon creation becomes great, for he makes the subjects a ransom for himself and uses them to achieve his own aims, and that leads to the ruin of the world and the occurrence of chaos and confusion among creation, and that ultimately leads to the destruction of that king. But if that king's rulings conform to the true divine law, the interests of the world are organized and the doors of goodness are widened in the best manner. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So judge between the people in truth,﴾ meaning: there must be a judge among the people by truth, so be you that judge.

Then He said: ﴿And do not follow [your] desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah,﴾ the verse. Its explanation is that following desire necessitates going astray from the way of Allah, and going astray from the way of Allah necessitates evil punishment; so it follows that following desire necessitates evil punishment.

As for the first station, that following desire necessitates going astray from the way of Allah: its establishment is that desire calls to immersion in bodily pleasures, and immersion in them prevents occupation with seeking spiritual felicities, which are the enduring good deeds, because these are two opposed states; as one increases, the other decreases.

As for the second station, that going astray from the way of Allah necessitates evil punishment: the matter in it is evident, because when a person's attachment to these bodily things becomes great and he completely forgets his spiritual states, then when he dies he has parted from what he loved and desired, and he enters abodes for which he has no familiarity with their people, and his eye has no capacity to behold the lights of those abodes; so it is as if he has lost the beloved and reached what he hates, and he is inevitably in the greatest hardship and affliction. Thus it is established that following desire necessitates going astray from the way of Allah, and it is established that going astray from the way of Allah necessitates punishment, and this is an explanation of utmost completeness.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning,﴾ meaning that the first cause of the occurrence of that straying is forgetting the Day of Reckoning, because if he were mindful of the Day of Reckoning he would not have turned away from preparing provision for the Day of Return, nor would he have become absorbed in these corrupt pleasures.

It is narrated from one of the caliphs of the Marwanid dynasty that he said to Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz: "Have you heard what has reached us, that the caliph is not recorded by the pen and no sin is written against him?" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, are the caliphs better or the prophets?!" Then he recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning.﴾

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them without purpose. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191], and His saying: ﴿Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth﴾ [al-Rum: 8]. And in it are issues:

The first issue: Al-Jubba'i used this verse to argue that He, exalted is He, cannot be the creator of the actions of the servants. He said: because they contain disbelief and wickedness, and all of them are falsehoods. When He, exalted is He, stated that He did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in vain, this indicates that He did not create the actions of the servants. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them except in truth.﴾ The Mujbira (determinists) hold that He created the disbeliever so that he would disbelieve, and disbelief is falsehood, and He has created falsehood. Then Allah, exalted is He, emphasized this by saying: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve,﴾ meaning: whoever says this statement is a disbeliever. This is an explicit declaration that the doctrine of the Mujbira is itself disbelief. Our companions, may Allah have mercy on them, argued that this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the creator of the actions of the servants. They said: this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the creator of everything between the heavens and the earth, and the actions of the servants occur between the heaven and the earth, so it is necessary that Allah, exalted is He, is their creator.

The second issue: This verse indicates the soundness of the doctrine of resurrection, gathering, and the Resurrection. That is because He, exalted is He, created creation in this world. Either it is said that He created them to harm them, or to benefit them, or neither to benefit nor to harm. The first is false because that is not befitting to the Merciful, Generous. The third is also false because this state obtains when they were non-existent. So nothing remains but that He created them to benefit them. We say: that benefit is either in the life of this world or in the life of the Hereafter. The first is false, because the benefits of this world are few and its harms are many, and bearing many harms for a few benefits is not befitting to wisdom. Since this division is invalid, the doctrine of the existence of another life after this worldly life is established, and that is the doctrine of resurrection, gathering, and the Resurrection. Know that this proof can be formulated in many ways, and we have summarized them exhaustively at the beginning of Surah Yunus, so there is no way to repeat them. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that He, exalted is He, did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them in vain; and if their creation is not in vain, then the doctrine of resurrection and gathering is necessary; and whoever denies the doctrine of resurrection and gathering is doubting the wisdom of Allah in creating the heaven and earth. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ And when Allah, exalted is He, had explained in summary that denying the gathering and resurrection necessitates doubt about the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, He explained that in detail, saying: ﴿Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ Its explanation: we see in this world those who obey Allah and refrain from His disobedience suffering poverty, disability, and various afflictions, and we see disbelievers and sinners in ease and comfort. If there were no gathering, resurrection, and return, then the state of the obedient would be lower than the state of the disobedient, and that is not befitting to the wisdom of the Wise, Merciful. And if that is detrimental to wisdom, it is established that denying the gathering and resurrection necessitates denying the wisdom of Allah.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿[This is] a Book We have revealed to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, only sent down this Qur'an for the sake of good, mercy, and guidance, and this implies two things:
One: that the acts of Allah are caused by the consideration of benefits.
The second: that He, exalted is He, wills faith, goodness, and obedience from everyone, unlike the view of one who says He wills disbelief from the disbeliever.

The second issue: Regarding the arrangement of these verses, we say: a questioner may ask and say: He, exalted is He, related at the beginning of the surah that the disbelievers who mocked had gone to extremes in denying resurrection and the Last Day, and said: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, related this about them, He did not mention the response, but said: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant David,﴾ and it is known that mentioning David, peace be upon him, has no connection with the truth of the doctrine of the Resurrection. Then He, exalted is He, elaborated at length on the explanation of David's story, then followed it with His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth,﴾ and it is known that the question of establishing Allah's wisdom has no connection with the story of David. Then, when He mentioned establishing Allah's wisdom and based upon it the establishment that the doctrine of gathering and resurrection is true, He mentioned after it that the Qur'an is a noble, virtuous Book abundant in benefit and good; and this section has no connection with the preceding words. And if that is so, these sections are separate, distinct sections, with no connection between some of them and others, so how is it fitting in this place to describe the Qur'an as a noble, virtuous Book? This is the complete question.

The answer: We say: the wise have said that whoever is afflicted with an ignorant, stubborn, fanatical opponent, and sees him deeply immersed in that fanaticism and obstinacy, must cut off discussion with him on that issue, because the more he persists in arguing his position, the greater his aversion to acceptance becomes. The proper course then is to cut off discussion with him on that issue, and to engage in another discourse entirely unrelated to the first issue, and to elaborate at length in that unrelated discourse, so that the fanatic forgets that first issue; and when his mind becomes occupied with this unrelated discourse and forgets the first issue, then at that point

Within the course of this discussion, he (God) includes a premise that is suitable for that first claim, a premise to which the biased opponent would assent. Once he assents to it, he will hold to it in establishing the first claim, and the opponent who was biased will then be left silenced and defeated. Knowing this, we say: the unbelievers went so far in denying the gathering and resurrection (al-hashr wa-al-nashr, the assembling of people and their rising for judgment) and the Return (al-ma'ad) that they said in mockery: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our portion before the Day of Reckoning﴾. So He said: "O Muhammad, cut off your speech with them on this question, and begin another discourse that is entirely unrelated to this matter, namely the story of David, peace be upon him." It is known that this story has no connection to the question of the gathering and resurrection. Then He elaborated at length in explaining that story, and then said at the end of the story: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor in the earth, so judge between the people with truth﴾. Everyone who hears this says: "How excellent what he did, in that He commanded him to judge with truth." Then it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "I do not only command you with truth; rather, I, being the Lord of the worlds, do not act except with truth, and I do not decide by falsehood." Here the opponent says: "How excellent what He did, in that He decided only with truth." At this point it is said: since you have granted that God's judgment must be with truth and not with falsehood, it necessarily follows that you must grant the soundness of the doctrine of the gathering and resurrection. For if that did not occur, it would follow that the unbeliever would be favored over the Muslim in bestowing benefits upon him, and that is contrary to wisdom and is pure falsehood. Thus, by this subtle method, God presented a decisive argument against the deniers of the gathering and resurrection, a presentation from which they cannot escape. So that opponent, who had reached the point of mockery in denying the Return, became silenced and obligated by this method. When God mentioned this subtle method of argumentation in the Qur'an, He therefore described the Qur'an with perfection and excellence, saying: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses, and that those of understanding may take heed﴾. Indeed, whoever does not reflect, does not contemplate, and is not aided by divine success, will not come to know these wondrous secrets mentioned in this mighty Qur'an, since he sees it in its outward appearance as joined with poor arrangement, while in reality it contains the most perfect aspects of arrangement. This is what occurred to us in the interpretation of these verses, and success is from God.

As for the second station, that going astray from the way of Allah necessitates evil punishment: the matter in it is evident, because when a person's attachment to these bodily things becomes great and he completely forgets his spiritual states, then when he dies he has parted from what he loved and desired, and he enters abodes for which he has no familiarity with their people, and his eye has no capacity to behold the lights of those abodes; so it is as if he has lost the beloved and reached what he hates, and he is inevitably in the greatest hardship and affliction. Thus it is established that following desire necessitates going astray from the way of Allah, and it is established that going astray from the way of Allah necessitates punishment, and this is an explanation of utmost completeness.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning,﴾ meaning that the first cause of the occurrence of that straying is forgetting the Day of Reckoning, because if he were mindful of the Day of Reckoning he would not have turned away from preparing provision for the Day of Return, nor would he have become absorbed in these corrupt pleasures.

And in it are issues:

He said: because they contain disbelief and wickedness, and all of them are falsehoods. When He, exalted is He, stated that He did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in vain, this indicates that He did not create the actions of the servants. And if that is detrimental to wisdom, it is established that denying the gathering and resurrection necessitates denying the wisdom of Allah.
* * *

One: that the acts of Allah are caused by the consideration of benefits.
The second: that He, exalted is He, wills faith, goodness, and obedience from everyone, unlike the view of one who says He wills disbelief from the disbeliever.

The second issue: Regarding the arrangement of these verses, we say: a questioner may ask and say: He, exalted is He, related at the beginning of the surah that the disbelievers who mocked had gone to extremes in denying resurrection and the Last Day, and said: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, related this about them, He did not mention the response, but said: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant David,﴾ and it is known that mentioning David, peace be upon him, has no connection with the truth of the doctrine of the Resurrection. Then He, exalted is He, elaborated at length on the explanation of David's story, then followed it with His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth,﴾ and it is known that the question of establishing Allah's wisdom has no connection with the story of David. Then, when He mentioned establishing Allah's wisdom and based upon it the establishment that the doctrine of gathering and resurrection is true, He mentioned after it that the Qur'an is a noble, virtuous Book abundant in benefit and good; and this section has no connection with the preceding words. This is the complete question.

The answer: We say: the wise have said that whoever is afflicted with an ignorant, stubborn, fanatical opponent, and sees him deeply immersed in that fanaticism and obstinacy, must cut off discussion with him on that issue, because the more he persists in arguing his position, the greater his aversion to acceptance becomes. The proper course then is to cut off discussion with him on that issue, and to engage in another discourse entirely unrelated to the first issue, and to elaborate at length in that unrelated discourse, so that the fanatic forgets that first issue; and when his mind becomes occupied with this unrelated discourse and forgets the first issue, then at that point

Within the course of this discussion, he (God) includes a premise that is suitable for that first claim, a premise to which the biased opponent would assent. Once he assents to it, he will hold to it in establishing the first claim, and the opponent who was biased will then be left silenced and defeated. Knowing this, we say: the unbelievers went so far in denying the gathering and resurrection (al-hashr wa-al-nashr, the assembling of people and their rising for judgment) and the Return (al-ma'ad) that they said in mockery: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our portion before the Day of Reckoning﴾. Thus, by this subtle method, God presented a decisive argument against the deniers of the gathering and resurrection, a presentation from which they cannot escape. So that opponent, who had reached the point of mockery in denying the Return, became silenced and obligated by this method. When God mentioned this subtle method of argumentation in the Qur'an, He therefore described the Qur'an with perfection and excellence, saying: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses, and that those of understanding may take heed﴾. Indeed, whoever does not reflect, does not contemplate, and is not aided by divine success, will not come to know these wondrous secrets mentioned in this mighty Qur'an, since he sees it in its outward appearance as joined with poor arrangement, while in reality it contains the most perfect aspects of arrangement. This is what occurred to us in the interpretation of these verses, and success is from God.

That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191], and His saying: ﴿Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth﴾ [al-Rum: 8]. And in it are issues:

The first issue: Al-Jubba'i used this verse to argue that He, exalted is He, cannot be the creator of the actions of the servants. He said: because they contain disbelief and wickedness, and all of them are falsehoods. When He, exalted is He, stated that He did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in vain, this indicates that He did not create the actions of the servants. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them except in truth.﴾ The Mujbira (determinists) hold that He created the disbeliever so that he would disbelieve, and disbelief is falsehood, and He has created falsehood. Then Allah, exalted is He, emphasized this by saying: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve,﴾ meaning: whoever says this statement is a disbeliever. This is an explicit declaration that the doctrine of the Mujbira is itself disbelief. Our companions, may Allah have mercy on them, argued that this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the creator of the actions of the servants. They said: this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the creator of everything between the heavens and the earth, and the actions of the servants occur between the heaven and the earth, so it is necessary that Allah, exalted is He, is their creator.

The second issue: This verse indicates the soundness of the doctrine of resurrection, gathering, and the Resurrection. That is because He, exalted is He, created creation in this world. Either it is said that He created them to harm them, or to benefit them, or neither to benefit nor to harm. The first is false because that is not befitting to the Merciful, Generous. The third is also false because this state obtains when they were non-existent. So nothing remains but that He created them to benefit them. We say: that benefit is either in the life of this world or in the life of the Hereafter. The first is false, because the benefits of this world are few and its harms are many, and bearing many harms for a few benefits is not befitting to wisdom. Since this division is invalid, the doctrine of the existence of another life after this worldly life is established, and that is the doctrine of resurrection, gathering, and the Resurrection. Know that this proof can be formulated in many ways, and we have summarized them exhaustively at the beginning of Surah Yunus, so there is no way to repeat them. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that He, exalted is He, did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them in vain; and if their creation is not in vain, then the doctrine of resurrection and gathering is necessary; and whoever denies the doctrine of resurrection and gathering is doubting the wisdom of Allah in creating the heaven and earth. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ And when Allah, exalted is He, had explained in summary that denying the gathering and resurrection necessitates doubt about the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, He explained that in detail, saying: ﴿Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ Its explanation: we see in this world those who obey Allah and refrain from His disobedience suffering poverty, disability, and various afflictions, and we see disbelievers and sinners in ease and comfort. If there were no gathering, resurrection, and return, then the state of the obedient would be lower than the state of the disobedient, and that is not befitting to the wisdom of the Wise, Merciful. And if that is detrimental to wisdom, it is established that denying the gathering and resurrection necessitates denying the wisdom of Allah.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿[This is] a Book We have revealed to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, only sent down this Qur'an for the sake of good, mercy, and guidance, and this implies two things:
One: that the acts of Allah are caused by the consideration of benefits.
The second: that He, exalted is He, wills faith, goodness, and obedience from everyone, unlike the view of one who says He wills disbelief from the disbeliever.

The second issue: Regarding the arrangement of these verses, we say: a questioner may ask and say: He, exalted is He, related at the beginning of the surah that the disbelievers who mocked had gone to extremes in denying resurrection and the Last Day, and said: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, related this about them, He did not mention the response, but said: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant David,﴾ and it is known that mentioning David, peace be upon him, has no connection with the truth of the doctrine of the Resurrection. Then He, exalted is He, elaborated at length on the explanation of David's story, then followed it with His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth,﴾ and it is known that the question of establishing Allah's wisdom has no connection with the story of David. Then, when He mentioned establishing Allah's wisdom and based upon it the establishment that the doctrine of gathering and resurrection is true, He mentioned after it that the Qur'an is a noble, virtuous Book abundant in benefit and good; and this section has no connection with the preceding words. And if that is so, these sections are separate, distinct sections, with no connection between some of them and others, so how is it fitting in this place to describe the Qur'an as a noble, virtuous Book? This is the complete question.

The answer: We say: the wise have said that whoever is afflicted with an ignorant, stubborn, fanatical opponent, and sees him deeply immersed in that fanaticism and obstinacy, must cut off discussion with him on that issue, because the more he persists in arguing his position, the greater his aversion to acceptance becomes. The proper course then is to cut off discussion with him on that issue, and to engage in another discourse entirely unrelated to the first issue, and to elaborate at length in that unrelated discourse, so that the fanatic forgets that first issue; and when his mind becomes occupied with this unrelated discourse and forgets the first issue, then at that point

Within the course of this discussion, he (God) includes a premise that is suitable for that first claim, a premise to which the biased opponent would assent. Once he assents to it, he will hold to it in establishing the first claim, and the opponent who was biased will then be left silenced and defeated. Knowing this, we say: the unbelievers went so far in denying the gathering and resurrection (al-hashr wa-al-nashr, the assembling of people and their rising for judgment) and the Return (al-ma'ad) that they said in mockery: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our portion before the Day of Reckoning﴾. So He said: "O Muhammad, cut off your speech with them on this question, and begin another discourse that is entirely unrelated to this matter, namely the story of David, peace be upon him." It is known that this story has no connection to the question of the gathering and resurrection. Then He elaborated at length in explaining that story, and then said at the end of the story: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor in the earth, so judge between the people with truth﴾. Everyone who hears this says: "How excellent what he did, in that He commanded him to judge with truth." Then it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "I do not only command you with truth; rather, I, being the Lord of the worlds, do not act except with truth, and I do not decide by falsehood." Here the opponent says: "How excellent what He did, in that He decided only with truth." At this point it is said: since you have granted that God's judgment must be with truth and not with falsehood, it necessarily follows that you must grant the soundness of the doctrine of the gathering and resurrection. For if that did not occur, it would follow that the unbeliever would be favored over the Muslim in bestowing benefits upon him, and that is contrary to wisdom and is pure falsehood. Thus, by this subtle method, God presented a decisive argument against the deniers of the gathering and resurrection, a presentation from which they cannot escape. So that opponent, who had reached the point of mockery in denying the Return, became silenced and obligated by this method. When God mentioned this subtle method of argumentation in the Qur'an, He therefore described the Qur'an with perfection and excellence, saying: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses, and that those of understanding may take heed﴾. Indeed, whoever does not reflect, does not contemplate, and is not aided by divine success, will not come to know these wondrous secrets mentioned in this mighty Qur'an, since he sees it in its outward appearance as joined with poor arrangement, while in reality it contains the most perfect aspects of arrangement. This is what occurred to us in the interpretation of these verses, and success is from God.

[p. 177 continues]

Know that this is the second story. His words, ﴿Excellent was the servant﴾, raise several discussions.

The first: The one praised in ﴿Excellent was the servant﴾ is omitted. It has been said that he is Solomon, and it has been said that he is David. The first view is preferable, because it is the nearer of the two mentioned, and because God said after it, ﴿indeed he was ever turning back﴾. It cannot be that David is meant, because his being described with this meaning was already mentioned in the preceding verse, where He said, ﴿And remember Our servant David, the possessor of strength; indeed he was ever turning back﴾. If we said that the word "ever turning back" here is also a description of David, it would entail repetition. And if we said it is a description of Solomon, it would entail that the son resembles his father in the attributes of perfection and excellence, so this is more fitting.

[p. 178]

The second discussion: He said first, ﴿Excellent was the servant﴾, and then after it, ﴿indeed he was ever turning back﴾. This word (inna, "indeed") indicates causation (ta'lil). This shows that he was "excellent servant" because he was ever turning back. It follows that everyone who frequently returns to God Most High in most times and in most important matters is described as ﴿excellent servant﴾. This is the truth about which there is no doubt, because human perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it. The head and chief of knowledge is the knowledge of God Most High, and the head and chief of acts of obedience is the acknowledgment that nothing of goodness is completed except by God's help. Whoever is like this is one who frequently returns to God Most High, and so he is ever turning back. Thus it is established that everyone who is ever turning back must be an ﴿excellent servant﴾.

As for His words, ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾, there are several opinions on it.

The first: The construction is: "Excellent was the servant" because of what he did from his deeds, namely that he did such and such.

The second: It is the beginning of a new statement. The construction is: "Remember, O Muhammad, when there were displayed before him such and such." Al-'Ashiyy is from the time of 'Asr to the end of the day. The horses were displayed before him so that he might look at them and observe the condition of their states. "Al-safinat al-jiyad" (the standing, swift horses) are described with two attributes:

The first attribute: "al-safinat." The author of al-Sihah (al-Jawhari) said: al-safin is the one who stands on three legs, or who joins his feet together, and in the hadith: "When we prayed behind him and he raised his head from the ruku' (bowing), we would stand in suful (rows)", that is, we would stand with our feet joined. I say: According to both interpretations, al-sufun is an attribute indicating the excellence of the horse.

The second attribute of the horses in this verse is "al-jiyad." Al-Mubarrad said: al-jiyad is the plural of jawad, which is one who runs very fast, just as the jawad among people is one who is quick to give. So the intent is to describe them with excellence and perfection in both states, standing and movement. As for the state of their standing, He described them with al-sufun; as for the state of their movement, He described them with goodness of gait. That is: when they stand, they are still and calm in their places in the best forms; when they run, they are swift in their running; when they are pursued, they overtake; and when they pursue, they are not overtaken. Then God Most High said, ﴿So he said, "Indeed I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord"﴾. There are several interpretations of this expression.

The first: Ahbabtu ("I loved") is taken to include the meaning of a verb that takes 'an (from), as if it were said: "I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord."

The second: Ahbabtu means "I bound myself to," and the meaning is: "I bound myself to the love of horses out of remembrance of my Lord," that is, out of the Book of my Lord, which is the Torah, because the tethering of horses is praised in the Qur'an and likewise praised in the Torah.

The third: A person may love something while loving that he should not love it, like the sick person who craves what increases his illness, and the father who loves his bad son. But whoever loves something and loves that he loves it, this is the utmost love. So His words, "I have loved the love of good," mean: "I have loved my love for these horses."

* * *

Then He said, "out of remembrance of my Lord," meaning that this intense love arose only out of the remembrance of God and His command, not out of desire and passion. This is the most apparent of the interpretations.

* * *

Then God Most High said, ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾. I say: the pronoun in His words ﴿until they were hidden﴾ and in His words ﴿Bring them back to me﴾ may each refer to the sun, since there was mention of what is connected to it, namely the afternoon ('ashiyy). It may also be that each refers to the safinat (horses). It may be that the first is connected to the sun and the second to the horses, and it may be the reverse. These are four possibilities, and there is nothing beyond them.

The first: Both pronouns refer to the horses, as if he said, "until the horses were hidden behind the veil; bring the horses back to me."

The second possibility: Both pronouns refer to the sun, as if he said, "until the sun was hidden behind the veil; bring back the sun." It has been narrated that when he (ﷺ) was occupied with the horses, the 'Asr prayer passed him by, so he asked God to return the sun. Thus His words, ﴿Bring them back to me﴾, are a reference to asking for the return of the sun. This possibility, in my view, is far-fetched. What indicates this is the following:

[p. 179]

First: The horses are explicitly mentioned, while the sun is not mentioned, and returning a pronoun to what is mentioned is preferable to returning it to what is implied.

Second: He said, ﴿Indeed I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord until they were hidden behind the veil﴾. The apparent sense of this wording indicates that Solomon, peace be upon him, was saying, "Indeed I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord," and he kept repeating these words until they were hidden behind the veil. So if we say the intent is "until the horses were hidden behind the veil," its meaning is that when his gaze fell upon them while they were running, he kept saying this phrase until they disappeared from his eye, and this is fitting. But if we say the intent is "until the sun was hidden behind the veil," its meaning is that he kept repeating the very same phrase from the time of 'Asr until the time of Maghrib, and this is extremely far-fetched.

Third: If we ruled that the pronoun in His words "until it was hidden" refers to the sun, and understood the wording to mean that he abandoned the 'Asr prayer, this would contradict His words, "I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord," for if that love were out of the remembrance of God, he would not have forgotten the prayer or abandoned the remembrance of God.

Fourth: Even on the assumption that he, peace be upon him, remained occupied with those horses until the sun set and the 'Asr prayer was missed, that would be a great sin and a serious offense. The fitting response to such a state is supplication, weeping, and great effort in displaying repentance. But to say, in a manner of recklessness and of self-importance toward the God of the worlds and Lord of the worlds, "Bring them back to me," with such a phrase stripped of every aspect of good manners, right after that great offense, is something that would not proceed even from the people most distant from goodness. How then is it permissible to attribute it to the purified and honored Messenger!

Fifth: The One able to move the spheres and the stars is God Most High, so he should have said "Bring it back to me" and not "Bring them back to me." If they say that he used the plural form to signal the honoring of the one addressed, we say: His words, "Bring them back," is an expression that indicates the greatest kind of humiliation, so how could the honoring of the addressee be fitting with this expression?!

Sixth: If the sun had returned after sunset, that would have been witnessed by all the people of the world, and if that were the case, the motives to transmit and publicize it would have been abundant. Since no one has said this, we know its falsehood.

Seventh: God Most High said, ﴿when there were displayed before him in the afternoon the standing, swift horses﴾, and then He said, ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾. Returning the pronoun to the nearer of the two mentioned is preferable, and the nearer of the two mentioned is "the standing, swift horses," while "al-'ashiyy" is the farther of the two. So it is preferable that this pronoun refer to the horses. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that interpreting His words, "until they were hidden behind the veil," as the hiding of the sun, and interpreting His words, "Bring them back," as meaning a request that God return the sun after its setting, is a statement far removed from the composition of the text.
