The second: Ahbabtu means "I bound myself to," and the meaning is: "I bound myself to the love of horses out of remembrance of my Lord," that is, out of the Book of my Lord, which is the Torah, because the tethering of horses is praised in the Qur'an and likewise praised in the Torah.

The third: A person may love something while loving that he should not love it, like the sick person who craves what increases his illness, and the father who loves his bad son. But whoever loves something and loves that he loves it, this is the utmost love. So His words, "I have loved the love of good," mean: "I have loved my love for these horses."

* * *

Then He said, "out of remembrance of my Lord," meaning that this intense love arose only out of the remembrance of God and His command, not out of desire and passion. This is the most apparent of the interpretations.

* * *

Then God Most High said, ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾. I say: the pronoun in His words ﴿until they were hidden﴾ and in His words ﴿Bring them back to me﴾ may each refer to the sun, since there was mention of what is connected to it, namely the afternoon ('ashiyy). It may also be that each refers to the safinat (horses). It may be that the first is connected to the sun and the second to the horses, and it may be the reverse. These are four possibilities, and there is nothing beyond them.

The first: Both pronouns refer to the horses, as if he said, "until the horses were hidden behind the veil; bring the horses back to me."

The second possibility: Both pronouns refer to the sun, as if he said, "until the sun was hidden behind the veil; bring back the sun." It has been narrated that when he (ﷺ) was occupied with the horses, the 'Asr prayer passed him by, so he asked God to return the sun. Thus His words, ﴿Bring them back to me﴾, are a reference to asking for the return of the sun. This possibility, in my view, is far-fetched. What indicates this is the following:

[p. 179]

First: The horses are explicitly mentioned, while the sun is not mentioned, and returning a pronoun to what is mentioned is preferable to returning it to what is implied.

Second: He said, ﴿Indeed I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord until they were hidden behind the veil﴾. The apparent sense of this wording indicates that Solomon, peace be upon him, was saying, "Indeed I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord," and he kept repeating these words until they were hidden behind the veil. So if we say the intent is "until the horses were hidden behind the veil," its meaning is that when his gaze fell upon them while they were running, he kept saying this phrase until they disappeared from his eye, and this is fitting. But if we say the intent is "until the sun was hidden behind the veil," its meaning is that he kept repeating the very same phrase from the time of 'Asr until the time of Maghrib, and this is extremely far-fetched.

Third: If we ruled that the pronoun in His words "until it was hidden" refers to the sun, and understood the wording to mean that he abandoned the 'Asr prayer, this would contradict His words, "I have loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord," for if that love were out of the remembrance of God, he would not have forgotten the prayer or abandoned the remembrance of God.

Fourth: Even on the assumption that he, peace be upon him, remained occupied with those horses until the sun set and the 'Asr prayer was missed, that would be a great sin and a serious offense. The fitting response to such a state is supplication, weeping, and great effort in displaying repentance. But to say, in a manner of recklessness and of self-importance toward the God of the worlds and Lord of the worlds, "Bring them back to me," with such a phrase stripped of every aspect of good manners, right after that great offense, is something that would not proceed even from the people most distant from goodness. How then is it permissible to attribute it to the purified and honored Messenger!

Fifth: The One able to move the spheres and the stars is God Most High, so he should have said "Bring it back to me" and not "Bring them back to me." If they say that he used the plural form to signal the honoring of the one addressed, we say: His words, "Bring them back," is an expression that indicates the greatest kind of humiliation, so how could the honoring of the addressee be fitting with this expression?!

Sixth: If the sun had returned after sunset, that would have been witnessed by all the people of the world, and if that were the case, the motives to transmit and publicize it would have been abundant. Since no one has said this, we know its falsehood.

Seventh: God Most High said, ﴿when there were displayed before him in the afternoon the standing, swift horses﴾, and then He said, ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾. Returning the pronoun to the nearer of the two mentioned is preferable, and the nearer of the two mentioned is "the standing, swift horses," while "al-'ashiyy" is the farther of the two. So it is preferable that this pronoun refer to the horses. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that interpreting His words, "until they were hidden behind the veil," as the hiding of the sun, and interpreting His words, "Bring them back," as meaning a request that God return the sun after its setting, is a statement far removed from the composition of the text.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he began to pass his hand over the legs and the necks﴾. That is, Sulayman (peace be upon him) began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks. Most of the commentators said its meaning is that he struck the sword against their shanks and necks, that is, he cut them. They said: when the afternoon prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿaṣr) escaped him because of his occupation with gazing at those horses, he took them back and hamstrung their shanks and necks, seeking nearness to Allah the Exalted. But in my view this too is far-fetched, and several points indicate this:

First: if the meaning of passing over the shanks and necks were cutting them, then the meaning of His words ﴿And wipe over your heads and your feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6] would be cutting them, and this is something no rational person would say. Rather, even if it were said "he wiped his head with the sword," perhaps beheading might be understood from it; but when the word "sword" is not mentioned, no slaughtering or hamstringing at all is understood from "wiping."

Second: those who hold this view have attributed to Sulayman (peace be upon him) several kinds of blameworthy acts.

The first of them: abandoning the prayer.

The second: that occupation with love of this world overcame him to the point that he forgot the prayer. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The love of the world is the root of every sin."

The third:

That after committing this great sin, he did not occupy himself with repentance and turning back to Allah at all.

The fourth: that he addressed the Lord of the worlds with His words ﴿Bring them back to me﴾, and this is a phrase that a wise man would not use except with a lowly servant.

The fifth: that he followed these sins with hamstringing the horses in their shanks and necks. And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he "forbade slaughtering an animal except for its eating." So these are kinds of major sins which they attributed to Sulayman (peace be upon him), although the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate any of them.

Sixth: that Allah the Exalted mentioned these stories following His words ﴿And they said: Our Lord, hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning﴾, and when the disbelievers reached such a degree of foolishness, Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): Be patient, O Muhammad, over their foolishness ﴿and remember Our servant Dawud﴾, and He mentioned the story of Dawud, then after the two of them He mentioned the story of Sulayman. The sense is that He said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): Be patient, O Muhammad, over what they say, and remember Our servant Sulayman. This statement is only fitting if we say that Sulayman (peace be upon him) in this story performed virtuous deeds and noble character, was patient in obedience to Allah, and turned away from desires and pleasures. But if the purpose of the story of Sulayman (peace be upon him) in this place were that he committed great sins and grave transgressions, then mentioning this story would not be fitting in this place. Thus it is established that the Book of Allah the Exalted calls for the rejection, refutation and nullification of these corrupt sayings. Rather, the interpretation that conforms to the truth of the words of the Qur'an is this: tethering horses was recommended in their religion, just as it is in the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then Sulayman (peace be upon him) needed to go out to war, so he sat and ordered the horses to be brought, and ordered them to be made to run, and said: I do not love them for the sake of this world and the portion of the self, but I love them for the command of Allah and seeking to strengthen His religion; and this is what is meant by his words ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾. Then he (peace be upon him) ordered them to be driven away and sent off until they were hidden by the veil, that is, they vanished from his sight. Then he ordered the trainers to bring those horses back to him, and when they returned to him, he began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks. The purpose of that wiping is several matters:

First: to honor them and show their esteem, since they are among the greatest helpers in repelling the enemy.

Second: that he wished to show that in governing and ruling he humbles himself to the point of personally attending to most affairs.

Third: that he was most knowledgeable about the conditions, diseases and defects of horses, so he would examine them and pass his hand over their shanks and necks in order to know whether there was anything indicating illness. This interpretation that we have mentioned fits the wording of the Qur'an exactly and in full agreement, and there is no necessity for us to attribute to him any of those reprehensible and forbidden things. I say: I am greatly astonished at how people accepted these feeble views, although both reason and transmission reject them, and they have no doubt in establishing them, let alone proof. If it is said: the majority interpreted the verse in that way, so what is your view of it? We say: here there are two positions.

The first position: we claim that the wording of the verse does not indicate any of those aspects which they mention, and it has become clear, praise be to Allah, that the matter is as we have stated, and no rational person doubts its clarity.

The second position: suppose that the wording of the verse does not indicate it, yet it is a statement that people have mentioned; so what is your view of it? Our answer: many proofs have established the infallibility (ʿiṣmah) of the prophets (peace be upon them), and no proof has indicated the soundness of these narrations; and a report of single transmitters (khabar al-āḥād) cannot be fit to oppose strong proofs. So how about narrations from groups of people who are not regarded and whose sayings are not given attention? And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verse 34:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did test Solomon, and We placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (in repentance).﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me; indeed You are the Bestower."﴾ ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, running gently by his command wherever he willed.﴾ ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver,﴾ ﴿and others bound together in chains.﴾ ﴿"This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without account."﴾ ﴿And indeed he has near access to Us and a good final return.﴾

Know that this verse describes a second incident concerning Solomon, peace be upon him. The scholars differed over the meaning of His saying, ﴿And We did test Solomon﴾. The people of ḥashw (the uncritical transmitters, ahl al-ḥashw) and narration have one view, and the people of knowledge and verification (ahl al-taḥqīq) have another. As for the view of the ahl al-ḥashw, they related certain narratives concerning it:

The first narrative: They said that news reached Solomon of a city in the sea, so he went out to it with his armies, carried by the wind. He seized it, killed its king, and took a daughter of his named Jarada, one of the most beautiful of people in appearance. He chose her for himself, and she became Muslim, and he loved her. She would constantly weep over her father, so Solomon ordered the devil to form for her an image of her father, and she dressed it in the same garment as his. She would go to that image in the morning and evening with her female attendants, and they would prostrate to it. Asaf informed Solomon of this, so he broke the image, punished the woman, and went out alone to a wilderness, spread ashes, and sat upon them, repenting to God, exalted is He. Solomon had a concubine called Amina, and whenever he entered for relieving himself or for intercourse with a woman, he would place his ring with her, and his sovereignty was in his ring. One day he placed it with her, and the devil of the sea came to her in the form of Solomon and said: "O Amina, my ring!" So she gave it to him, he put it on, and he sat upon Solomon's throne. The birds, the jinn, and humankind came to him, while Solomon's appearance had changed. Solomon then came to Amina to ask for the ring, but she denied him and drove him away. He realised that the sin had overtaken him, so he went around the houses begging for food, and whenever he said, "I am Solomon," they threw dust upon him and reviled him. Then he began to serve fishermen, carrying fish for them, and they would give him two fish each day. He remained in this state for forty days, equal to the number of days the idol had been worshipped in his house. Asaf and the leading men of the Children of Israel then rejected the devil's rule, and Asaf asked Solomon's wives. They said: "He does not leave any woman among us in her blood, nor does he wash from impurity." It was also said: "Rather, his rule was carried out in everything except concerning them." Then the devil flew away and threw the ring into the sea, and a fish swallowed it. The fish fell into the hand of Solomon, who split open its belly and found the ring in it. He put it on, fell prostrate to God, his sovereignty returned to him, and he seized that devil, confined him in a rock, and cast it into the sea.

The second narrative of the ḥashwiyya: When that woman undertook to worship that image, Solomon was tested, and the ring kept slipping from his hand and would not stay on it. Asaf said to him: "Indeed you are tested because of your sin, so repent to God."

The third narrative of theirs: They said that Solomon said to one of the devils: "How do you seduce people?" The devil said: "Show me your ring and I will tell you." When he gave it to him, the devil threw it into the sea, his sovereignty went away, and this devil sat upon his throne. Then he mentioned the story to its end.

Page 182

Having known these narratives, these people said: the meaning of His saying, ﴿And We did test Solomon﴾, is that God, exalted is He, afflicted him, and His saying, ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body﴾, is the sitting of that devil upon his throne.

The fourth narrative: The cause of his trial was that he veiled himself from the people for three days, so his sovereignty was taken away, and a devil was placed upon his throne as a punishment for him.

Know that the people of verification (ahl al-taḥqīq) found this account implausible for several reasons:

The first: If the devil were able to take the form and bodily appearance of the prophets, then no reliance could be placed on any of the laws. Perhaps those whom people saw in the form of Muhammad, Jesus and Moses, peace be upon them, were not those men at all, but devils who took their form in order to mislead and lead astray. It is well known that this would completely nullify the religion.

The second: If the devil were able to deal with the Prophet of God, Solomon, in this manner, it would necessarily follow that he could do the same with all the scholars and ascetics. In that case he would be able to kill them, tear up their books, and ruin their homes. Since this is impossible with respect to ordinary scholars, it is even more impossible with respect to the great prophets.

The third: How does it befit God's wisdom and benevolence to empower the devil over the wives of Solomon? Without doubt, this is ugly.

The fourth: If we say that Solomon permitted that woman to worship that image, this would be disbelief on his part; and if he did not permit it at all, then the sin lies with that woman. So how would God hold Solomon accountable for an act that did not proceed from him?

As for the matters which the people of verification mentioned in this respect, they are as follows:

The first: The trial of Solomon was that a son was born to him, and the devils said: "If he lives, he will become empowered over us like his father, so our course is to kill him." Solomon learned of this, so he would raise him in the clouds. While he was occupied with his affairs, that child was cast dead upon his throne. He then became aware of his error, namely that he had not relied upon God in that matter, so he sought forgiveness from his Lord and turned back in repentance.

The second: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Solomon said: 'Tonight I shall go around to seventy women, each of whom will bear a horseman who will fight in the way of God.' He did not say, 'If God wills.' So he went around to them, and none conceived except one woman, who bore half a man. He was brought upon his throne and placed in his lap. By Him in whose hand is my soul, had he said, 'If God wills,' they would all have fought in the way of God as horsemen, all of them." That is His saying: ﴿And We did test Solomon﴾.

The third: His saying, ﴿And We did test Solomon﴾, refers to a severe sickness which God inflicted upon him. ﴿And We placed upon his throne﴾, from him, ﴿a body﴾, and that was because of the severity of the illness. The Arabs say of a weak person that he is "flesh on a bone and a body without a soul." ﴿Then he turned back﴾, meaning he returned to the state of health. Thus the wording is open to these meanings, and there is absolutely no need to interpret it in those feeble ways.

The fourth: I say that it is also not far-fetched to say that God afflicted him by imposing upon him fear, or the expectation of a calamity from some quarter, and because of the intensity of that fear he became like a weak body laid upon that throne. Then God removed that fear from him and restored him to his former strength and tranquillity of heart.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me"﴾: know that those who took the preceding account to mean that a lapse had indeed proceeded from him relied upon this verse, for if a sin had not preceded, he would not have sought forgiveness. It may be answered that a person never wholly refrains from leaving what is better and more fitting, and therefore needs to seek forgiveness, since the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near (to God), and because they are always in a state of humbling the self and displaying lowliness and submission, as he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I seek forgiveness from God seventy times a day and night." It is not far-fetched that this word means this meaning. And God knows best.

[Page 183]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾. This verse indicates that the affair of religion (*muhimm al-din*) must be given precedence over the affair of worldly life (*muhimm al-dunya*), because Solomon first asked for forgiveness and after that asked for the kingdom. The verse also indicates that asking God for forgiveness is a cause for the opening of the gates of good in this world, because Solomon first asked for forgiveness and then used it as a means (*tawassul*) to ask for the kingdom. Noah, peace be upon him, did the same, for God related of him that he said: ﴿So I said, "Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain, and will provide you with wealth and children"﴾ [Nuh 71:10–12]. And He said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:132].

If it is said: His saying, peace be upon him, ﴿a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾ suggests envy. The answer is that those who hold that Satan seized his kingdom said that the meaning of his saying "that shall not belong to anyone after me" is that God would give him a kingdom which the devils could never take over in its place at all. As for those who deny this, they have answered it in several ways:

The first: kingdom (*mulk*) means power (*qudra*), so the intended meaning is: "Empower me over things which no one other than me can have power over at all, so that my power over them becomes a miracle (*mu'jiza*) indicating the truth of my prophethood and my message." The proof of the correctness of this statement is that God said right after it: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed﴾. The wind running by his command is a wondrous power and a wondrous kingdom, and there is no doubt that it is a miracle indicating his prophethood. So his saying, "Grant me a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me," means this meaning, because the condition of a miracle is that no one else can oppose it. Thus His saying ﴿that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾ means that no one can oppose it.

The second answer: when he, peace be upon him, fell ill and then returned to health, he knew that the good things of this world pass to others by inheritance or by some other cause. So he asked his Lord for a kingdom that cannot pass from him to anyone else. This is what he asked for by his saying ﴿a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾, that is, a kingdom that cannot pass from me to another.

The third answer: restraint from the good things of this world while having the power over them is harder than restraint from them when one lacks the power over them. So it is as if he said: "O my God, give me a kingdom surpassing all the kingdoms of mankind entirely, so that I may refrain from them while having power over them, so that my reward may be more perfect and more excellent."

The fourth: Some people say that restraint from the pleasures of this world is difficult and arduous, because these pleasures are present while the felicities of the Hereafter are deferred, and ready cash is hard to sell on credit. So Solomon said: "Give me, O Lord, a kingdom that is the greatest of the kingdoms possible for mankind, so that I may remain, with that complete power, in the utmost restraint from it, so that it may become manifest to creation that attaining the world does not prevent one from serving the Master."

The fifth: whoever has no power over the world remains with his heart inclined toward it, and thinks that it contains great felicities and beneficial goods. So Solomon said: "O Lord of might, give me the greatest of kingdoms, so that people may stand upon the full reality of its condition. Then it will become clear to the intellect that there is no benefit in it, and then the heart will turn away from it and not incline toward it, and I will occupy myself with worship, tranquil in soul, with my heart not preoccupied with the ties of this world." Then He said: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed﴾. *Rukhaan* means soft and gentle, and it derives from *rakhawa* (softness). When the wind is gentle, it does not shake violently and does not resist him; it is pleasant.

If it is said: Did not God say in another verse: ﴿And to Solomon the wind, violent, running by his command﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:81]? We say: the answer is in two ways:

The first: there is no contradiction between the two verses, for the intended meaning is that the wind had the strength of violent winds, but when it ran by his command it became delicious and pleasant, and so it was gentle.

The second answer: that the wind was gentle at one time and violent at another, and there is no contradiction between the two matters. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wherever he directed﴾ means "where he intended and aimed." Al-Asma'i related from the Arabs that they say: "He hit the correct thing but missed the answer" (*asaba al-sawab fa-akhta al-jawab*). It is related from Ru'ba that two men of the people of language intended him to ask him about this word, and he came out to them and said: "Where do you aim (*tusibaan*)?" They said: "This is what we are seeking." In sum, the point is that God made the wind subservient to him until it ran by his command in accordance with his will. Then He said: ﴿and the devils, every builder and diver﴾. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "The devils" is in apposition (*'atf*) to "the wind," "every builder" is a substitute (*badal*) for "the devils," and "and others" (*wa-akhirina*) is coordinated (*'atf*) with His saying ﴿every builder﴾, and it is a substitution of the whole for the whole (*badal al-kull min al-kull*). They used to build for him whatever he wished of structures, and they used to dive for him and extract pearls. His saying ﴿bound together﴾ (*muqarranin*) is said of binding them with ropes, and the doubling of the letter is for multiplicity. *Al-asfad* means shackles, whose singular is *safad*, and *safad* also means a gift. The poet al-Nabigha said:

*"And I have not, may you be cursed, deflected with a gift."*

According to this meaning, *safad* is a fetter. Whoever you bind firmly, you have shackled (*saffadtahu*), and whoever you give a lavish gift, you have given him generously (*asfadtahu*).

Here there is a discussion: these verses indicate that the devils have great power, and by that power they were able to build strong structures that humans cannot build, and they were able to dive into the seas. Solomon, peace be upon him, needed to bind them. One may say: these devils either have dense bodies or subtle bodies. If the first, then whoever has sound senses must see them, for if it were permissible that we do not see them despite the density of their bodies, then it would be permissible that there be high mountains and terrifying sounds in our presence which we neither see nor hear, and that is entry into sophistry (*sufsata*). If the second, namely that their bodies are not dense but subtle and fine, then such a being cannot be described as possessing great strength. Moreover, it would follow that their bodies would be scattered and torn apart by strong winds and die immediately, and that prevents describing them as building strong structures. Also, if the jinn and devils are described with this strength and power, why do they not kill the scholars and ascetics in our time? Why do they not ruin people's homes, even though Muslims are extreme in expressing their curse and enmity toward them? Since none of that is perceived, we know that the claim of affirming jinn and devils is weak.

Know that our companions (the Ash'aris) allow that their bodies may be dense even though we do not see them. Also, it is not far-fetched to say their bodies are subtle in the sense of lacking color, but solid in the sense that they do not accept dispersion and tearing apart. As for al-Jubba'i, he conceded that their bodies were dense, and he claimed that people used to see them in the time of Solomon. Then, when Solomon, peace be upon him, died, God caused those jinn and devils to die, and created another kind of jinn and devils whose bodies are extremely fine and who have no strength at all. And what exists in our time of jinn and devils is nothing but of this kind.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Give to whom you wish and withhold from whom you wish, without account," that is, there is no blame on you for what you give and for what you withhold.

The second: that this is specifically about the devils, and the meaning is: "These devils who are subjected are Our gift; so grant favor to whomever of the devils you wish, releasing him, and detain whomever of them you wish in labor without account."

When God, exalted is He, mentioned what He had bestowed upon Solomon in this world, He followed it with His bestowal upon him in the Hereafter, and said: ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has with Us an near station and a good return﴾. Its interpretation has already preceded.

According to this meaning, *safad* is a fetter. Whoever you bind firmly, you have shackled (*saffadtahu*), and whoever you give a lavish gift, you have given him generously (*asfadtahu*).

Here there is a discussion: these verses indicate that the devils have great power, and by that power they were able to build strong structures that humans cannot build, and they were able to dive into the seas. Solomon, peace be upon him, needed to bind them. One may say: these devils either have dense bodies or subtle bodies. If the first, then whoever has sound senses must see them, for if it were permissible that we do not see them despite the density of their bodies, then it would be permissible that there be high mountains and terrifying sounds in our presence which we neither see nor hear, and that is entry into sophistry (*sufsata*). If the second, namely that their bodies are not dense but subtle and fine, then such a being cannot be described as possessing great strength. Moreover, it would follow that their bodies would be scattered and torn apart by strong winds and die immediately, and that prevents describing them as building strong structures. Also, if the jinn and devils are described with this strength and power, why do they not kill the scholars and ascetics in our time? Why do they not ruin people's homes, even though Muslims are extreme in expressing their curse and enmity toward them? Since none of that is perceived, we know that the claim of affirming jinn and devils is weak.

Know that our companions (the Ash'aris) allow that their bodies may be dense even though we do not see them. Also, it is not far-fetched to say their bodies are subtle in the sense of lacking color, but solid in the sense that they do not accept dispersion and tearing apart. As for al-Jubba'i, he conceded that their bodies were dense, and he claimed that people used to see them in the time of Solomon. Then, when Solomon, peace be upon him, died, God caused those jinn and devils to die, and created another kind of jinn and devils whose bodies are extremely fine and who have no strength at all. And what exists in our time of jinn and devils is nothing but of this kind.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿This is Our gift, so grant or withhold without account﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Give to whom you wish and withhold from whom you wish, without account," that is, there is no blame on you for what you give and for what you withhold.

The second: that this is specifically about the devils, and the meaning is: "These devils who are subjected are Our gift; so grant favor to whomever of the devils you wish, releasing him, and detain whomever of them you wish in labor without account."

When God, exalted is He, mentioned what He had bestowed upon Solomon in this world, He followed it with His bestowal upon him in the Hereafter, and said: ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has with Us an near station and a good return﴾. Its interpretation has already preceded.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾. This verse indicates that the affair of religion (*muhimm al-din*) must be given precedence over the affair of worldly life (*muhimm al-dunya*), because Solomon first asked for forgiveness and after that asked for the kingdom. The verse also indicates that asking God for forgiveness is a cause for the opening of the gates of good in this world, because Solomon first asked for forgiveness and then used it as a means (*tawassul*) to ask for the kingdom. Noah, peace be upon him, did the same, for God related of him that he said: ﴿So I said, "Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain, and will provide you with wealth and children"﴾ [Nuh 71:10–12]. And He said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:132].

If it is said: His saying, peace be upon him, ﴿a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾ suggests envy. The answer is that those who hold that Satan seized his kingdom said that the meaning of his saying "that shall not belong to anyone after me" is that God would give him a kingdom which the devils could never take over in its place at all. As for those who deny this, they have answered it in several ways:

The first: kingdom (*mulk*) means power (*qudra*), so the intended meaning is: "Empower me over things which no one other than me can have power over at all, so that my power over them becomes a miracle (*mu'jiza*) indicating the truth of my prophethood and my message." The proof of the correctness of this statement is that God said right after it: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed﴾. The wind running by his command is a wondrous power and a wondrous kingdom, and there is no doubt that it is a miracle indicating his prophethood. So his saying, "Grant me a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me," means this meaning, because the condition of a miracle is that no one else can oppose it. Thus His saying ﴿that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾ means that no one can oppose it.

The second answer: when he, peace be upon him, fell ill and then returned to health, he knew that the good things of this world pass to others by inheritance or by some other cause. So he asked his Lord for a kingdom that cannot pass from him to anyone else. This is what he asked for by his saying ﴿a kingdom that shall not belong to anyone after me﴾, that is, a kingdom that cannot pass from me to another.

The third answer: restraint from the good things of this world while having the power over them is harder than restraint from them when one lacks the power over them. So it is as if he said: "O my God, give me a kingdom surpassing all the kingdoms of mankind entirely, so that I may refrain from them while having power over them, so that my reward may be more perfect and more excellent."

The fourth: Some people say that restraint from the pleasures of this world is difficult and arduous, because these pleasures are present while the felicities of the Hereafter are deferred, and ready cash is hard to sell on credit. So Solomon said: "Give me, O Lord, a kingdom that is the greatest of the kingdoms possible for mankind, so that I may remain, with that complete power, in the utmost restraint from it, so that it may become manifest to creation that attaining the world does not prevent one from serving the Master."

The fifth: whoever has no power over the world remains with his heart inclined toward it, and thinks that it contains great felicities and beneficial goods. So Solomon said: "O Lord of might, give me the greatest of kingdoms, so that people may stand upon the full reality of its condition. Then it will become clear to the intellect that there is no benefit in it, and then the heart will turn away from it and not incline toward it, and I will occupy myself with worship, tranquil in soul, with my heart not preoccupied with the ties of this world." Then He said: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed﴾. *Rukhaan* means soft and gentle, and it derives from *rakhawa* (softness). When the wind is gentle, it does not shake violently and does not resist him; it is pleasant.

If it is said: Did not God say in another verse: ﴿And to Solomon the wind, violent, running by his command﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:81]? We say: the answer is in two ways:

The first: there is no contradiction between the two verses, for the intended meaning is that the wind had the strength of violent winds, but when it ran by his command it became delicious and pleasant, and so it was gentle.

The second answer: that the wind was gentle at one time and violent at another, and there is no contradiction between the two matters. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wherever he directed﴾ means "where he intended and aimed." Al-Asma'i related from the Arabs that they say: "He hit the correct thing but missed the answer" (*asaba al-sawab fa-akhta al-jawab*). It is related from Ru'ba that two men of the people of language intended him to ask him about this word, and he came out to them and said: "Where do you aim (*tusibaan*)?" They said: "This is what we are seeking." In sum, the point is that God made the wind subservient to him until it ran by his command in accordance with his will. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 38, verse 41:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called upon his Lord: "Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾ ﴿"Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink."﴾ ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder to those of understanding.﴾ ﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it and do not break your oath. Indeed, We found him patient; an excellent servant. Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah).﴾

Know that this is the third of the stories mentioned in this surah. Know also that Dawud and Sulayman were among those upon whom Allah bestowed all kinds of blessings and favours, while Ayyub was among those whom Allah the Exalted singled out with all kinds of trials. The purpose of all these stories is admonition. It is as if Allah the Exalted said: "O Muhammad, be patient with the folly of your people, for there was no one in this world with more blessing, wealth and status than Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, and no one with more affliction and tribulation than Ayyub. So reflect upon the conditions of these men, so that you may know that the conditions of this world are not constant for anyone, and that the wise person must be patient in the face of hardships." There are several issues here:

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "*Ayyub* is an *ʿatf bayān* (an explanatory apposition) and *idh* is a *badal ishtimal* (a substitution of inclusion) from it. ﴿*Annī massanī*﴾ means "that he had touched me," as a quotation of his words with which he called upon (his Lord). Had it not been a quotation, it would have said "that he had touched him," because he is in the third person." The word ﴿*bi-nuṣbin*﴾ has been read with a *ḍamma* or *fatḥa* on the *nūn*, together with a sukūn, *fatḥa* or *ḍamma* on the *ṣād*, so the readings are *nuṣb* and *naṣab*, like *rushd* and *rashad*, *ʿudm* and *ʿadam*, and *suqm* and *saqam*. *Nuṣb* is on the pattern of the original verbal noun, and *naṣab* is a heavier form of *nuṣb*. The meaning is one: weariness, hardship, torment and pain.

Know that he had two kinds of hardship: intense grief caused by the loss of blessings and the occurrence of hateful things, and intense physical pain. When both of these occurred, Allah the Exalted mentioned two words, namely *nuṣb* and *ʿadhāb* (torment).

**The second issue:** Scholars have two opinions on this point:

The first: the pains and illnesses that afflicted his body were caused by the action of Satan.

The second: they were caused by the action of Allah, and the "torment" attributed to Satan in this verse is the torment of whispering and the casting of corrupt thoughts.

As for the first opinion, its argument is what has been related: that Iblis asked his Lord, saying, "Is there among Your servants anyone who, if You gave me power over him, would resist me?" Allah said, "Yes, My servant Ayyub." So Iblis began to bring him his whisperings, while he saw Iblis plainly and paid no attention to him. Iblis said, "O Lord, he has resisted me, so give me power over his wealth." Iblis would come to him and say, "So-and-so of your wealth has perished," and he would say, "Allah gave and Allah took," and then praise Allah. Iblis said, "O Lord, Ayyub does not care about his wealth, so give me power over his children." So he came and shook the house, and all his children perished entirely. He came to him and informed him of this, but he paid no attention to him. He said, "O Lord, he does not care about his wealth and his children, so give me power over his body." So He permitted him, and he blew upon the skin of Ayyub, and great illnesses and severe pains arose in him. He remained in that affliction for years, until he became such that the people of his town found him repulsive. He went out into the desert, and no one came near him. Then Satan came to his wife and said, "If your husband had sought my help, I would have freed him from this affliction." The woman mentioned that to her husband, and he swore by Allah that if Allah restored his health, he would flog her one hundred lashes. At this event he said: ﴿"Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾ So Allah answered his supplication and revealed to him that ﴿"Strike with your foot"﴾. Allah then caused a cool, pure spring to gush forth from beneath his foot, and he bathed in it. Allah removed from him every ailment, outwardly and inwardly, and returned to him his family and his wealth.

The second opinion: Satan has absolutely no power to cause people to fall into illnesses and pains. The proofs for this are several:

**First:** If we allowed that death, life, health and sickness could come from Satan, then perhaps each of us finds life through the action of Satan, and perhaps all the good things and happiness we have are by the action of Satan. In that case we would have no way of knowing that the Giver of life and death, health and sickness, is Allah the Exalted.

**Second:** If Satan were able to do that, why does he not strive to kill the prophets and the saints, why does he not ruin their homes, and why does he not kill their children?

**Third:** Allah the Exalted related of Satan that he said: ﴿"I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me."﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. Thus he declared that he has no power over human beings except to cast whisperings and corrupt thoughts. This indicates the view of those who say that Satan is the one who inflicted those illnesses and afflictions. If someone says: "Why is it not permissible to say that the agent of these conditions is Allah the Exalted, but in accordance with Satan's request?" We reply: If it is necessary to acknowledge that the creator of those pains and illnesses is Allah the Exalted, then what is the benefit of making Satan an intermediary in that? Rather, the truth is that what is meant by His saying ﴿"Satan has touched me with hardship and torment"﴾ is that, through the casting of corrupt whisperings and inner thoughts, he would cast him into various kinds of torment and weariness. Then, those who hold this view differ over how those whisperings were, and they have mentioned several aspects:

The first: his illness was very painful, and its duration was long; people found him repulsive and recoiled from being near him, and he no longer had any wealth at all. His wife used to serve people and obtain for him just enough food, but then the people's aversion to him grew until they prevented his wife from entering among them and from working for them. Satan kept reminding him of the blessings he had once enjoyed and the calamities that had befallen him, and he would scheme to drive away those whisperings. When those whisperings grew strong in his heart, he feared and humbled himself before Allah, saying: ﴿"Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾ Because the more those thoughts increased, the greater the pain in his heart became.

The second: when the duration of the illness was prolonged, Satan came to him and would make him despair of his Lord and make him think it proper to despair. He feared that the thought of despair would take firm root in his heart, so he humbled himself before Allah the Exalted and said: ﴿"Satan has touched me"﴾.

The third: It was said that when Satan said to his wife, "If your husband obeyed me, I would remove these afflictions from him," the woman mentioned that to him. He then became convinced that Satan had desired his religion, and this grieved him, so he humbled himself before Allah the Exalted and said: ﴿"Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾

The fourth: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Ayyub remained in affliction for eighteen years, until both the near and the far abandoned him, except for two men. Then one of them said to his companion: 'Ayyub has committed a sin that no one in all the worlds has committed, and had it not been for that, he would not have fallen into such an affliction.' They mentioned that to Ayyub, peace be upon him, and he said: 'I do not know what you are saying, except that Allah knows that I used to pass by the two men when they were quarrelling and mentioning Allah the Exalted, and I would return to my house and withdraw from them, disliking that Allah the Exalted be mentioned except in truth.'"

The fifth: It was said that his wife used to serve people and take from them just enough food and bring it to Ayyub. It happened that they no longer employed her at all. Some women asked her to cut off one of her two locks of hair in exchange for enough food, and she did so. Then on the second day she did the same, until she no longer had any lock of hair. Whenever Ayyub, peace be upon him, wanted to move on his bed, he would hold on to that lock, but when he could not find the lock, harmful thoughts entered his heart and his grief intensified. At that point he said: ﴿"Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾

The sixth: He said on one of the days: "O Lord, You know that two matters never came together upon me without my preferring Your obedience. When You gave me wealth, I was a guardian to the widows, a helper to the wayfarer, and a father to the orphans!" Then he was called from a cloud: "O Ayyub, from whom was that success?" Ayyub took dust and placed it upon his head and said: "From You, O Lord." Then he feared the first thought, and so he said: ﴿"Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾ They have related other opinions as well, and Allah knows best the reality of the matter.

I heard some of the Jews say that Musa ibn Imran, peace be upon him, had a separate book concerning the event of Ayyub. The essence of that book is that Ayyub was a man of great obedience to Allah the Exalted, constant in worship, exceedingly reverent of the command of Allah the Exalted, and compassionate toward the creatures of Allah. Then he fell into severe affliction and great hardship. Was that for a wisdom or not? If it was for a wisdom, then it is known that he had committed no sin in the past for which that torment would be a recompense. And if it was for the abundance of reward, then the Wise and Merciful God is capable of delivering every good and benefit to him without the intermediary of those long pains and hateful diseases. In that case, there would be no benefit in those illnesses and afflictions. These are clear and manifest words, and they indicate that the acts of the Majestic are exalted above being explained by interests and harms. The clear truth is that ﴿"He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23].

**Third issue:** The wording of the verse indicates that this hardship and suffering came from Satan. On the first view, this suffering refers to the illnesses that afflicted his body. On the second view, it refers to the griefs that arose in his heart because of the insinuations (*wasawis*) that Satan cast. On either view, the act is attributed to Satan. Our companions (the Ash'arite scholars), may God have mercy on them, replied: We do not deny that the act is attributed to Satan, but we say that the act of the servant is created by God, Exalted is He, in the detailed manner that is well known.

As for God's words, ﴿Strike with your foot﴾, the meaning is that when he complained about Satan, it was as if he asked his Lord to remove that affliction from him, and God answered him by saying to him, ﴿Strike with your foot﴾. *Rakd* (striking) is a forceful thrust with the foot, as in "his striking the horse" (*rakdukum al-faras*). The implied meaning is: We said to him, "Strike with your foot." It was said that he struck the earth with his foot, and a spring gushed forth, and it was said to him, ﴿This is a cool bath and drink﴾, that is, this is water in which you may bathe, so that your inward part is healed. The apparent wording indicates that a single spring of water gushed forth for him, in which he bathed and from which he drank.

The exegetes said that two springs gushed forth for him: he bathed in one and drank from the other, and the illness left him both outwardly and inwardly by God's permission. It was also said that he struck with his right foot and a hot spring gushed forth, in which he bathed, and then he struck with his left foot and a cold spring gushed forth, from which he drank.

* * *

Then God said, ﴿And We gave him his family﴾. It has been said that they were his own family and an equal number besides them; and it has been said that they were others like them. The first is preferable, because it is the apparent meaning, and it is not permissible to depart from it without necessity. Then they differed. Some said: the meaning is that We removed the sickness from them, and they returned to health. Others said: rather, they came to him after they had been absent from him, and they were reunited after they had been scattered. Others said: rather, he was given authority over them and they over him in matters related to companionship and service.

As for His words, ﴿and the like of them with them﴾, the closest view is that God granted him enjoyment of his health, his wealth, and strength, until his offspring multiplied and his family became double what they had been, and many times that. Al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, said: the meaning of the granting of the family is that God brought them back to life after they had died.

Then He said, ﴿as a mercy from Us﴾, meaning: We did all these acts by way of grace and mercy, not by way of obligation.

Then He said, ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾, meaning: We first made the affliction fall upon him, and he was patient; then We removed the affliction from him and brought him to blessings and favors, as an admonition to those of understanding that whoever is patient succeeds. The purpose of this is to draw attention to what the discourse began with, which is His saying to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud﴾.

The Mu'tazilites (a theological school holding that God's acts are subject to rational good and purposes) said: God's words, ﴿as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding﴾, mean that We did these things for these purposes and aims, and this indicates that God's acts and rulings are grounded in purposes and benefits. The discussion of this matter has already occurred more than once.

As for His words, ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (*ḍighth*)﴾, it is connected to "strike." A *ḍighth* is a small bundle of grass, or sweet herbs, or something similar. Know that this statement indicates that he had previously taken an oath. According to the report, he swore to strike his wife. The exegetes differed about the reason for which he swore against her, and it is unlikely that what is said is true, that she encouraged him to obey Satan; and it is also unlikely what is related, that she cut off her locks of hair from her head, because one who is compelled by need for food is permitted to do that. Rather, the most likely explanation is that she opposed him in some important matters: she went off on some important errand and was late, so he swore during his illness that he would strike her one hundred times once he was healed. Since she was excellent in serving him, God, by the most lenient means for him and for her, dissolved his oath. This concession remains in effect. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a leper who had committed adultery with a female slave was brought to him, and he said: "Take a palm-stalk bearing one hundred shoots and strike him once with it."

Then God said, ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾. If it is asked: how did He find him patient when he complained to Him? The answer has several aspects:

First: he complained to Him about Satan, and he did not complain about it to anyone else.

Second: while the pain was on the body, he did not mention anything; when the insinuations became severe, he feared for the heart and the religion, so he humbly implored.

Third: Satan is an enemy, and complaining about the enemy to the Beloved does not detract from patience. Then He said, ﴿What an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to God)﴾. This indicates that the honor of "what an excellent servant" was earned only because he was ever turning back. I heard some of them say: When God's words, ﴿What an excellent servant﴾, were revealed concerning Sulayman, peace be upon him, at one time, and concerning Ayyub, peace be upon him, at another time, great grief settled into the hearts of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). They said: God's words, ﴿What an excellent servant﴾, concerning Sulayman are a great honor; if we need to attain a kingdom like Sulayman's to attain this honor, we cannot do it; and if we need to bear a trial like Ayyub's, we cannot do it either. So how is the way to attain it? Then God revealed His words, ﴿What an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper﴾ (Al-Anfal: 40). The meaning is: if you are not ﴿an excellent servant﴾, then I am ﴿an excellent Protector﴾ (Al-Anfal: 40). If there is excess from you, there is bounty from Me; if there is shortcoming from you, there is mercy and facilitation from Me.

Then God said, ﴿And We gave him his family﴾. It has been said that they were his own family and an equal number besides them; and it has been said that they were others like them. The first is preferable, because it is the apparent meaning, and it is not permissible to depart from it without necessity. Then they differed. Some said: the meaning is that We removed the sickness from them, and they returned to health. Others said: rather, they came to him after they had been absent from him, and they were reunited after they had been scattered. Others said: rather, he was given authority over them and they over him in matters related to companionship and service.

As for His words, ﴿and the like of them with them﴾, the closest view is that God granted him enjoyment of his health, his wealth, and strength, until his offspring multiplied and his family became double what they had been, and many times that. Al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, said: the meaning of the granting of the family is that God brought them back to life after they had died.

* * *

Then He said, ﴿as a mercy from Us﴾, meaning: We did all these acts by way of grace and mercy, not by way of obligation.

* * *

Then He said, ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾, meaning: We first made the affliction fall upon him, and he was patient; then We removed the affliction from him and brought him to blessings and favors, as an admonition to those of understanding that whoever is patient succeeds. The purpose of this is to draw attention to what the discourse began with, which is His saying to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud﴾.

The Mu'tazilites (a theological school holding that God's acts are subject to rational good and purposes) said: God's words, ﴿as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding﴾, mean that We did these things for these purposes and aims, and this indicates that God's acts and rulings are grounded in purposes and benefits. The discussion of this matter has already occurred more than once.

As for His words, ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (*ḍighth*)﴾, it is connected to "strike." A *ḍighth* is a small bundle of grass, or sweet herbs, or something similar. Know that this statement indicates that he had previously taken an oath. According to the report, he swore to strike his wife. The exegetes differed about the reason for which he swore against her, and it is unlikely that what is said is true, that she encouraged him to obey Satan; and it is also unlikely what is related, that she cut off her locks of hair from her head, because one who is compelled by need for food is permitted to do that. Rather, the most likely explanation is that she opposed him in some important matters: she went off on some important errand and was late, so he swore during his illness that he would strike her one hundred times once he was healed. Since she was excellent in serving him, God, by the most lenient means for him and for her, dissolved his oath. This concession remains in effect. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a leper who had committed adultery with a female slave was brought to him, and he said: "Take a palm-stalk bearing one hundred shoots and strike him once with it."

Then God said, ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾. If it is asked: how did He find him patient when he complained to Him? The answer has several aspects:

First: he complained to Him about Satan, and he did not complain about it to anyone else.

Second: while the pain was on the body, he did not mention anything; when the insinuations became severe, he feared for the heart and the religion, so he humbly implored.

Third: Satan is an enemy, and complaining about the enemy to the Beloved does not detract from patience. Then He said, ﴿What an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to God)﴾. This indicates that the honor of "what an excellent servant" was earned only because he was ever turning back. I heard some of them say: When God's words, ﴿What an excellent servant﴾, were revealed concerning Sulayman, peace be upon him, at one time, and concerning Ayyub, peace be upon him, at another time, great grief settled into the hearts of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). They said: God's words, ﴿What an excellent servant﴾, concerning Sulayman are a great honor; if we need to attain a kingdom like Sulayman's to attain this honor, we cannot do it; and if we need to bear a trial like Ayyub's, we cannot do it either. So how is the way to attain it? Then God revealed His words, ﴿What an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper﴾ (Al-Anfal: 40). The meaning is: if you are not ﴿an excellent servant﴾, then I am ﴿an excellent Protector﴾ (Al-Anfal: 40). If there is excess from you, there is bounty from Me; if there is shortcoming from you, there is mercy and facilitation from Me.

**Third issue:** The wording of the verse indicates that this hardship and suffering came from Satan. On the first view, this suffering refers to the illnesses that afflicted his body. On the second view, it refers to the griefs that arose in his heart because of the insinuations (*wasawis*) that Satan cast. On either view, the act is attributed to Satan. Our companions (the Ash'arite scholars), may God have mercy on them, replied: We do not deny that the act is attributed to Satan, but we say that the act of the servant is created by God, Exalted is He, in the detailed manner that is well known.

As for God's words, ﴿Strike with your foot﴾, the meaning is that when he complained about Satan, it was as if he asked his Lord to remove that affliction from him, and God answered him by saying to him, ﴿Strike with your foot﴾. *Rakd* (striking) is a forceful thrust with the foot, as in "his striking the horse" (*rakdukum al-faras*). The implied meaning is: We said to him, "Strike with your foot." It was said that he struck the earth with his foot, and a spring gushed forth, and it was said to him, ﴿This is a cool bath and drink﴾, that is, this is water in which you may bathe, so that your inward part is healed. The apparent wording indicates that a single spring of water gushed forth for him, in which he bathed and from which he drank.

The exegetes said that two springs gushed forth for him: he bathed in one and drank from the other, and the illness left him both outwardly and inwardly by God's permission. It was also said that he struck with his right foot and a hot spring gushed forth, in which he bathed, and then he struck with his left foot and a cold spring gushed forth, from which he drank.

[Page 189]

The words of the Most High: ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, men of strength and vision.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: the remembrance of the Abode.﴾ ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent.﴾ ﴿And remember Ishmael, Elisha and Dhul-Kifl, each of them among the excellent.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir read ﴿ʿabdanā﴾ (His servant, in the singular), which is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas. He said: the phrase ﴿ʿabdanā﴾ is a great honour, so this honour must be specific to the greatest of the people mentioned in this verse, who is Abraham. The rest read ﴿ʿibādanā﴾ (His servants, in the plural). They said: other prophets too have been described by this attribute. About Jesus it came: ﴿He was only a servant upon whom We bestowed favour﴾ (al-Zukhruf 59). About Job: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. About Noah: ﴿Indeed he was a grateful servant﴾ (al-Isra 3). Whoever reads ﴿ʿabdanā﴾ makes Abraham alone the explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) for it, and then links his offspring to ﴿ʿabdanā﴾, namely Isaac and Jacob. Whoever reads ﴿ʿibādanā﴾ makes Abraham, Isaac and Jacob an explanatory apposition for ﴿ʿibādanā﴾.

The second issue: The sense of the verse is as if He, the Most High, said: "So be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud," until He said: ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham﴾. That is, O Muhammad, remember the patience of Abraham when he was thrown into the fire, the patience of Isaac for the sacrifice, and the patience of Jacob when he lost his son and his sight was lost. Then He said: ﴿men of strength and vision﴾. Know that the hand is the instrument for most actions, and the eye is the instrument for the strongest kinds of perception. So it is fitting to express action by the hand and perception by the eye. Having understood this, we say: the rational human soul has two powers, the active and the cognitive. The noblest thing that issues from the active power is obedience to God, and the noblest thing that issues from the cognitive power is knowledge of God. Whatever actions and knowledge lie outside these two categories are like frivolity and falsehood. Thus His words ﴿men of strength and vision﴾ point to these two states.

* * *

Then the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: the remembrance of the Abode.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: His words ﴿bi-khāliṣah﴾ have been read both with tanwin and with the construct (iḍāfah). Whoever reads it with tanwin, the implied meaning is "We purified them", that is, "We made them sincere to Us by means of a pure quality without any admixture, namely the remembrance of the Abode." Whoever reads it with the construct, the meaning is "by means of what was purified of the remembrance of the Abode", meaning that the remembrance of the Abode may be for God and may be for other than God, so the sense is: "We purified them by means of what was purified of this remembrance."

The second issue: There are several opinions about ﴿the remembrance of the Abode﴾:

The first: The meaning is that they were absorbed in the remembrance of the Hereafter and went so far in this remembrance that they forgot the world.

The second: The meaning is that they attained a great and exalted remembrance in the Hereafter.

The third: The meaning is that God preserved for them a good remembrance in this world, and accepted their supplication in His words: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ (al-Shuʿara 84).

* * *

Then the Most High said: ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent.﴾ That is, the chosen ones from among their kind. The word ﴿al-akhyār﴾ is the plural of ﴿akhyar﴾ or ﴿khayr﴾ (lightened), like ﴿amwāt﴾ as the plural of ﴿mayyit﴾ or ﴿mayt﴾. The scholars have used this verse to establish the infallibility (ʿiṣmah, the doctrine that prophets are preserved from sin) of the prophets. They said: since He, the Most High, judged them to be excellent in an absolute sense, this encompasses excellence in all actions and attributes, as evidenced by the validity of the exception (istithnāʾ) and by the removal of ambiguity.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And remember Ishmael, Elisha and Dhul-Kifl, each of them among the excellent.﴾ They are other prophets who bore hardships in the religion of God. We have already discussed the explanation of these names, and the attributes of these prophets, in Surat al-Anbiya and Surat al-Anʿam, so there is no benefit in repeating it. Here ends the discussion of the stories of the prophets in this surah.

Know that in His saying ﴿Dhikr [a reminder]﴾ there are two interpretations.

The first: Exalted is He only mentioned the circumstances of these prophets, peace be upon them, so that Muhammad, peace be upon him, would endure the folly of his people with patience. When He had completed the explanation of this path and wished to mention, after it, another path that requires patience in the face of the folly of the ignorant, and wished to distinguish one of the two sections from the other, He said, without doubt, ﴿This is a reminder﴾. Then He began to establish the second section, saying ﴿And indeed, for the God-fearing [muttaqin]﴾. This is like an author who, having completed a passage, says "This is a section," then begins another section. And when a writer finishes a chapter of his book and wishes to begin another, he says: "This is what was, and such-and-such." The proof of this is that when He completed the mention of the people of Paradise and wished to follow it with the mention of the people of Hell, He said: ﴿This, and indeed for the rebellious there is an evil return﴾ [Sad: 55].

The second interpretation: what is meant is that this is an honour and a good remembrance for these prophets, peace be upon them, by which they will be mentioned forever. The first is the correct one.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, for the God-fearing is a good return﴾.

Know that when Exalted is He related about the disbelievers of Quraysh their folly toward the Prophet ﷺ, in that they described him as a sorcerer and a liar, and said to him in mockery, ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our portion [of punishment]﴾, at this point He commanded Muhammad to be patient with that folly, and He made clear that this patience is obligatory for two reasons:

The first: Exalted is He, having shown that the earlier prophets endured hardships and afflictions with patience, it is obligatory for you to follow them in this matter.

The second: Exalted is He, in this verse, made clear that whoever obeys God will have such-and-such reward, and whoever disobeys Him will have such-and-such punishment, and all of this requires patience in observing the obligations of God, Exalted is He. This is a fine arrangement and a subtle sequence.

As for the saying of Exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, for the God-fearing is a good return﴾: al-ma'ab means the place of return. Those who hold the view of the eternity of souls [qidam al-arwah] have used this verse as evidence, and every verse that contains the word "return" (rujū'). The basis of their argument is that the word "return" applies only if these souls existed before the bodies and were in the presence of God's majesty, and then became attached to the bodies; so when they are separated from the bodies, that is called a return. The answer to this is: if it indicates anything, it indicates only that souls existed before bodies, and it does not indicate the eternity of souls.

* * *

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾, which is a substitution [badal] for His saying ﴿a good return﴾. Then He said: ﴿with gates opened for them﴾. In this there are several issues:

Issue one: They have mentioned several interpretations of this expression:

The first: al-Farra' said: its meaning is "with its gates opened for them." The Arabs use the definite article (al-alif wa-l-lam) as a replacement for the possessive construction (idafa). The Arabs say: "I passed by a man whose face is good [hasan al-wajh]," so the al- in al-wajh is a substitute for the possessive.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "with its gates opened for them" from it.

The third: the author of al-Kashshaf [al-Zamakhshari] said: ﴿al-abwab [the gates]﴾ is a substitution [badal] for the pronoun, and its implied sense is: "opened, they, the gates," like your saying "Zayd struck the hand and the foot," and this is badal al-ishtimal [substitution of inclusion/comprehension].

Issue two: It was read: "Gardens of Eden, opened" in the nominative, on the basis that the phrase ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is the subject [mubtada'] and "opened" is its predicate [khabar], and both are the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "it is ﴿Gardens of Eden, opened for them﴾."

Issue three: Know that Exalted is He described, in this verse, several aspects of the state of the people of Paradise:

The first: the state of their dwellings. His saying ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ indicates two matters:

One of them: that they are gardens and orchards.

The second: that they are lasting, safe from coming to an end.

As for His saying ﴿with gates opened for them﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: that the meaning is that the angels assigned to the gardens, when they see the owner of the garden, open its gates for him and greet him with peace. Thus he enters, surrounded by the angels, in the most honoured state and most beautiful form. Exalted is He said: ﴿Until, when they come to it and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it to abide therein"﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

The second: that whenever they wish those gates to open, they open for them, and whenever they wish them to close, they close for them.

The third: the purpose of this opening is to describe those dwellings as spacious, with the eyes wandering freely through them, and the witnessing of pleasant and delightful states.

* * *

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿Reclining therein, calling therein for [various] fruit and drink﴾. In this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: In this verse He mentioned their reclining in Paradise, and in other verses He mentioned the manner of that reclining. He said in one verse: ﴿reclining on couches﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56], and in another verse: ﴿reclining on green cushions [rafraf]﴾ [al-Rahman: 76].

The second discussion: His saying ﴿reclining therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) placed before its governing element, which is His saying ﴿calling therein﴾. The meaning is: they call in the Gardens, ﴿reclining therein﴾. Then He said: ﴿for abundant fruit and drink﴾, meaning: for varieties of fruit and varieties of drink; the implied sense is: for abundant fruit and abundant drink. The reason for mentioning this meaning is that the lands of the Arabs are hot and have few fruits and drinks, so God encouraged them toward it.

When Exalted is He had made clear the matter of the dwelling and the matter of food and drink, He mentioned after that the matter of marriage, saying: ﴿And with them are those who restrain their gaze [qasirat al-tarf]﴾. Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Saffat. In sum, the meaning of "restraining their gaze" is that they do not look at others, and their hearts are confined to love for them. His saying ﴿of equal age [atrab]﴾ means of one age. It is possible that the maidens are of equal age, and it is possible that they are of equal age to their husbands. Al-Qaffal said: the reason for considering this attribute is that when they resemble one another in attribute, age, and adornment, inclination toward them is equal, and that requires the absence of jealousy.

* * *

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾. He means that God, Exalted is He, promised the God-fearing a reward described with this attribute. Then Exalted is He informed about the permanence of the reward, saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾.

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾. He means that God, Exalted is He, promised the God-fearing a reward described with this attribute. Then Exalted is He informed about the permanence of the reward, saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾.
